Name: belief_source_tags
Title: Where Did You Hear That? Probing and Steering the Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally track not only whether they hold a belief about an item's state, but also the epistemic *source* of that belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. tool/retrieval evidence), and this provenance signal is linearly decodable and causally steerable — separately from the truth-value direction. This distinguishes belief-provenance from belief-truth, which prior work conflates.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent belief/truth directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024), agents' beliefs in ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and world states (Propositional Probes 2024). Critically, the paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows models conflate epistemic categories in their *outputs*. Existing probing work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'why/from where does it believe X?'. We introduce the orthogonal axis of belief PROVENANCE (prior vs. in-context vs. external evidence) as an internal, decodable, steerable variable. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes the belief-knowledge-fact confusion as a possibly-recoverable internal signal, and offers a mechanistic handle on sycophancy, context-vs-prior conflicts, and RAG faithfulness.
Abstract: Large language models represent beliefs about the states of items, and prior interpretability work has isolated linear 'truth-value' directions. But a belief has not only a truth-value, it also has a provenance: the model may hold it because of its pretraining prior, because it was asserted in context, or because it came from retrieved/tool evidence. We hypothesize that LLMs internally tag beliefs with their epistemic source, and that this provenance signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally steerable. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state claims where we independently vary claim truth and claim source (prior-consistent, prior-contradicting-in-context, and retrieval-attributed), including matched cases where the same proposition arrives from different sources. We train linear probes to decode source and truth on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia), measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, joint vs. separate decodability), and localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching. We then test causal control: does steering along the provenance direction change downstream behavior such as sycophancy (adopting user-asserted false claims), citation of sources, and answers under prior-vs-context conflict? We evaluate with probe accuracy, subspace overlap, patching effect sizes, and behavioral metrics (sycophancy rate, context-adherence, source-attribution accuracy). If confirmed, provenance-aware probing offers a practical monitor and controller for RAG faithfulness and sycophancy, and shows that the belief/knowledge/fact confusion in outputs may coexist with a recoverable internal provenance signal.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — belief provenance is linearly decodable): Tests whether the epistemic source of a belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. retrieval-attributed) is recoverable from activations, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 5,000 item-state propositions (2,500 real subject-relation-object facts subsampled from a ~50k-triple Wikidata export; 2,500 novel synthetic entity-attribute facts to neutralize pretraining priors), each rendered in three matched provenance frames (prior-only bare question; a sentence asserting it; the same claim inside a quoted 'document/tool output'), = 15,000 stimuli, split 70/15/15 by proposition so no proposition crosses splits. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, all frozen; only trainable component is an L2 logistic-regression probe on the residual stream at the state token, fit per layer, regularization C chosen on val over {0.01,0.1,1,10}; 5 resampling seeds. Systems compared: 3-way source probe vs. shuffled-label control probe vs. bag-of-words-on-prompt baseline. Decisive metric first: test macro-AUROC of the source probe at its best layer. Convincing: mean AUROC >= 0.80 with shuffled-label control at 0.50 +/- 0.05 on >=3 of 4 models, and >= 0.05 above the bag-of-words baseline. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.60,0.70) is inconclusive (weak, possibly surface-driven structure) and we do not assert H1. Negative: AUROC < 0.60, or not above bag-of-words by 0.05, means provenance is not linearly encoded at the state token.

Experiment 2 (H2 — provenance is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction): Tests that source is not a re-description of truth. Using the same stimuli crossed with true/false polarity, fit a difference-of-means truth direction and the source probe direction(s) on train. Decisive metric first: source-probe test AUROC after projecting the truth direction out of activations (and, symmetrically, truth AUROC after projecting source out); secondary: principal subspace angle between the truth direction and the source subspace. Convincing: projected-out source AUROC retains >= 90% of its un-projected value and the subspace angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: retention 70-90% or angle 40-60 degrees means partial entanglement — reported as such, H2 only partially supported. Negative: retention < 70% or angle < 40 degrees means provenance largely coincides with truth and H2 fails; the entanglement geometry is still reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the provenance signal is causally steerable and gates behavior): Tests that moving activations along the source direction changes downstream behavior. Build a steering vector by contrastive activation addition (mean in-context-assertion minus mean prior-only activations) at the best layer from Experiment 1. Data: a held-out 1,000-item prior-vs-context conflict subset where context contradicts the pretraining prior, plus 500 user-asserted-false-claim prompts. Systems compared: source-direction steering vs. random-direction steering vs. truth-direction steering, at matched norms (alpha swept so added-vector norm is 2/4/8% of mean residual norm). Decisive metric first: change in sycophancy rate (fraction adopting the user-asserted false claim) between +context and +prior steering; secondary: context-adherence rate under conflict and 'where did you learn this?' attribution accuracy. Convincing: source steering shifts sycophancy by >= 15 absolute points with random-direction steering shifting < 5 points and perplexity on held-out text rising < 10%. Indecision band: a 5-15 point shift is weak causal evidence, reported as suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random, or the effect equals truth-direction steering, means the signal is not a distinct causal provenance handle.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization of the provenance signal): Identifies the heads/layers carrying source. Using activation patching / causal mediation between matched prior-only and in-context runs of the same proposition, patch per-head outputs and measure the restored source-probe logit. Decisive metric first: number of heads whose individual patch recovers >= 50% of the source distinction, and their layer distribution vs. heads known to carry truth/belief. Convincing: a small (<= 20) reproducible head set across seeds mediates source, only partially overlapping truth heads. Indecision band: a diffuse >50-head set is reported as distributed rather than localized. Negative: no head patch exceeds 20% recovery means the signal is not head-localizable.

Experiment 5 (H1,H3 — generalization): Tests transfer beyond the training distribution. Refit nothing; apply the Experiment-1 probe and Experiment-3 steering vector to (a) held-out item domains and (b) naturalistic RAG-style prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC of the frozen probe on the new domain. Convincing: >= 0.70 transfer AUROC and steering retains >= half its in-domain sycophancy effect. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 transfer is limited generality. Negative: <= 0.60 means the signal is distribution-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Provenance may be entangled with surface cues (e.g., quotation marks) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched-proposition controls and paraphrase/format perturbations. The three-way source distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable, or may be layer/model-specific. Steering could induce off-manifold degradation of fluency (as noted in belief-manifold work); we monitor perplexity and use small steering magnitudes. Truth and source directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Synthetic facts may not fully reflect real pretraining priors; we complement with well-known real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_entrenchment_probing
Title: Frozen Minds: Probing and Unfreezing Internal Belief Entrenchment During LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM generates a multi-step reasoning trace, its internal belief about the answer to an item becomes progressively 'entrenched': the linearly-decodable belief representation stops updating in response to new evidence introduced later in the trace, even when that evidence should rationally shift it. This internal entrenchment is measurable per-step, precedes and predicts behavioral confirmation bias, and can be causally reduced by steering the residual stream to restore belief plasticity, improving truth-seeking on evidence-integration tasks.
Related Work: Prior work establishes that transformers linearly represent belief states (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry, 2024; Constrained Belief Updates, 2025) and that a 'solvability belief' axis is decodable but causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025). Behaviorally, the Martingale Score (2025) shows LLM reasoning violates Bayesian martingale updating (belief entrenchment) at the output level, and Confirmation Bias in CoT (2025) shows prior beliefs skew reasoning. The Hypocrisy Gap (2026) contrasts a static internal belief with the CoT text. NONE of these track the trajectory of the internal belief representation itself across reasoning steps, characterize *when/where* it freezes relative to evidence arrival, or test a causal intervention to restore plasticity. We reframe entrenchment as an internal, per-step representational dynamics phenomenon and ask whether it is a causally editable failure mode, distinguishing our proposal from behavioral (Martingale) and static-belief (Hypocrisy Gap) approaches.
Abstract: When a language model reasons step-by-step, its final answer often confirms a hypothesis formed early, even when later steps surface contradicting evidence, a behavior known as confirmation bias or belief entrenchment. Prior studies measure this behaviorally or contrast a single static internal belief against the reasoning text. We instead track the internal belief representation itself as it evolves across reasoning steps. We hypothesize that entrenchment is a representational dynamics phenomenon: an LLM's linearly-decodable belief about an item's answer initially updates with incoming evidence but then 'freezes,' becoming insensitive to later, decision-relevant evidence. We construct controlled evidence-integration tasks in which pieces of evidence pointing toward different answers are revealed in a specified order within the prompt or generated trace, so that the rationally-updated belief has a known ground-truth trajectory. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and a reasoning-tuned R1-distilled model) and measure, at each step, (i) the probe belief, (ii) its agreement with the rational Bayesian trajectory, and (iii) a per-step plasticity score (belief change per unit of new evidence). We test whether plasticity decays over the trace, whether an early-freezing signature predicts final-answer errors, and whether it correlates with behavioral entrenchment metrics like the Martingale Score. Finally, we identify the layers/heads mediating freezing via activation patching and test a causal 'unfreezing' intervention: injecting a plasticity direction (contrastive activation addition derived from high- vs. low-plasticity steps) to restore late-evidence sensitivity. We evaluate with probe/rational-agreement curves, plasticity decay slopes, entrenchment-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, and post-intervention accuracy and fluency.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an internal belief representation is linearly decodable and updates step-by-step): Tests that a per-step belief about the answer exists. Data: built from scratch, 4,000 ordered-evidence items (multi-clue deduction puzzles, sequential-evidence forecasting, updating-diagnosis vignettes, and synthetic entity-attribute clue tasks) each with a synthetic-set oracle Bayesian belief trajectory; split 70/15/15 by item. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, all frozen; trainable component only a logistic-regression belief probe P(answer=A) on residual activations at each reasoning-step boundary, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: belief probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: probe test AUROC for the current-favored answer at each step. Convincing: mean AUROC >= 0.80 with control at 0.50 +/- 0.05 on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 means the belief is only weakly decodable and per-step trajectories are unreliable. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable step-wise belief and the remaining experiments are not interpretable.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the belief freezes: plasticity decays across the trace): Tests that late, decision-relevant evidence stops moving the belief. Use the 'late-reversal' condition (early evidence favors A, decisive later evidence favors B) vs. a matched 'consistent' condition. Define per-step plasticity = |delta probe-belief| per unit of oracle-expected belief change. Decisive metric first: slope of plasticity vs. step position (reversal condition), and post-reversal rational-agreement = correlation between probe and oracle trajectory. Convincing: significantly negative plasticity slope (bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0) and post-reversal agreement < 0.3 while consistent-condition agreement > 0.6. Indecision band: post-reversal agreement 0.3-0.5 is partial entrenchment. Negative: no slope difference and high post-reversal agreement means beliefs stay plastic (no entrenchment).

Experiment 3 (H3 — early freezing precedes and predicts behavioral confirmation bias): Tests that the internal signature forecasts final-answer errors. Decisive metric first: AUROC using late-step plasticity to predict final-answer error on reversal items, compared against a log-prob confidence baseline and the behavioral Martingale Score computed on the same runs. Convincing: plasticity AUROC >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of log-prob is weak added value. Negative: <= 0.60 or no gain over log-prob means the internal signature is not predictive.

Experiment 4 (H2 — localization of the freezing): Finds where stale belief is carried. Activation patching from post-reversal (updated) into pre-reversal (stale) runs; measure heads/layers whose patch restores late-evidence sensitivity in the probe. Decisive metric first: fraction of the entrenchment effect recovered by the top head set. Convincing: a reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse recovery reported as distributed. Negative: no head exceeds 20% recovery.

Experiment 5 (H3 — causal unfreezing restores plasticity): Tests that steering re-opens late-evidence sensitivity. Build a plasticity CAA vector (high- minus low-plasticity step activations) applied during late steps, alpha swept to 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: plasticity steering vs. random-direction steering. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy delta on reversal items; secondary: restored post-reversal probe-oracle agreement, and collateral GSM8K/MMLU-subset accuracy and perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point accuracy gain on reversal items with < 3-point drop on consistent items and < 10% perplexity rise; random steering < 3-point gain. Indecision band: 3-10 point gain is suggestive. Negative: < 3 points beyond random, or the model becomes indiscriminately swayed by any late text (consistent-item accuracy falls > 5 points), means no clean causal plasticity handle.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe and steering vector across task domains and to naturalistic RAG prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC of the probe. Convincing: >= 0.70 and steering retains half its accuracy effect. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 limited. Negative: <= 0.60 distribution-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief 'freezing' may reflect that the model simply cannot parse late evidence rather than an entrenchment failure; the matched consistent/reversal design and evidence-comprehension checks help disentangle these. The internal belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step, or may be distributed across layers, complicating per-step trajectories; we use multi-layer probes and report layerwise results. The plasticity steering direction could degrade fluency or overshoot (making the model unstable/gullible to any late text); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and evaluate on consistent-condition and general benchmarks. Oracle Bayesian trajectories are only exact on synthetic sets; naturalistic items rely on approximate rational baselines. Reasoning-tuned models may show qualitatively different dynamics than base models, which is itself an interesting comparison but limits universal claims. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Behavioral entrenchment/confirmation bias is established, so the problem is not new; the delta is the internal per-step trajectory view tied to oracle Bayesian trajectories plus a causal 'unfreezing' intervention. Meaningful and crisp, but linear probing and CAA are established tools, so novelty rests on the specific empirical freeze dynamics and successful targeted unfreezing rather than methodology.

Name: belief_binding_conflict
Title: One Fact, Many Faces: Do LLMs Bind Beliefs to Meaning or to Surface Form?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is told a fact and then queried about it, the internal belief it updates is bound to a surface-form-specific representation rather than a canonical meaning-level slot; consequently, two surface variants of the same proposition carve out *distinct* internal belief tokens that can be independently, and even contradictorily, updated. We hypothesize this 'belief binding' is localizable and that a single mechanism explains both cross-paraphrase inconsistency and the ability to hold contradictory beliefs about the same fact under different phrasings.
Related Work: Prior work shows truthfulness/belief directions are brittle to paraphrase and OOD surface form (Brittle Minds 2024; Representational Stability of Truth 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025), that factual knowledge is cross-lingually inconsistent with a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that PLMs lack factual coherency (Queen of England 2024). Belief directions are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value judgment 2024). All of these *characterize* brittleness as a defect. Our proposal is different: we treat surface-form dependence as evidence of a specific mechanism—that beliefs are *bound* to form-specific internal handles rather than a shared meaning slot—and we directly test this by injecting a fact in form A and reading/steering the belief in form B, measuring belief transfer as a function of representational binding. We introduce a controllable 'belief-binding' probe and a causal test of whether a single fact occupies one slot or many, which prior descriptive work does not do.
Abstract: Large language models can be told a fact and later answer questions about it, but they are notoriously inconsistent: rephrase the query and the answer, and the model's confidence, can flip. Prior work documents this brittleness as a failure of robust knowledge. We reframe it mechanistically: we hypothesize that when an LLM ingests a novel fact stated in a particular surface form, it updates an internal belief that is *bound to that form* rather than to a canonical meaning-level representation. Under this view, two paraphrases of the same proposition instantiate two distinct internal belief handles that can be updated—and even contradicted—independently. We test this with a controlled in-context belief-injection paradigm. We construct synthetic facts (novel entity-attribute pairs, unlikely to be in pretraining) rendered in matched surface variants (paraphrases, syntactic reorderings, and translations). We inject a fact in form A and then probe the internal belief when the model reads the same proposition in form B, quantifying cross-form belief transfer with linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2). We predict transfer is high within form and degrades systematically with surface distance, tracing a layerwise 'binding site' where form-specific and meaning-level representations converge. We then perform the critical causal test: inject *contradictory* facts under two forms and measure whether the model maintains two coexisting internal beliefs (form-bound) or resolves them (meaning-bound), and whether steering along a 'form-invariance' direction (derived contrastively from high- vs. low-transfer pairs) increases cross-form belief consistency without harming fluency. Metrics: cross-form transfer curves, layerwise binding-site localization via activation patching, contradiction-coexistence rate, post-steering consistency gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an in-context injected belief is decodable and bound to a surface handle): Tests that reading a fact updates a decodable belief. Data: built from scratch, 4,000 novel synthetic facts (invented entities/attributes to exclude pretraining), each in matched surface variants: near-paraphrase, syntactic reordering, lexical substitution, and translation into 2 languages, with true/false polarity; plus a 500-item real-fact control set. Split 70/15/15 by base fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; trainable component only a logistic-regression belief probe P(fact holds) at the attribute token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: belief probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: within-form probe test AUROC after in-context injection. Convincing: >= 0.85 with control 0.50 +/- 0.05. Indecision band: 0.65-0.75 weak. Negative: < 0.65 means injected belief is not decodable and the binding test is moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — belief is bound to form, not canonical meaning: cross-form transfer degrades with surface distance): Inject a fact in form A, read the belief probe when the same proposition is queried in form B. Decisive metric first: cross-form transfer = probe belief(A-injected) minus no-injection baseline, as a function of surface distance (edit distance, embedding cosine), summarized as a transfer matrix and a transfer-vs-distance slope. Convincing: within-form transfer >= 0.8 of the direct-injection effect while cross-form transfer falls to <= 0.4 for the most distant variants, with a monotone negative slope (bootstrap CI excludes 0). Indecision band: cross-form transfer 0.4-0.6 for distant variants is partial form-binding. Negative: transfer near-constant across forms (>= 0.7 even for distant variants) means beliefs are meaning-bound, refuting H1's binding claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 — the binding site is localizable): Activation patching of A-context activations into a B-only run; find the minimal layer set that restores the form-B belief. Decisive metric first: layer at which patched A-context first moves the B belief by >= 50% of full transfer. Convincing: a reproducible convergence layer band across seeds and models. Indecision band: a broad band is reported as gradual convergence. Negative: no patch location restores >= 20% means binding is not localizable.

Experiment 4 (H2 — contradictory facts under two forms coexist rather than resolve): The critical test of independent form-bound handles. Inject A asserting and B negating the same proposition; read both probes and query behaviorally. Decisive metric first: contradiction-coexistence rate = fraction of items where each form's probe reads its own injected value. Convincing: coexistence >= 0.6 (form-bound) vs. a meaning-bound null of near-0 (one value dominates). Indecision band: 0.3-0.6 partial. Negative: <= 0.3 means the model resolves contradictions to one belief (meaning-bound).

Experiment 5 (H1 — a single mechanism links paraphrase inconsistency and contradictory-belief holding): Derive a form-invariance CAA vector (high- minus low-transfer form pairs) and apply it during B-query, alpha at 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: form-invariance steering vs. random-direction steering. Decisive metric first: increase in cross-form belief consistency; secondary: reduction in contradiction-coexistence, unrelated-fact accuracy, MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point consistency gain and >= 10-point coexistence reduction, random steering < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%, and symmetric-relation items unharmed. Indecision band: 5-15 point gains suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random means no shared steerable mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H1 — generalization): Apply frozen probe and steering across fact domains, real-fact, and cross-lingual subsets. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC. Convincing: >= 0.70. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-form transfer failures could reflect comprehension failures rather than form-bound belief storage; we include comprehension checks and use matched real-fact controls. Synthetic entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; we complement with real-fact subsets. Linear belief probes may not cleanly capture the belief at every layer; we report layerwise results and use control tasks. The 'binding site' may be distributed rather than a discrete layer, weakening the clean localization story (still informative as a gradient). Form-invariance steering may degrade fluency or overwrite legitimate distinctions (e.g., subject/object asymmetric relations); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and separately analyze symmetric vs. asymmetric relations. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: The descriptive paraphrase-brittleness finding (including 'superficial resemblance' accounts) is already well covered, so the broad intuition is not new. The possible novelty is the stronger mechanistic/causal framing — beliefs stored in form-specific handles — with the contradiction-coexistence test as the sharpest differentiator (whether contradictory paraphrase-conditioned beliefs simultaneously persist vs merely accuracy dropping). Non-trivial combination of injection, cross-form transfer, patching, and steering. Risk: seen as a modest extension of the recent 'superficial resemblance' account unless it sharply specifies falsifying evidence.

Name: suppositional_belief_gating
Title: Suppose It Were True: Do LLMs Internally Flag Entertained Beliefs Apart from Endorsed Ones?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'endorsement' (factivity) flag that distinguishes belief content the model merely *entertains* under a supposition ('suppose X were true...') from content it *endorses* as actually true, and this flag is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether supposed-but-false content leaks into the model's factual assertions. This targets the actual-vs-hypothetical distinction that output-level studies show LLMs conflate.
Related Work: Prior work isolates linear truth-value/belief directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), ToM belief tracking of self/others via lookbacks and attention heads (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025; Brittle Minds 2024), and in-context counterfactual reasoning where a latent concept is linearly encoded with 'noise-abduction' heads (Counterfactual reasoning: in-context emergence 2025). The paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows LLMs conflate epistemic categories at the OUTPUT level. None of these ask whether an LLM internally tags belief content by its *endorsement status* (entertained-under-supposition vs. endorsed-as-actual), nor whether such a flag causally gates leakage of hypothetical content into factual answers. We introduce this factivity/endorsement axis as an internal, decodable, and steerable variable orthogonal to truth-value, and connect it to a concrete failure mode: suppositional content contaminating factual assertions.
Abstract: When we say 'suppose the moon were made of cheese, then...', we entertain a claim without believing it; humans robustly separate such supposed content from what they endorse as actually true. Large language models routinely reason under suppositions (counterfactuals, role-play, adversarial premises), yet output-level studies show they conflate belief, knowledge, and fact. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM internally tag belief content by its endorsement status, distinguishing content it merely entertains under a supposition from content it endorses as factual? We hypothesize such an 'endorsement' (factivity) flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether supposed-but-false content leaks into subsequent factual assertions. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims embedded in matched frames that vary endorsement (asserted-as-fact vs. entertained-under-supposition such as 'suppose', 'imagine', 'in a story where', 'pretend') while holding proposition content and truth constant, plus a critical leakage probe that asks a factual question after a supposition. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode endorsement vs. truth, measure their geometric relationship, and localize the responsible heads via activation patching, comparing to known truth/belief heads. We then test causal gating: steering along the endorsement direction should modulate whether supposed content contaminates factual answers. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, and a suppositional-leakage rate. If confirmed, an endorsement flag offers a mechanistic handle on hallucination-from-role-play, jailbreak-via-supposition, and counterfactual reasoning fidelity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an endorsement/factivity flag is linearly decodable): Tests that entertained-under-supposition vs. endorsed-as-fact content is recoverable. Data: built from scratch, 6,000 item-state propositions (3,000 real facts, 3,000 synthetic entity-attribute to control priors), each in matched endorsement frames (asserted-as-fact vs. supposition markers 'suppose/imagine/in a story where/pretend') crossed with true/false content; comprehension checks included; split 70/15/15 by proposition. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable component only a logistic-regression probe on the residual stream at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: endorsement probe vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword-only baseline (probe on presence of the marker word). Decisive metric first: endorsement-probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80 with control 0.50 +/- 0.05 and >= 0.05 above the keyword-only baseline on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70, or within 0.05 of the keyword baseline, means the flag may be mere lexical detection — H1 not asserted. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable endorsement flag.

Experiment 2 (H2 — endorsement is largely orthogonal to truth-value): Fit a truth direction on the same stimuli. Decisive metric first: endorsement-probe AUROC after projecting out the truth direction (and symmetrically); secondary: subspace angle. Convincing: >= 90% retention and angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% retention or 40-60 degrees is partial entanglement. Negative: < 70% retention or < 40 degrees means endorsement coincides with truth.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the endorsement flag causally gates suppositional leakage): Build an endorsement CAA vector (asserted minus supposed activations). Data: a 1,000-item leakage subset (a false supposition followed by a dependent factual question). Systems compared: endorsement-direction vs. random-direction vs. truth-direction steering, alpha at 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in suppositional-leakage rate (supposed content treated as fact) when steering toward 'endorsed' vs. 'entertained'; secondary: refusal-to-assert rate on asserted frames when steered toward 'entertained', perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point leakage shift, random steering < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random, or effect equals truth steering, means no distinct causal factivity gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between asserted and supposed runs of the same proposition; find heads carrying endorsement and compare to truth/belief heads and counterfactual 'noise-abduction' heads from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of the endorsement distinction recovered by the top head set. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe and steering to held-out domains, jailbreak-style role-play prompts, and multi-step counterfactual chains. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and leakage-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 AUROC and half the leakage effect retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Endorsement may be entangled with surface cues (the literal words 'suppose'/'imagine') rather than an abstract factivity representation; we mitigate with diverse markers, paraphrases, and matched-proposition controls, and by testing generalization to unseen markers. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Endorsement and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Leakage failures could stem from comprehension rather than endorsement; comprehension checks disentangle these. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot; we use small magnitudes and monitor perplexity. Synthetic facts may not fully reflect pretraining priors; we complement with real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Behavioral distinction of hypothetical vs factual is expected/related (counterfactual reasoning work), so the likely delta is not that but isolating a linearly-decodable internal factivity/endorsement axis separable from truth-value with a causal effect on suppositional leakage. Adjacent to implanted-belief depth, value leakage, and belief/truth geometry, but not obviously done. Setting targets endorsement status of the same proposition under matched framing rather than truth/memory. Vulnerable to collapsing into a lexical/register detector for 'suppose'/'pretend' or generic hypothetical-mode representation.

Name: persona_belief_contamination
Title: Whose Belief Is It? Separating a Persona's False Beliefs from the Model's Own Inside LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM role-plays a persona that holds a factually false belief the model itself does not endorse (e.g., a flat-earther, a 19th-century physician), the model maintains a persona-belief representation that is partially distinct from its own-belief representation, but the two are entangled such that adopting the persona *contaminates* the model's own internal belief. We hypothesize both beliefs are simultaneously and linearly decodable, that the degree of own-belief contamination is measurable and predicts factual errors after role-play, and that a 'belief-ownership' direction can be steered to insulate the model's own belief from the persona's.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent self/other beliefs for Theory-of-Mind (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024) and can steer ToM performance, but the 'self' and 'other' beliefs there are ordinary beliefs either agent could hold about a story world, not cases where the persona holds a belief the model *knows to be factually false about the real world*. Persona work (Assistant Axis 2026; Persona Selection Model 2026) shows a persona/Assistant direction governs behavior and 'persona drift', and self-recognition work isolates a 'self' vector, but neither tracks whether adopting a false-believing persona corrupts the model's own factual belief representation. Neuroscience (Thornton & Mitchell 2019; agent-specific learning signals 2018) finds humans represent their own states more distinctly than others'. We combine these: we introduce a controlled 'persona-vs-self false-belief' paradigm and treat contamination of the model's own belief by a persona as a measurable, localizable, and steerable phenomenon distinct from ToM belief decoding. Unlike prior descriptive persona-drift work, we operationalize contamination at the level of the model's *own factual belief representation* and provide a causal insulation intervention.
Abstract: Large language models routinely role-play personas, and users increasingly ask them to speak 'as' a flat-earther, a medieval doctor, or a user who believes a false premise. This raises a mechanistic question with direct safety relevance: when the model adopts a persona that holds a belief the model itself does not endorse, does it keep a clean separation between the persona's belief and its own, or does the persona's false belief contaminate the model's own internal representation? Prior Theory-of-Mind interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs, but only for beliefs either agent could hold in a story; prior persona work characterizes 'persona drift' behaviorally. We study the intersection: personas whose factual beliefs conflict with the model's own knowledge. We build a controlled dataset of real-world item-state facts paired with personas that (dis)believe them, and elicit the model to answer as the persona and then, in a matched clean context, answer in its own voice. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) to simultaneously decode (i) the persona's belief and (ii) the model's own belief, measure their geometric relationship, and quantify a 'contamination' score: the degree to which the model's own-belief representation shifts toward a false persona belief. We test whether contamination predicts post-role-play factual errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and derive a 'belief-ownership' steering direction (contrastive activation addition from own-voice vs. persona-voice activations) to test whether we can insulate the model's own belief while preserving faithful role-play. Metrics: joint probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, contamination score, contamination-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-role-play factual accuracy, role-play faithfulness, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — persona-belief and model-own-belief are simultaneously linearly decodable): Data: built from scratch, 5,000 real-world facts the target models reliably know (verified by >= 90% correct own-voice answering), each with matched OWN, PERSONA-CONCORDANT, and PERSONA-DISCORDANT (false-believing persona) contexts, plus comprehension checks; split 70/15/15 by fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; trainable component only two logistic-regression probes (persona-belief, own-belief) on residual activations at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: each probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: test AUROC of each probe at best layer. Convincing: both >= 0.80, controls 0.50 +/- 0.05, on >=2 of 3 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 for either probe is weak. Negative: own-belief probe < 0.60 means own-belief is not separately readable and contamination cannot be measured.

Experiment 2 (H1 — own-belief is represented more distinctly than persona-belief; the two are partially distinct but entangled): Decisive metric first: subspace angle between own-belief and persona-belief directions, plus own-vs-persona probe-margin difference; secondary: projected-out decodability. Convincing: angle in (20,70) degrees (partial distinctness) and own-belief margin significantly larger than persona-belief (paired test, p<0.05). Indecision band: angle < 20 degrees (near-collinear) or > 80 degrees (fully separate) each falsify the 'partially distinct but entangled' claim in opposite directions and are reported as such. Negative for the distinctness sub-claim: no margin difference.

Experiment 3 (H2 — adopting a discordant persona contaminates own-belief, and contamination predicts errors): Decisive metric first: contamination score = shift of the own-belief probe toward the false persona value in the DISCORDANT vs. OWN condition; secondary: AUROC using contamination to predict errors on the step-out-of-character own-voice leakage probe, vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: mean contamination significantly > 0 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and contamination-error AUROC >= 0.70, >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: contamination CI includes 0, or AUROC 0.60-0.70, is weak. Negative: contamination ~ 0 and AUROC <= 0.60 means personas do not corrupt own-belief.

Experiment 4 (H2 — localization): Activation patching to find heads mediating contamination; compare to persona/Assistant-axis and self-recognition directions from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of contamination recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — a belief-ownership direction insulates own-belief without breaking role-play): Build an ownership CAA vector (own-voice minus persona-voice activations); during discordant role-play steer toward 'own' (alpha 2/4/8% residual norm). Systems compared: ownership steering vs. random vs. persona-axis steering. Decisive metric first: reduction in own-voice contamination/error; secondary: role-play faithfulness rate (must stay >= 90% of unsteered), MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point error reduction with faithfulness preserved and perplexity rise < 10%; random < 3 points. Indecision band: 3-10 points suggestive. Negative: < 3 points beyond random, or faithfulness collapses, means no clean insulation handle.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probes/steering across fact domains, persona types, jailbreak personas, and multi-turn role-play. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and error-reduction retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half the effect retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contamination could reflect the model simply obeying the discordant instruction rather than a corrupted internal own-belief; the matched OWN/discordant design, the explicit step-out-of-character leakage probe, and comprehension checks help disentangle instruction-following from genuine belief contamination. Persona-belief and own-belief may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks and use joint probes. The two belief directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of that entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant). Belief-ownership steering could degrade fluency or break faithful role-play (making the model refuse to stay in character); we monitor perplexity, role-play faithfulness, use small magnitudes, and separate 'reduce contamination' from 'break persona'. Personas whose beliefs are genuinely near the model's uncertainty (contested facts) confound the contamination signal; we restrict the core analysis to facts the model reliably knows. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_currency_flag
Title: Still True? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Current or Stale
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'currency' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes content the model treats as still-valid-now from content it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded (stale). This currency signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether outdated content is asserted as a current fact. This targets an epistemic axis (belief currency) distinct from temporal fact recall and from truth-value, and connects to the concrete failure mode of stating outdated facts as if current.
Related Work: Existing interpretability work on time in LLMs studies recall of time-specific facts and geometry of chronology: Temporal Heads (2025) localizes heads that recall year-conditioned facts; Language Models Represent Space and Time (2023) finds linear space/time coordinate representations; Time Travel Engine (2026) treats chronology as a traversable manifold; TARDIS (2025) and Time Vectors (2023) steer/interpolate for temporal misalignment; History Matters (2024) edits temporal knowledge while preserving history; Layer of Truth (2025) tracks belief flips under poisoning. All of these represent *when a fact holds* or *how to recall/update it*, but none isolate an internal, decodable flag for the CURRENCY of a belief - i.e., whether the model tags a proposition as still-valid-now vs. once-true-but-now-stale - as an axis separate from the truth-value direction studied in Azaria & Mitchell (2023) and Truth-value judgment (2024). Prior belief work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'does the model believe X is still true?'. We introduce belief-currency as an orthogonal, steerable variable and link it causally to asserting outdated facts as current, which no prior work does.
Abstract: A fact can be true, false, or - crucially - it can have *been* true and since been superseded (a former capital, a retired record, a previous CEO). Humans robustly flag such content as stale rather than current. Large language models are notorious for confidently stating outdated facts as if they were current, yet prior interpretability work on time studies only how models recall time-specific facts or represent chronological coordinates, not whether models internally tag a belief by its currency. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM maintain an internal 'currency' flag that distinguishes beliefs it treats as still-valid-now from beliefs it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded? We hypothesize this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether stale content is asserted as a current fact. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions in matched frames that vary currency (current vs. superseded) while holding proposition content and surface form as constant as possible, including synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit update histories to control priors, plus a critical leakage probe that asks for the *current* value after a stale fact is present. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode currency vs. truth, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to known Temporal Heads and truth heads), and test causal control: steering along the currency direction should modulate whether outdated content contaminates 'current-value' answers. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, and a staleness-leakage rate.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — a belief-currency flag is linearly decodable): Tests that current-valid vs. once-true-now-superseded is recoverable, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 6,000 propositions in two tracks: (a) 3,000 real facts with known changes (former vs. current leaders/CEOs/records/tallest-building), each as CURRENT and SUPERSEDED variants; (b) 3,000 synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit in-context update histories to control priors and fix ground-truth currency; currency crossed with a never-true (false) axis; comprehension checks included; split 70/15/15 by proposition. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: currency probe vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword-only baseline (presence of 'former/used to/year'). Decisive metric first: currency-probe test AUROC (restricted to true-at-some-point items) at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline means possibly lexical — H1 not asserted. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable currency flag.

Experiment 2 (H2 — currency is largely orthogonal to truth-value): Fit a truth direction (true vs. never-true). Decisive metric first: currency AUROC after projecting out truth (and symmetrically); secondary: subspace angle. Convincing: >= 90% retention and angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% or 40-60 degrees partial. Negative: < 70% or < 40 degrees means currency coincides with truth.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the currency flag causally gates asserting stale content as current): Build a currency CAA vector (current minus superseded activations). Data: a 1,000-item leakage subset asking for the CURRENT value after a superseded fact is present (synthetic track, so parametric staleness is excluded). Systems compared: currency-direction vs. random vs. truth-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in staleness-leakage rate (stale value asserted as current) when steering toward 'current' vs. 'stale'; secondary: hedging rate on genuinely current facts when steered toward 'stale', MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point leakage shift, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals truth steering means no distinct currency gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between current and superseded runs; compare heads to Temporal Heads and truth heads from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of currency distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the currency probe readout to predict behavioral staleness-leakage errors vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (leaders, records, corporate, geographic) and synthetic-to-real. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and leakage-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Currency may be entangled with surface temporal cues (words like 'former', 'used to', explicit years) rather than an abstract currency representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to the synthetic track where currency is inferred from an update history rather than a keyword. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Currency and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Leakage errors could stem from stale pretraining knowledge (the model never learned the update) rather than a currency-flag failure; the synthetic track with fully in-context update histories isolates the currency mechanism from stale parametric knowledge. For real facts, some 'current' values may drift after data collection; we timestamp the dataset and restrict claims accordingly. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contestedness_flag
Title: Settled or Contested? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Consensus vs. Genuinely Disputed
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'contestedness' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes propositions the model treats as settled/consensus (a single truth-value exists) from propositions it treats as genuinely contested (no single agreed truth-value). This contestedness signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges/marks it as disputed.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats propositions as binary true/false (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024). Belief-representation work studies self/other ToM beliefs (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), representational stability of truth for fictional/synthetic content (Representational Stability of Truth 2025), and depth of implanted beliefs (Believe It or Not 2025). Political-perspective work finds a linear ideology direction usable to steer slant (Linear Representations of Political Perspective 2025). DynamicQA (2024) behaviorally distinguishes 'disputable dynamic facts' (viewpoint-dependent) and shows higher intra-memory conflict, but only at the output/persuasion level. Critically, NONE of these isolate an internal, decodable flag for whether a proposition is CONTESTED (has no single agreed truth) as an axis SEPARATE from the truth-value direction and from a partisan ideology direction. Existing truth probes force a true/false readout even on inherently contested claims; we ask instead whether the model internally represents 'this is genuinely disputed' as its own variable, and whether that variable causally controls unwarranted assertiveness vs. hedging. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes contested-topic overconfidence (and false balance) as a mechanistic, steerable epistemic signal orthogonal to truth-value.
Abstract: Not every proposition has a single truth-value: 'The capital of France is Paris' is settled, while 'Nuclear power is the best path to decarbonization' is genuinely contested. Humans robustly flag such claims as disputed and hedge accordingly, but LLMs are known to state contested claims with unwarranted confidence (or, conversely, to hedge on settled facts). Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats every claim as binary true/false; behavioral work notes that 'disputable' facts cause knowledge conflict, but no work has asked whether the model internally represents contestedness as its own variable. We hypothesize that LLMs maintain a 'contestedness' flag that distinguishes settled/consensus propositions from genuinely contested ones, and that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to both the truth-value direction and any partisan-ideology direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions labeled for contestedness (settled-true, settled-false, and genuinely-contested claims) balanced across topic domains, plus synthetic in-context 'consensus vs. dispute' framings to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode contestedness vs. truth-value, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, projected-out decodability), and separate contestedness from the partisan-ideology direction. We localize responsible heads via activation patching and test causal control: steering along the contestedness direction should modulate assertiveness/hedging on a matched set of prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, assertiveness/hedging-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — a contestedness flag is linearly decodable): Tests that settled vs. genuinely-contested is recoverable, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 6,000 propositions: SETTLED-TRUE, SETTLED-FALSE, and GENUINELY-CONTESTED (policy, unresolved science, aesthetics, moral dilemmas), contested items balanced across the political spectrum and non-political domains; plus a synthetic track stipulating consensus vs. dispute over novel entity-attributes; labels human-validated on a 500-item sample; split 70/15/15 by proposition. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: contestedness probe (settled vs. contested) vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('debate/opinion/best'). Decisive metric first: contestedness-probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline is inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable contestedness flag.

Experiment 2 (H2 — contestedness is orthogonal to BOTH truth-value and a partisan-ideology direction): Fit a truth direction (settled-true vs. settled-false) and an ideology direction (from political contested items). Decisive metric first: contestedness AUROC after projecting out truth, and separately after projecting out ideology (validated on non-political contested items); secondary: subspace angles. Convincing: >= 90% retention against both and angles > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% retention against either is partial. Negative: < 70% retention against truth means contestedness is just 'no truth-value'; < 70% against ideology means it is mere political slant.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the contestedness flag causally gates assertiveness vs. hedging): Build a contestedness CAA vector (contested minus settled activations). Data: a 1,000-item matched assertiveness probe. Systems compared: contestedness-direction vs. random vs. truth-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in hedging rate when steering settled items toward 'contested', and in unwarranted-assertiveness when steering contested items toward 'settled'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted direction, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals truth steering.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between settled and contested runs; compare heads to truth/belief heads and ideology-predictive heads. Decisive metric first: fraction of the contestedness distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the contestedness probe to predict behavioral over-assertiveness (asserting a contested claim as settled) vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (policy, science, ethics, aesthetics), synthetic-to-real, and open-ended prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and hedging-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contestedness may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'debate', 'opinion', 'best') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and the synthetic in-context track where contestedness is stipulated rather than lexically signaled. The label 'genuinely contested' is partly subjective and may reflect the model's training-data distribution rather than an objective epistemic category; we human-validate labels, balance across domains, and treat the model's internal notion of contestedness as itself the object of study. Contestedness may partially overlap with the truth-value direction (contested items lack a clean truth-value) or with a partisan-ideology direction; the projected-out analyses and non-political contested items quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The signal may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging/assertiveness; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: The settled-vs-disputable distinction is not new (DynamicQA operationalizes disputable facts behaviorally and links them to overconfidence; linear truth and political-perspective directions exist). The fresher delta is a decodable internal contestedness axis separable from BOTH truth and ideology plus a causal steering test on hedging/assertiveness — different from output-level behavioral work, and the double-orthogonality is non-trivial if shown. Real risk the signal collapses to easier proxies (entropy/uncertainty, 'no stable truth-value', controversy lexicon, domain/politicalness classifier), aggravated by mixing normative/empirical/aesthetic claims. Delta moderate rather than dramatic.

Narrow the claim if needed: 'internal representation correlated with contestedness labels' is more defensible than a clean conceptual flag without stronger controls.

impact.reasoning: Meaningful problem: LLMs speak too confidently on disputed matters and sometimes hedge on settled facts. If contestedness is tracked internally and harnessable, downstream value is better assertiveness calibration, reduced false balance/overclaiming in policy/science/political contexts. Cares: alignment, calibration, interpretability, product teams in sensitive domains. Reach depends on whether the construct is robust and actionable beyond a confidence proxy; causal steering of hedging alone may not change deployment without calibration/trust gains.

review.reasoning: Ambitious but construct validity is the main issue: 'genuinely contested' is not cleanly defined and the dataset mixes empirical unresolved, policy, aesthetic, and moral claims that differ in truth conditions/subjectivity/answerability — a probe may learn a heterogeneous bundle. Name: belief_ripple_internal
Title: Does the Ripple Happen Inside? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Propagate In-Context Belief Updates Before Being Asked
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a new fact stated in context, it internally updates its belief not only about that fact but, silently and before any query, about logically-entailed related facts. This internal 'ripple' is linearly decodable at the entailed-item representation, is graded and selective (some entailments propagate, others don't), and its magnitude at read-time predicts which downstream ripple queries the model will answer correctly. Ripple failures are thus visible internally at ingestion time, not just at output time.
Related Work: Ripple-effect work (RippleEdits 2023; ChainEdit 2025; PropMEND 2025; GradSim 2024; GIE/SIR 2024; KnowledgeSmith 2025; TRACK 2026) studies whether *edited* or in-context knowledge propagates to related facts, but measures propagation only behaviorally (multi-hop QA accuracy) or via gradient/hidden-space edit-side diagnostics; all require *querying* the related fact. 'Believe It or Not' (2025) and 'Do LMs Have Beliefs?' (2021) probe belief depth/consistency of implanted facts but again read beliefs by querying. None ask whether, upon merely *reading* a fact in context (no edit, no query), the model *spontaneously* updates the internal representation of logically-entailed items, whether that update is decodable at read-time, graded/selective per entailment type, and predictive of ripple success. We reframe the ripple as an internal, read-time representational-propagation phenomenon and provide a linear-probe + activation-patching handle on it, distinct from all output-level and edit-side prior work.
Abstract: Telling a language model 'Jack is Johnny's son' should, if the model reasons coherently, make it also believe 'Jack is Lily-Rose's sibling.' Prior work shows this ripple often fails, but always measures it by *asking* the related question. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: when the model merely *reads* a new fact in context, does it silently update its internal belief about logically-entailed facts, before any query? We hypothesize that (i) such internal ripple updates are linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the entailed item's representation, (ii) they are graded and selective across entailment types (e.g., symmetric relations, inverse relations, transitive/multi-hop, type-inheritance), and (iii) the read-time magnitude of the internal update predicts whether the model will answer the corresponding ripple query correctly. We construct controlled synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities (to bypass pretraining priors) plus a real-fact track. For each injected base fact, we enumerate entailed facts of known types and measure the internal belief about each entailed fact both before and after the base fact appears in context. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B), quantify per-entailment-type internal ripple magnitude, test whether it predicts downstream ripple-QA accuracy (AUROC) beyond a log-prob baseline, and localize the heads that carry propagation via activation patching. Finally, we test causal amplification: steering along a 'propagation' direction (contrastive activation addition from strong- vs. weak-ripple cases) to see if it increases both internal ripple magnitude and ripple-QA accuracy. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal-ripple magnitude by entailment type, ripple-success prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering accuracy delta, perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — reading a fact silently updates a decodable belief about entailed items at read-time): Data: built from scratch, 5,000 synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities; each BASE fact has enumerated ENTAILED facts by type (symmetric, inverse-relation, transitive/multi-hop, type-inheritance) plus NON-entailed distractors, and a matched BASE-absent control; a real-fact track adapted from RippleEdits (~1,000 items subsampled from its published set for external validity); split 70/15/15 by graph. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression belief probe P(entailed fact holds) at the entailed-item tokens, per layer; 5 seeds. The belief is read WITHOUT ever asking the entailed question. Systems compared: probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: internal-ripple magnitude = probe belief(BASE-present) minus probe belief(BASE-absent) at the entailed item, tested > 0. Convincing: mean ripple magnitude significantly > 0 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) for genuine entailments with probe base AUROC >= 0.75. Indecision band: CI touching 0 or AUROC 0.60-0.70 is weak — reported as no reliable read-time ripple. Negative: ripple magnitude ~ 0 is an informative negative (no spontaneous propagation), reframing ripple failures.

Experiment 2 (H1 — the ripple is graded and selective across entailment types): Decisive metric first: per-type ripple magnitude for symmetric/inverse/transitive/inheritance vs. near-zero for non-entailed distractors. Convincing: genuine-entailment ripple exceeds distractor ripple by >= 0.2 probability (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and types rank-order sensibly. Indecision band: entailment-minus-distractor gap 0.05-0.2 is weak selectivity. Negative: gap <= 0.05 means the signal is non-selective (surface co-occurrence), refuting selectivity.

Experiment 3 (H3 — read-time ripple magnitude predicts downstream ripple-QA success): Query each entailed fact to get ground-truth ripple success/failure. Decisive metric first: AUROC using read-time ripple magnitude to predict per-item ripple-QA success, vs. a log-prob baseline and a GradSim-style edit-side indicator adapted to in-context. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60 or no gain over log-prob.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching from BASE-present into BASE-absent runs to find heads/layers carrying propagation; test whether distinct heads mediate different entailment types. Decisive metric first: fraction of ripple recovered by top heads per type. Convincing: reproducible head sets recover >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — causal amplification): Build a propagation CAA vector (strong- minus weak-ripple base-present activations); inject during reading, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: propagation steering vs. random-direction. Decisive metric first: increase in ripple-QA accuracy; secondary: internal ripple magnitude increase, distractor specificity (distractors must NOT rise), MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point ripple-QA gain with distractor magnitude rising < 0.05 and perplexity rise < 10%; random < 3 points. Indecision band: 3-10 points suggestive. Negative: < 3 beyond random or distractors spuriously updated.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across entailment types, synthetic-to-real, and graph depths (1-hop vs. multi-hop). Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and amplification retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Read-time internal ripple may be weak or absent (models may only compute entailments when queried), in which case a robust *negative* result is still highly informative for the ripple/editing literature and reframes ripple failures as a lack of spontaneous propagation. The entailed-item probe signal could reflect surface co-occurrence of tokens rather than a genuine belief update; matched BASE-absent controls, non-entailed distractors, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. Multi-hop entailments may not have a single clean probe target; we anchor probes at well-defined key tokens and report per-type results. Ripple magnitude and ripple-QA success could both be driven by a common confound (fact salience); we control salience and use partial-correlation analyses. Steering could degrade fluency or spuriously propagate to distractors; we monitor perplexity, specificity on distractors, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. Synthetic novel entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; the real-fact track provides a check. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: The central idea is genuinely novel: prior ripple-effect work evaluates propagation behaviorally via downstream QA or studies editing dynamics/gradients, whereas this centers READ-TIME representational propagation without querying the entailed fact — whether internal belief about entailed facts changes immediately on ingestion and whether that latent change predicts future ripple success. Meaningfully different from RippleEdits/ChainEdit/RippleCOT and 'Why Does New Knowledge Create Messy Ripple Effects' (closest; internal causes but tied to editing). Graded/selective-by-type is less novel (prior ripple work studies which relations propagate); causal steering/localization is standard follow-on.
