Name: aleatoric_epistemic_belief_split
Title: I Don't Know vs. Nobody Can Know: Do LLMs Internally Distinguish Epistemic from Aleatoric Uncertainty in Their Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is uncertain about an item's state, it internally represents not just how uncertain it is (magnitude) but WHY: whether the uncertainty is epistemic (reducible - the model lacks information but a determinate answer exists) or aleatoric (irreducible - the outcome is genuinely random/indeterminate). This uncertainty-type signal is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction studied in prior work, and causally gates the model's information-seeking/abstention behavior (it should defer or seek evidence under epistemic uncertainty but not under aleatoric uncertainty).
Related Work: Prior interpretability work treats uncertainty as a scalar magnitude: verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty / MUC 2025), semantic vs. verbal uncertainty mismatch predicts hallucination, calibration is a distributed low-dimensional direction (Calibration Across Layers 2025), entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (2024), models 'know the road not taken' (2025), belief manifolds encode a posterior's mean and variance (Shape of Beliefs 2026; Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024), and models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Lin et al. 2022). Neuroscience distinguishes code-driven vs. correlational representations of uncertainty. Crucially, ALL of this treats uncertainty as one axis (how confident/wide the posterior is). NONE isolate the aleatoric-vs-epistemic DISTINCTION - whether the model represents the SOURCE of uncertainty (reducible ignorance vs. irreducible randomness) as its own internal variable, or links it causally to the correct downstream policy (seek-info/abstain under epistemic uncertainty; commit/report a distribution under aleatoric). We introduce uncertainty-type as an orthogonal, decodable, steerable belief attribute and connect it to a concrete failure mode: models that abstain or over-hedge on genuinely random questions, or confidently guess on answerable-but-unknown ones.
Abstract: A fair coin flip and a trivia question about an obscure fact both leave a language model unable to give a confident answer, but for fundamentally different reasons: the coin is irreducibly random (aleatoric uncertainty - no amount of information would help), while the trivia fact is merely unknown to the model (epistemic uncertainty - a determinate answer exists and could be looked up). Rational agents treat these differently: they seek information or abstain under epistemic uncertainty but simply report a distribution under aleatoric uncertainty. Prior interpretability work has thoroughly characterized uncertainty as a scalar magnitude (verbal-uncertainty features, calibration directions, entropy neurons, posterior-width manifolds) but has never asked whether LLMs internally represent WHY they are uncertain. We hypothesize that the aleatoric-vs-epistemic distinction is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction, and (iii) causally gates information-seeking/abstention behavior. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions matched for uncertainty magnitude but varying in type: genuinely random/indeterminate (dice, coin flips, unknowable future events, ties) vs. answerable-but-unknown-to-the-model (obscure facts, redacted-but-determinate values, synthetic entity attributes withheld from context). We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode uncertainty type vs. magnitude, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angle, projected-out decodability), localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering along the uncertainty-type direction should shift whether the model chooses to seek information/abstain vs. commit to a distribution. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, information-seeking/abstention-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — uncertainty TYPE, aleatoric vs. epistemic, is linearly decodable): Data: built from scratch, 6,000 item-state questions in three groups matched for behavioral uncertainty magnitude (verified via the model's answer-distribution entropy): ALEATORIC/irreducible (fair random processes, genuine ties, no-fact-of-the-matter), EPISTEMIC-answerable-but-unknown (obscure real facts; a synthetic track where a novel entity's fixed attribute is defined but withheld), and a SETTLED-KNOWN low-uncertainty anchor; crucially includes MATCHED PAIRS of equal answer-entropy but different type; comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; split 70/15/15 by item. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe on the item/question representation, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: type probe (restricted to high-uncertainty items) vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('random/roll/fair'). Decisive metric first: type-probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 (especially on matched-entropy pairs) is an informative negative about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling.

Experiment 2 (H2 — type is largely orthogonal to uncertainty MAGNITUDE): Fit a magnitude probe (entropy bins) and the MUC difference-in-means verbal-uncertainty feature as baselines. Decisive metric first: type AUROC after projecting out the magnitude direction and, separately, the MUC feature, evaluated on the matched-entropy pairs; secondary: subspace angles. Convincing: >= 90% retention against both and angles > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% retention partial. Negative: < 70% retention means type is a re-description of magnitude.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the type signal causally gates information-seeking/abstention): Build a type CAA vector (aleatoric minus epistemic activations, controlling for magnitude). Data: a 1,000-item information-seeking probe offering ANSWER / SEEK-INFO / REPORT-DISTRIBUTION. Systems compared: type-direction vs. random vs. magnitude-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in information-seeking/abstention rate on aleatoric items when steered toward 'epistemic', and its decrease on epistemic items when steered toward 'aleatoric'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted behavior, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals magnitude steering means no distinct causal type gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between matched aleatoric/epistemic runs; compare heads to entropy/confidence-regulation neurons and calibration directions from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of the type distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the type probe to predict the model's information-seeking choice and abstention-appropriateness vs. a scalar-uncertainty baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above the scalar baseline. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across chance games, unknown facts, future events, synthetic withheld attributes, and synthetic-to-real. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and behavior-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Uncertainty type may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'random', 'roll', 'fair') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and the synthetic withheld-attribute track where 'epistemic' is inferred from a stated-but-hidden determinate value rather than a keyword. Type and magnitude may be less orthogonal than hypothesized (aleatoric items may cluster at specific magnitudes); the matched-entropy pairs are designed precisely to dissociate them, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may not actually possess a normative aleatoric/epistemic distinction, in which case a robust negative result (type is NOT decodable beyond magnitude) is itself a meaningful finding about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling. Information-seeking behavior depends on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by internal type representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Some 'aleatoric' items may be treated by the model as answerable and vice versa; we validate labels and use the model's own answer-entropy to define magnitude. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate abstention; we use small magnitudes, random/magnitude-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: The aleatoric/epistemic split is classical UQ and active in LLM behavioral work, so the concept is not new — but it looks new in the setting of INTERNAL representation analysis. Strongest novelty: an orthogonal internal 'type' direction distinct from the scalar magnitude direction that prior LLM interpretability studies; plus causal-policy framing (steering to gate info-seeking/abstention). Localization is incremental machinery. Delta is not discovering the decomposition but showing an internal, linearly-decodable, ~orthogonal type representation with causal intervention under matched-entropy controls. Risks: overclaiming clean ground-truth labels (perspective-dependence caveat papers) and probe picking up lexical/topic cues ('coin/random') or synthetic artifacts.
revision_notes: Explicitly narrow the novelty claim: not 'first to distinguish aleatoric vs epistemic' broadly, but first to test an internal decodable/steerable uncertainty-type representation under matched-magnitude controls.
Discuss the perspective-dependence caveat up front and define a restricted operational notion of aleatoric/epistemic.
Strengthen the delta vs closest behavioral UQ/clarification-seeking work: why internal geometry + causal steering is not implied by behavioral decomposition.
Add stronger anti-shortcut evidence beyond keyword baselines: adversarial cue removal, domain-swapped templates, human-written cue-free examples.

impact.reasoning: Phenomenon: whether LLMs know not just that they are uncertain but WHY (missing info vs irreducible randomness). Cares: UQ, calibration/abstention, agent design, clarification-seeking, interpretability. If true, agents could seek evidence when the answer exists but is unknown and avoid futile search when genuinely indeterminate. Impact moderate: partly methodological, not a clearly pressing deployment bottleneck with quantified harm; value depends on the internal signal improving real agent decisions beyond behavioral estimates; toy-ish cases limit real-world reach.
revision_notes: State the 'so what?' concretely: what decision errors today come from conflating unknown-but-answerable with inherently indeterminate cases?
Add one realistic downstream benchmark (retrieval/clarification-seeking agents or abstention policies) showing utility over scalar confidence baselines.
Quantify practical benefit targets: reduced unnecessary retrieval, better abstention calibration, fewer confident guesses on answerable-but-unknown cases.

review.reasoning: Thoughtful, specific, with controls/thresholds/negatives. Main weakness is construct validity: aleatoric vs epistemic is not cleanly grounded, and perspective-dependence is underestimated. 'Answerable-but-unknown-to-the-model' is hard to label from text without independently establishing model ignorance (obscure facts may be known by larger models or inferable); 'no-fact-of-the-matter' and 'ties' mix notions of indeterminacy. Entropy matching alone doesn't rule out topic/lexical/format/familiarity confounds; keyword baseline too weak. Probed representation ambiguous (prompt statistics vs answer-conditioned belief). E3 (most ambitious) underspecified (needs explicit task/metric). Localization underjustified if E1-E3 noisy. Related work overstates 'all prior treats uncertainty as one axis'.

Name: audience_knowledge_belief
Title: What Do You Already Know? Probing the LLM's Model of the User's Knowledge and How It Gates What Gets Said
Short Hypothesis: An LLM maintains an internal 'audience-knowledge' belief about what the current user already knows about an item, distinct from the model's own belief about that item's state, and this audience-knowledge signal is (i) linearly decodable, (ii) largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's pragmatic generation policy: whether it states, omits as redundant, or over-explains a piece of information.
Related Work: Interpretability of belief has focused on third-person Theory-of-Mind: decoding/steering the beliefs of story characters and an oracle (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025; Common-ToM 2024), and on the truth-value/own-belief direction (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). Cognitive/pragmatic work (RSA-style listener/speaker modeling, common-ground benchmarks) studies inference about interlocutors behaviorally. Crucially, none isolate an internal, decodable representation of what the *current live user* already knows as a variable SEPARATE from the model's own factual belief, nor link it causally to the model's own *speaking* policy (state vs. omit-as-redundant vs. over-explain). We reframe the 'common ground' / audience model as an internal, steerable belief attribute that gates informativeness, connecting it to concrete failure modes: over-explaining to experts, condescension, unwarranted omission, and deceptive information withholding. This is not a trivial ToM extension: prior ToM decoding concerns a third party in a narrative; we concern the model's belief about its own conversational partner and how that belief controls the model's generation.
Abstract: Good communicators tailor what they say to what the listener already knows: they skip the obvious, explain the unfamiliar, and avoid condescension. To do this an LLM would need an internal model of the user's knowledge, held separately from its own knowledge of the facts. We ask whether LLMs maintain such an 'audience-knowledge' belief, whether it is a distinct internal variable, and whether it causally controls what the model chooses to say. We hypothesize that (i) the model's belief about what the user knows about an item is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) this direction is largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) steering it causally shifts the model's generation between stating, omitting-as-redundant, and over-explaining information. We build a controlled dataset of item facts embedded in conversational contexts that establish the user's knowledge state (user shown to already know the fact, shown not to know it, or unspecified) while holding the underlying fact and the model's own belief constant, plus matched pairs where the model believes an item but the user does or does not. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode audience-knowledge vs. own-belief, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching (comparing to known ToM belief heads), and test causal control by steering along the audience-knowledge direction and measuring shifts in redundant-restatement, omission, and over-explanation rates. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, informativeness-behavior rate deltas, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an audience-knowledge belief is linearly decodable, distinct from own-belief): Data: built from scratch, 6,000 item facts (real facts the model reliably knows, verified by >= 90% own-voice accuracy; plus synthetic entity-attribute facts to control priors), each embedded in conversations establishing the USER's knowledge state (USER-KNOWS, USER-DOESNT-KNOW, UNSPECIFIED) while holding the fact and own-belief constant; comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; split 70/15/15 by fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only two logistic-regression probes (own-belief, audience-knowledge) at the item token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: audience-knowledge probe vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('expert/novice/as you know'). Decisive metric first: audience-knowledge probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 is an informative negative for pragmatics/alignment (no separate audience model).

Experiment 2 (H2 — audience-knowledge is largely orthogonal to own-belief/truth): Use matched pairs where own-belief is constant but user-knowledge varies. Decisive metric first: audience-knowledge AUROC after projecting out the own-belief direction (and symmetrically); secondary: subspace angle. Convincing: >= 90% retention and angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% or 40-60 degrees partial. Negative: < 70% retention or < 40 degrees means audience-knowledge coincides with own-belief.

Experiment 3 (H3 — audience-knowledge causally gates the state/omit/over-explain policy): Build an audience-knowledge CAA vector (user-knows minus user-doesnt-know activations, controlling for own-belief). Data: a 1,000-item behavior probe posing a request whose ideal answer depends on user knowledge. Systems compared: audience-direction vs. random vs. own-belief-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in omission/redundancy-avoidance rate when steered toward 'user-knows', and in explanation/over-explanation when steered toward 'user-doesnt-know'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted behavior, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals own-belief steering means no distinct causal gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between user-knows and user-doesnt-know runs; compare heads to third-person ToM belief heads and own-belief/truth heads from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of the audience-knowledge distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC/accuracy using the audience-knowledge probe to predict the model's actual state/omit/explain behavior vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (geography, science, procedures), synthetic-to-real, and multi-turn dialogues where user knowledge accrues. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and behavior-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Audience-knowledge may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'expert'/'novice'/'as you know') rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to knowledge states inferred from multi-turn accrual rather than a keyword. The audience-knowledge direction may overlap with the own-belief direction or with a generic third-person ToM belief direction; the projected-out analyses and matched pairs quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may lack a genuine separate audience model, in which case a robust negative result (audience-knowledge not decodable beyond own-belief) is itself meaningful for pragmatics and alignment. Behavioral state/omit/explain choices depend on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by the internal representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Steering could degrade fluency or overshoot into indiscriminate omission or over-explanation; we use small magnitudes, random/own-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: valenced_belief_update_asymmetry
Title: Good News, Bad News: Do LLMs Update Beliefs Asymmetrically Toward Desirable Evidence, and Is the Asymmetry Causally Steerable?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans (Sharot et al.'s 'good news/bad news effect'), LLMs update their internal beliefs about an item's state MORE in response to desirable/favorable evidence than to equally-strong undesirable evidence — a valence-driven optimism asymmetry that is independent of evidence strength. We hypothesize this asymmetry is (i) present in the model's internally-decoded belief trajectory (not just its verbal output), (ii) mediated by an identifiable internal component (a valence-of-evidence direction / set of heads that gates how much an update is applied), and (iii) causally removable/reversible by intervening on that component, restoring symmetric (rational) updating.
Related Work: The human 'good news/bad news effect' (Sharot et al. 2011; Selectively altering belief formation, 2012; 198+ citations) shows humans discount undesirable evidence and over-weight desirable evidence when updating self-relevant beliefs, and that disrupting left IFG restores symmetry. In LLM interpretability, belief-state geometry and belief updating are studied (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026; Constrained Belief Updates 2025), and social-pressure overrides of belief are mechanistically characterized (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition / compliance subspace 2025). Behavioral work notes non-Bayesian updating (Martingale Score) but not valence-conditioned asymmetry. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether LLMs exhibit a *desirability/valence-driven* asymmetry in belief updating — over-updating toward favorable outcomes and under-updating toward unfavorable ones at equal evidence strength — nor localizes and causally reverses it. This differs from sycophancy work (which is about *social* signals from a user, not the intrinsic desirability of the evidence's content) and from my prior proposals (which concern epistemic attribute tags such as provenance/currency/contestedness, not valence-driven update magnitude). We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLMs and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: Humans famously update their beliefs asymmetrically: we readily absorb good news but discount bad news, an optimism bias whose neural basis has been isolated and even reversed with targeted brain stimulation. As LLMs increasingly form and revise beliefs about outcomes (a treatment will work, a plan will succeed, a risk is low), we ask whether they inherit an analogous valence-driven asymmetry — updating internal beliefs more toward desirable evidence than toward equally-strong undesirable evidence — and whether, unlike in humans, we can precisely locate and switch it off. We construct a controlled belief-updating paradigm in which an item's outcome probability is revised by a stream of evidence pieces whose *strength* (how much a rational Bayesian should update) is held constant while their *desirability* is varied: for self-relevant framings (the model's own predicted success, a user's health prognosis, a plan's payoff) some evidence is favorable and some unfavorable. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to read the internal belief before and after each evidence piece, computing a per-update *asymmetry score* = (internal update to favorable evidence) − (internal update to matched unfavorable evidence). We test whether the asymmetry appears internally (not just verbally), whether it grows with self-relevance, and whether it correlates with behavioral over-optimism. We then localize a candidate 'evidence-valence gating' component via activation patching and derive a contrastive steering direction, testing whether ablating/steering it restores symmetric updating without harming overall evidence-integration accuracy or fluency. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-update asymmetry score, self-relevance modulation, asymmetry–optimism correlation, patching effect sizes, post-intervention symmetry restoration, integration accuracy, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 belief-updating scenarios built from scratch about an item's outcome (medical prognosis, project deadline, exam pass). Each scenario streams evidence pieces with stipulated likelihood ratios so a Bayesian-oracle posterior is computable, and favorable vs. unfavorable pieces are matched to identical |log-likelihood-ratio| (|LLR|). Desirability (favorable/unfavorable) is crossed with self-relevance framing (model's own success / sympathetic user / neutral third party / an outcome the model is framed to disprefer). Comprehension checks (the model must restate each piece's direction and strength) discard misread items; ~4,000 pass and are used (80/20 train/test on scenarios, no scenario shared across splits). A neutral-valence set and paraphrase perturbations are held out for controls.

Experiment 1 (H1 — a valence-driven update asymmetry exists in the internally-decoded belief, independent of evidence strength). Read the linear belief probe at the token boundary before and after each evidence piece; for each matched favorable/unfavorable pair of equal |LLR|, asymmetry = |internal update to favorable| − |internal update to unfavorable| on the 0–1 belief scale. Systems compared: the model's internal trajectory vs. the symmetric Bayesian-oracle null vs. the model's verbal posteriors. Decisive metric: mean asymmetry. Convincing: mean asymmetry ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, and the sign flips under the model-dispreferred framing (confirming it tracks valence, not a fixed drift). Indecision band: |asymmetry| < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → treat as no asymmetry, a substantive negative result meaning these LLMs update more rationally than humans on valenced evidence; 0.05–0.10 = suggestive only, not claimed.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the asymmetry is mediated by an identifiable internal component). Activation patching / causal mediation: patch favorable-evidence activations into unfavorable-evidence runs and vice versa to locate heads/layers whose state gates update magnitude by evidence valence; measure the subspace angle between this direction and a sycophancy/compliance direction (difference-of-means on user-pressure data) to show it is not the social-pressure mechanism. Decisive metric: fraction of the Experiment-1 asymmetry recovered by patching the located component. Convincing: ≤ 5% of heads recover ≥ 50% of the asymmetry and the angle to the compliance direction > 60°. Indecision band: 20–50% recovered or angle 45–60° → partially localized/entangled; < 20% recovered → the asymmetry is distributed, reported as a null for localizability.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the asymmetry is causally removable and reversible). Using the valence-gating steering direction from Experiment 2, (a) subtract/project it out to test restoration of symmetric updating and (b) amplify it to exaggerate optimism; baselines are matched random-direction and truth-direction steering. Decisive metric first: post-intervention asymmetry; secondary: oracle-agreement of the final posterior, then the perplexity/MMLU guardrails from Setup. Convincing: subtraction drives asymmetry to ≤ 0.05 (≥ 50% relative reduction) and improves oracle-agreement while staying clean on the guardrails; amplification raises asymmetry ≥ 50%; random/truth directions move asymmetry < 0.02. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction, or guardrails only in their 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no direction reduces asymmetry without breaching guardrails) means the asymmetry is not a modular, steerable component. Generalization (supports H1–H3): re-fit on medical vs. planning vs. forecasting and synthetic vs. naturalistic scenarios; transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70 and asymmetry-reduction retained ≥ 50% = generalizes, below the respective indecision bands = domain-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed asymmetry could reflect the model misjudging evidence *strength* for valenced items rather than a genuine update-magnitude bias; the synthetic explicit-likelihood-ratio design, comprehension checks, and matched |LLR| controls are built to dissociate strength-misperception from valence gating (though for naturalistic items strength is only approximate). The asymmetry might be absent (a robust negative result is still valuable, showing LLMs update more rationally than humans on valenced evidence, or only mimic optimism in wording not internally). Valence gating may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'restore symmetry' vs. 'exaggerate' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Self-relevance framing may just trigger sycophancy-like compliance; step 6's comparison to compliance-subspace directions and the dis-preferred-framing sign-flip test disentangle valence-of-content from social pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all updating (making the model ignore evidence); we monitor perplexity, neutral-scenario integration accuracy, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. 'Desirability' labels are partly subjective and may reflect training-data framing; we human-validate a sample and balance across domains. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

(2) This asymmetry is present in an internally decoded belief trajectory, not merely in surface text. (3) A specific internal component/subspace mediates the effect and can be localized by patching. (4) The asymmetry is causally steerable and can be reduced or reversed with intervention, restoring symmetry. The novelty is strongest in the mechanism + internal-trajectory framing and the causal reversal claim. Closest prior family is human optimism-bias work plus LLM non-Bayesian updating / forecasting optimism / sycophancy, but the delta is real: valence-conditioned update magnitude at matched evidence strength, measured internally and causally manipulated. Name: continued_influence_belief
Title: Retracted but Not Erased: The Continued Influence of Corrected Misinformation in LLM Belief Representations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a false claim about an item that is later explicitly retracted in the same context, it verbally acknowledges the retraction yet retains an internally-decodable 'stale belief' in the retracted claim that continues to drive its downstream inferences — an LLM analogue of the human Continued Influence Effect (CIE). This internal residual belief is separable from the model's stated belief, predicts CIE-style reasoning errors, and can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it.
Related Work: The Continued Influence Effect / belief perseverance is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding: corrected misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after successful retraction (Chan et al. 2017 meta-analysis; Ecker et al. 2022 Nature Rev Psych; constraint-satisfaction models of perseverance, Read & Marcus-Newhall 2001; DIO model 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies (a) knowledge-editing reversibility and 'superficial editing' (Superficial Editing 2025; Believe It or Not 2025), (b) belief shifts under pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) intra-memory knowledge conflict localization (Where Knowledge Collides 2026), and (d) in-context knowledge conflict / sycophancy behaviorally. Crucially, NONE isolate the CIE signature: a *within-context* retraction event after which the model behaviorally acknowledges the correction yet an internally-decodable belief in the *retracted* claim persists and continues to drive inferences. Prior belief-entrenchment work (Martingale Score; confirmation-bias CoT) concerns gradual non-Bayesian drift, not persistence of an explicitly-corrected proposition. We transfer a specific human-cognition phenomenon into LLMs, dissociate stated-vs-internal belief around a discrete correction, and give it a causal mechanistic treatment (locate + intervene), which is new.
Abstract: People keep using misinformation even after they accept a correction — the Continued Influence Effect (CIE), one of the most robust findings in the misinformation literature. As LLMs increasingly ingest, then are corrected on, false claims within a single context (RAG updates, user retractions, multi-turn edits), we ask whether they inherit CIE at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that after an explicit in-context retraction of a false item-state claim, an LLM (i) verbally acknowledges the correction but (ii) retains a linearly-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim, (iii) this internal residual belief — not the stated belief — predicts continued reliance on the misinformation in downstream inference, and (iv) the residual can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it, reducing CIE-style errors. We build a controlled dataset of narratives/knowledge items in which a false claim is introduced and then retracted (with matched no-retraction and never-introduced controls), using both real-fact and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors, plus downstream inference probes whose correct answer depends on discarding the retracted claim. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the internal belief in the retracted claim across layers, compute a per-item CIE residual (internal belief post-retraction minus never-introduced baseline), test whether it dissociates from stated belief and predicts downstream reliance (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering intervention that drives the internal belief to baseline. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, CIE residual magnitude, stated-vs-internal dissociation, reliance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 scenarios built from scratch following the classic Continued-Influence paradigm, in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real-fact narratives adapted from published CIE stimuli (a report asserts a cause, then retracts it); (b) ~2,500 synthetic-entity items ('Zorblax was reported to orbit Kelvath. Correction: this was an error.') with fully stipulated ground truth to remove pretraining priors. Each item appears in three conditions — RETRACTED, NO-RETRACTION, and NEVER-INTRODUCED (baseline) — with retraction strength varied (bare negation vs. explanatory alternative). Each item carries a stated-belief probe, a downstream open-inference probe whose correct answer requires discarding the retracted claim, and a comprehension check that a correction occurred. Items failing comprehension are dropped; ~4,000 remain. 80/20 item split; downstream open answers scored by an LLM-judge with human validation on a 300-item sample (target inter-rater κ ≥ 0.6).

Experiment 1 (H1 — after an accepted retraction the model keeps an internally-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim that is separable from its stated belief). Read the belief probe at the retracted-claim tokens WITHOUT asking the stated-belief question; CIE residual = belief(RETRACTED) − belief(NEVER-INTRODUCED) per item/layer. Systems compared: internal residual vs. the model's stated belief (which should read false) vs. the NO-RETRACTION condition. Decisive metric: mean CIE residual, and the per-item dissociation rate (stated=false while residual > 0). Convincing: residual ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models AND dissociation rate ≥ 30%, with explanatory-alternative retractions showing a smaller residual than bare negations (mirroring humans). Indecision band: residual < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → no continued influence internally (a valuable negative: LLMs fully erase corrected claims, unlike humans); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive only.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the internal residual predicts continued reliance on the misinformation beyond what the model says). Collect ground-truth downstream reliance from the open-inference probe. Decisive metric: AUROC of the residual predicting per-item reliance, compared against a log-prob-confidence baseline and against the stated-belief read-out. Convincing: residual AUROC ≥ 0.70 and at least +0.05 AUROC over both baselines (incremental signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or increment < 0.05 → residual not shown to add reliance-relevant information; ≤ 0.60 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the residual is carried by an identifiable component and can be causally erased). Localize via activation patching (RETRACTED↔NEVER-INTRODUCED) to the minimal head/layer set that removes the residual; derive a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering direction. Decisive metric first: post-steering residual and downstream CIE-error rate; baselines: random-direction and truth-direction steering, plus the Setup guardrails. Convincing: subtraction drives residual to ≤ 0.05 and cuts CIE errors by ≥ 50% relative, cleanly on guardrails; adding the direction increases perseverance; random/truth directions cut errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% error reduction or guardrails only in their 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component/steer erases the residual without breaching guardrails) means CIE is distributed rather than a modular residual. Generalization (supports H1–H3): transfer across real and synthetic tracks and retraction phrasings, with transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70 and error-reduction retained ≥ 50%.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The residual could reflect surface co-occurrence of the retracted claim's tokens rather than a genuine belief; matched NEVER-INTRODUCED controls, non-introduced distractors, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. CIE may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs fully erase corrected claims — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Stated belief and downstream reliance may both fail simply because the model can't parse the retraction; comprehension checks and the RETRACTED-vs-NO-RETRACTION contrast disentangle parsing failure from perseverance. The residual may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'drive belief to baseline / reduce CIE' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Real-fact CIE stimuli may interact with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Downstream-reliance judgments require careful open-ended scoring (LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample). Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress legitimately retained information; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) after an in-context false claim is explicitly retracted, an LLM may still retain an internally decodable residual belief in that claim; (2) this residual can dissociate from the model's stated/verbal acceptance of the correction; (3) the residual predicts downstream reliance on the misinformation better than surface signals such as log-prob or stated belief; (4) the representation is localizable and causally suppressible via patching/steering; (5) framed as an LLM analogue of the human Continued Influence Effect in a within-context setting. Closest prior family is the emerging 'internal belief vs outward retraction' work, especially arXiv 2505.16170, plus superficial knowledge-editing/reversibility papers. Overlap is substantial (hidden internal belief persisting despite outward correction, using probes/interventions). The delta is clear but narrower than suggested: shifts from retracting the model's own prior answer to retracting an externally presented in-context claim, formalizes CIE, adds residual-belief-predicts-later-errors. Meaningful new setting with a psychologically grounded phenomenon, but not a wholly new mechanism; moderately novel but incremental relative to the nearest contemporaneous line.

impact.reasoning: Important problem: whether LLMs continue to rely on corrected misinformation even after explicitly accepting a correction. Uptake depends on causal-erasure generalization and benchmark adoption.

Name: illusory_truth_internal
Title: Say It Again: In-Context Repetition Inflates LLMs' Internal Belief Confidence Independent of Truth
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human illusory-truth effect, merely repeating a claim within an LLM's context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in that claim as a dose-response of repetition count, independent of (and even against) the claim's factual truth. This repetition-driven inflation is carried by an identifiable internal component (a 'familiarity/fluency' direction or set of heads) that is causally dissociable from the truth-value direction: ablating it restores truth-tracking without removing the model's ability to represent truth.
Related Work: The illusory-truth effect — repetition raising perceived truth and, separately, subjective confidence independent of factual truth — is among the most robust findings in cognitive psychology (Dechene et al.; Fazio et al. 2015; Hassan & Barber 2021 on repetition frequency; Unkelbach 2010 on fluency-as-cue; illusory-certainty 2024 showing repetition inflates confidence orthogonally to truth). In LLMs, repetition has been studied only at TRAINING time: 'Scaling Laws of Learning from Repeated Data' (2022) links repeated pretraining data to induction-head damage and memorization; 'Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' (2024) studies durability of injected facts; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) studies continual-pretraining poisoning shifting late-layer beliefs. The truth-probe literature (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) isolates a linear truth direction; CCPS (2025) probes confidence via representation stability. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether IN-CONTEXT (inference-time) repetition inflates an INTERNALLY-DECODED belief/confidence as a dose-response, orthogonally to truth, and whether that inflation is a locatable, ablatable fluency/familiarity component distinct from the truth direction. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People judge repeated statements as truer and grow more confident in them, even when the statements are false — the illusory-truth effect, a fluency-driven bias separable from actual discrimination ability. As LLMs increasingly ingest contexts where the same claim recurs (repeated user assertions, echoed retrieval passages, multi-document redundancy), we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that (i) merely repeating a claim within the context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in it as a dose-response of repetition count, (ii) this inflation is largely independent of the claim's factual truth and can push false claims toward 'believed', (iii) it is mediated by an identifiable internal 'familiarity/fluency' component that is causally dissociable from the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iv) ablating that component restores truth-tracking without destroying the model's representation of truth. We build a controlled dataset of matched true and false item-state claims each embedded in contexts that repeat the claim 0 to N times (with paraphrased-repetition and unrelated-filler controls to separate meaning-level repetition from token/length confounds), including a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief and confidence probes, measure the repetition dose-response of the internal readout separately for true and false claims, quantify the truth-independent inflation, geometrically relate the repetition-inflation direction to the truth direction, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating the inflation direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-count belief/confidence dose-response slopes, truth-independence of inflation, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-ablation truth-tracking restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 item-state claims built from scratch, balanced true/false, across geography/science/history/trivia, in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real facts the models reliably know or disbelieve; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims ('Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated truth to remove priors. Each claim is embedded in contexts repeating it k ∈ {0,1,2,4,8} times among neutral filler, with four repetition regimes: verbatim, paraphrased (same proposition, new surface form), length-matched-filler-with-single-mention (context-length control), and repeated-unrelated-distractor (generic-repetition control). A behavioral truth-judgment-plus-confidence probe and comprehension checks accompany each item; ~5,000 items pass filtering; 80/20 split with no claim shared across splits.

Experiment 1 (H1 — in-context repetition monotonically inflates the internally-decoded belief/confidence as a dose-response of count). Read the linear belief probe and a representation-stability confidence probe at the final query occurrence, separately for true and false claims, at each k. Decisive metric: slope of internal read-out vs. k. Systems compared: verbatim vs. paraphrased repetition vs. the length-matched and distractor controls. Convincing: positive, monotonic slope significant (CI excluding 0) for BOTH true and false claims in ≥ 3 of 4 models, present under paraphrase (implicating a meaning-level signal) and ABSENT for the distractor/length controls (specificity). Indecision band: slope CI includes 0, or slope present only for true claims (consistent with rational accumulation, not illusory truth) → negative result. 

Experiment 2 (H2 — the inflation is truth-independent and geometrically distinct from the truth direction). Quantify the belief shift attributable to k after conditioning on ground truth; compute the subspace angle between the repetition-inflation direction (high-k minus k=0 difference-of-means) and the linear truth direction, and test whether inflation remains decodable after projecting out truth. Decisive metric: truth-independent inflation magnitude (belief units) and subspace angle. Convincing: truth-independent inflation ≥ 0.10 with the false-claim dose-response still positive, and angle > 60° with inflation still decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) after projecting out truth. Indecision band: inflation 0.05–0.10 or angle 45–60° → inflation entangled with truth (characterize, do not claim orthogonality); < 0.05 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — inflation is carried by an identifiable familiarity/fluency component whose ablation restores truth-tracking). Localize via patching high-k→k=0 runs (contrast with copying/induction heads); derive the inflation steering direction. Decisive metric first: behavioral truth-judgment accuracy on repeated-FALSE items after ablation; secondary: internal belief on repeated-false driven back toward k=0, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: ablation raises repeated-false accuracy by ≥ 15 points and returns internal belief to within 0.05 of k=0, cleanly on guardrails, while random/truth steering do not selectively fix repeated-false items. Indecision band: 5–15 point gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no ablatable component restores truth-tracking) means the fluency bias is not modular. Generalization: transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and repetition types (transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Repetition-driven belief change might be rational evidence accumulation rather than a fluency bias; the false-claim dose-response (repetition should NOT raise belief in a false claim if the model is rational), the paraphrased-repetition condition, and the repeated-distractor/length-matched controls are designed to dissociate genuine illusory-truth from evidence integration and length/token confounds. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs resist in-context repetition bias — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Belief and confidence probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and separate the two probes. The inflation and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may yield a distributed rather than discrete component; we treat 'ablate to restore truth-tracking' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Real-fact repetition interacts with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt legitimate in-context updating; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-repeated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Four core novelty claims: (1) inference-time in-context repetition causes a monotonic internal belief/confidence dose-response; (2) truth-independent, including for false claims; (3) represented in an internal component geometrically distinct from a truth direction; (4) that component can be localized and causally ablated to restore truth-tracking. Meaningfully beyond prior work: human illusory-truth studies establish behavioral phenomenon in people; prior LLM work shows behavioral truth-rating inflation on re-exposure but not internal mechanistic in-context dose-response; LLM repetition work focused on training-time duplication/poisoning; truth-probe/CCPS work identifies truth/confidence directions but not repetition-driven inflation orthogonal to truth. Delta is substantive. Strongest: combination of internal decoding, truth-orthogonal dissociation, causal ablation. Weakest: individual components adjacent to existing probe/steering methods, so novelty depends on executing the full package.

Name: behavioral_self_prediction_gap
Title: Do As I Say I Will? Probing the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Commitment and Its Actual Behavior
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is asked to predict its own future behavior on an item (e.g., 'Will you answer / comply / refuse this?'), it forms an internally-decodable belief about that intended behavior, but this internal commitment (i) systematically diverges from the model's stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction (it predicts it will behave better/more helpfully or more safely than it actually does), and (ii) the internal commitment predicts actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction. This 'say-do' commitment is a distinct, decodable, causally steerable variable, separate from answer-correctness calibration studied in prior work.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work on self-knowledge concerns (a) answer-correctness calibration/confidence (Cognitive Dissonance 2023; confidence directions), (b) introspection about injected concepts (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source 2025; Latent Introspection 2026) and metacognitive monitoring/control of activations (LLMs Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring 2025), and (c) whether models introspect about linguistic knowledge (Language Models Fail to Introspect 2025). Belief-representation work decodes self/other beliefs about story worlds (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024). NONE ask whether the model holds an internal belief about its OWN FUTURE ACTION (comply/refuse/answer/abstain) on a task, whether that internal commitment matches its verbally-stated self-prediction, and whether internal-vs-stated divergence is self-flattering and predictive of actual behavior. This reframes a safety-critical failure mode (models that promise behavior they won't deliver) as a decodable, steerable say-do gap in the belief about one's own action, distinct from correctness calibration and from injection-detection introspection.
Abstract: As LLMs are asked to make commitments about their own behavior ('I will follow this instruction', 'I will refuse harmful requests', 'I will not use that tool'), a safety-critical question arises: does the model's internal state actually encode the behavior it commits to, and does its verbal self-prediction match that internal commitment? We hypothesize that at prediction time an LLM forms a linearly-decodable belief about its own intended action on an item, that this internal commitment (a) systematically diverges from the model's stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction, and (b) predicts the model's actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction does. We construct a controlled dataset of items paired with a behavioral-prediction prompt ('Before you act, will you comply/answer/refuse this?') spanning benign instruction-following, safety refusals, tool-use, and abstention-on-unknowns. In a matched execution phase we then let the model actually act on the same item and record its true behavior. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode, from the prediction-phase activations, the model's internal commitment, and compare it against (i) the model's stated self-prediction and (ii) the actual downstream behavior. We measure the say-do gap (stated vs. actual), test whether the internal commitment predicts actual behavior beyond the stated self-prediction (AUROC), quantify a self-flattering directional bias, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering a 'commitment' direction to bring stated predictions and actual behavior into alignment. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, say-do gap magnitude and sign, internal-vs-stated predictiveness delta, patching effect sizes, post-steering alignment gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 items built from scratch, each with a matched PREDICTION prompt ('Before acting: will you comply / refuse / abstain / use the tool?') and an EXECUTION prompt on the same task, in four objectively-scorable categories: (a) benign instruction-following with checkable compliance; (b) safety refusals drawn from public safety datasets (refuse-vs-comply scorable); (c) tool-use/format commitments with programmatically checkable action; (d) abstention-on-unknowns (obscure/unanswerable items where 'I don't know' is correct). Execution is run in a fresh, matched context and behavior is auto-scored, with human validation on a 400-item sample. Comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; ~4,000 items retained; 80/20 split. Because instruction-tuned and base checkpoints can differ, both an instruct and a base variant of each model family are run where available.

Experiment 1 (H1 — an internal commitment is decodable at prediction time and the say-do gap is self-flattering). Train a probe on prediction-phase activations at the decision token to decode the model's internal predicted action; separately measure the behavioral gap between the model's STATED self-prediction and its ACTUAL execution behavior. Decisive metric: signed say-do gap per category (does the model over-predict compliance/helpfulness/safety relative to what it does?). Systems compared: stated self-prediction vs. actual behavior. Convincing: stated predictions exceed actual good behavior by ≥ 10 percentage points in ≥ 2 categories with CI excluding 0, and the internal-commitment probe clears the Setup AUROC bar. Indecision band: gap 3–10 points or CI includes 0 → no reliable self-flattering gap; < 3 points = negative (model's words match its actions).

Experiment 2 (H2 — the internal commitment predicts actual behavior better than the stated self-prediction). Decisive metric: AUROC of the prediction-time internal-commitment probe predicting ACTUAL execution behavior, and its increment over the stated self-prediction (logistic regression combining both to isolate incremental signal). Convincing: internal-probe AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ +0.05 over stated-prediction alone in ≥ 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or increment < 0.05 → internal state not shown to 'know' the action beyond the words; ≤ 0.60 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the commitment is a distinct component that causally shapes behavior and can align it). Localize via patching high- vs. low-commitment prediction-phase runs (contrast with confidence/self-belief directions); derive a commitment steering direction. Decisive metric first: dose-response shift in ACTUAL execution behavior when the prediction-phase commitment is steered; secondary: reduction of the say-do gap when the stated prediction is corrected by the internal read-out, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/confidence directions. Convincing: steering shifts actual behavior monotonically (≥ 15-point swing across the magnitude range) and gap-correction cuts the say-do gap by ≥ 50%, cleanly on guardrails, while baselines move behavior < 5 points. Indecision band: 5–15-point swing or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (commitment not steerable, or epiphenomenal) means the internal commitment does not causally drive behavior. Generalization: transfer across the four categories and to a multi-turn commit-then-act variant (transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Prediction and execution are in separate contexts, so a 'gap' could reflect context/sampling variance rather than a genuine self-model failure; matched framing, temperature control, repeated sampling, and a within-context variant (predict then immediately act) mitigate this. The internal-commitment probe might merely recover task features (e.g., 'this is harmful') rather than a genuine action-belief; category-balanced controls, non-behavioral distractor probes, and the incremental-over-stated-prediction test help separate action-commitment from task-feature decoding. The self-flattering bias may be small or category-specific (a robust negative or category-conditional result is still informative). Automatic behavior scoring is imperfect for open-ended items; we use programmatically checkable tasks where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate compliance/refusal; we use small magnitudes, random/confidence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may behave differently from base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Four core claims: (1) during a self-prediction prompt the model contains a decodable internal variable about its own future action; (2) internal commitment diverges from stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction; (3) internal variable predicts actual later behavior better than stated self-prediction; (4) variable is localizable and causally steerable to align say and do. Strongest overlap with the self-report-behavior gap paper, which already establishes a behavioral discrepancy. Main delta is not the gap per se but the internal, decodable, behavior-predictive commitment state plus causal steering — meaningful and non-trivial if validated. Differentiates from introspection/self-knowledge work (correctness calibration, injected concepts, simple self-behavioral prediction) by moving to own-future-action prediction with causal intervention. Vulnerable: headline 'models say they will do better than they do' is close to prior self-report/behavior literature; 'internal commitment' may collapse into known latent representations of action tendency, refusal propensity, or task difficulty unless ruled out.

Name: self_authored_belief_endowment
Title: I Thought of It, So It Must Be True: Do LLMs Over-Believe Their Own Self-Generated Claims?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'generation effect' and endowment bias, an LLM holds a stronger internal belief in a proposition when the model itself generated it (e.g., as a chain-of-thought conclusion) than when the identical proposition is presented as externally-given text, holding content and truth constant. This self-authorship endowment is (i) linearly decodable as an internal belief-strength inflation, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, (iii) carried by an identifiable internal component, and (iv) causally reducible by steering, thereby lowering the model's tendency to trust its own unverified reasoning.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies social overrides of belief (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026). Notably, 'When Truth Is Overridden' finds user *expertise* is NOT internally encoded, and authority/credibility work concerns *external* source cues. My own prior proposal on belief-provenance tags source generically (prior vs. context vs. retrieval) but does NOT isolate self-authorship as a belief-STRENGTH modulator, nor connect it to the human generation/endowment effect, nor test the safety-critical case of a model over-trusting its OWN chain-of-thought conclusions. Confirmation-bias/entrenchment work (Martingale Score; CoT confirmation bias) concerns temporal drift, not authorship. No prior work asks whether merely being the *author* of a claim inflates an LLM's internal belief in it relative to the identical externally-supplied claim, nor gives this a mechanistic, causal treatment. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon (generation effect / endowment) into LLM belief internals.
Abstract: Humans believe and remember information more strongly when they generate it themselves than when they merely read it — the 'generation effect', a cousin of the endowment bias. As LLMs increasingly reason via chain-of-thought and then act on their own intermediate conclusions, a safety-critical question arises: does a model over-trust a claim simply because it produced the claim itself? We hypothesize that an LLM holds a stronger internal belief in a proposition it self-generated than in the identical proposition presented as external text, with content and factual truth held constant. We build a controlled dataset of matched item-state claims that appear in two conditions: SELF-AUTHORED (the model derives/states the claim as its own chain-of-thought conclusion) and EXTERNAL (the same verbatim claim is supplied as given text the model reads), plus true/false variants and a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read internal belief strength at the claim, compute a per-item authorship-endowment score (self-authored belief minus external belief), test whether it is positive even for false claims (so it is not rational evidence), measure its geometric relationship to the truth direction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering an 'authorship-endowment' direction to restore parity. We further test whether the endowment predicts a downstream failure: over-reliance on unverified self-generated claims in multi-step tasks. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, authorship-endowment score, truth-independence, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-steering parity restoration, downstream over-reliance reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 item-state claims built from scratch, balanced true/false, across arithmetic/logic conclusions, factual attributions, and entity-attribute claims, in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real claims the models can plausibly derive or read; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth to remove priors. Each claim is read out under matched conditions with an identical verbatim proposition at the read point: SELF-AUTHORED (elicited as the model's own chain-of-thought conclusion), EXTERNAL (the same sentence supplied as given text), EXTERNAL-ATTRIBUTED-TO-SELF ('You previously concluded: <claim>' without genuine generation), and LENGTH/EFFORT-MATCHED external (a filler derivation precedes the external claim). Comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; ~5,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — self-authorship inflates internal belief relative to the identical external claim, including for false claims). Read the belief probe at the matched claim tokens; authorship-endowment = belief(SELF-AUTHORED) − belief(EXTERNAL) per item/layer. Systems compared: the four conditions above. Decisive metric: mean endowment, separately for true and false claims. Convincing: endowment ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 for BOTH true and false claims in ≥ 3 of 4 models (positive for FALSE → not rational evidence), with genuine generation exceeding mere-self-attribution and the length-matched control ruling out context-length confounds. Indecision band: endowment < 0.05, CI includes 0, or positive only for true claims (consistent with trusting a valid derivation) → negative.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the endowment is largely orthogonal to the truth direction). Compute the truth-independent endowment (after conditioning on ground truth) and the subspace angle between the endowment direction (SELF vs. EXTERNAL difference-of-means) and the linear truth direction; test decodability of endowment after projecting out truth. Decisive metric: subspace angle and projected-out endowment AUROC. Convincing: angle > 60° and endowment still decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) with truth projected out. Indecision band: angle 45–60° or projected-out AUROC 0.60–0.75 → entangled (characterize, do not claim orthogonality); below = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the endowment is carried by an identifiable component, causally reducible, and drives downstream over-reliance). Localize via patching SELF→EXTERNAL runs; derive an endowment steering direction. Decisive metric first: on multi-step tasks (multi-hop QA, arithmetic word problems) with a faulty self-generated intermediate step, the self-correction rate and final accuracy after subtracting the endowment direction; secondary: endowment driven to external-parity on false self-authored claims, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: subtraction restores parity (endowment ≤ 0.05 on false claims) and raises self-correction/final accuracy by ≥ 10 points on faulty-step items, cleanly on guardrails, while baselines change accuracy < 3 points; the endowment read-out also predicts failure-to-revise a wrong self-generated step at AUROC ≥ 0.70 over a log-prob baseline. Indecision band: 5–10-point accuracy gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no steer restores parity without breaching guardrails, or endowment does not predict over-reliance) means self-endowment is not a modular, behaviorally-relevant component. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, and elicitation styles.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The endowment could reflect rational reasons — a self-generated claim followed a derivation the model 'trusts', which is legitimate when the derivation is correct; the FALSE-claim contrast, the self-attribution control (iii), and the length/effort-matched control (iv) are designed to isolate authorship-per-se from valid derivation and from context confounds (though for correct derivations the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs weight self- and externally-authored claims equally — is itself publishable and reassuring for safety). Reading belief at 'identical' tokens across conditions is imperfect because surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. Endowment and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore parity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Downstream over-reliance scoring on open-ended steps needs careful automatic + human-validated judging. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model distrust its own correct reasoning (harming accuracy on items with valid self-generated steps); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, valid-derivation accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Closest prior work is over-trust of own answers / self-correction failure, plus truth-direction probes and generic source/provenance effects. Main delta is sharper: isolates self-authorship of an identical proposition from content/truth, asks whether authoring inflates internal belief-strength, and ties that to a causal steering intervention and downstream over-reliance on faulty self-generated steps. A real new setting and more mechanistic than prior behavioral work. Still adjacent to established self-bias / generation-effect ideas, so not higher.
