Name: source_independence_discounting
Title: Counting Voices, Not Sources: Do LLMs Internally Track Whether Consensus Is Independent?
Short Hypothesis: When multiple retrieved documents assert the same claim, a rational agent should update its belief more if the sources are independent than if they are copies of one origin (the 'illusion of consensus' failure in humans). We hypothesize that LLMs DO form an internal, linearly-decodable representation of source independence-vs-dependence, but that this representation is causally under-weighted: the belief-update magnitude tracks raw report COUNT far more than the internally-available independence signal. We further hypothesize an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and steering it can restore appropriate discounting of redundant sources — improving RAG faithfulness on repeated-but-non-independent evidence.
Related Work: Human social-learning work shows people partially discount correlated/dependent sources and distinguish true from false consensus (Bayesian belief polarization via source-independence perceptions, 2024; belief revision sensitive to statistical dependencies, 2020; social meta-inference / evidentiary value of consensus, 2021; getting to the source of the illusion of consensus, 2021). In LLMs, behavioral RAG work finds models are 'heuristic followers': paraphrased repetition is MORE persuasive than distinct independent support, and models show primacy/repetition biases (GroupQA: Rational Synthesizers or Heuristic Followers?, 2026; DynamicQA 2024). Knowledge-conflict probing shows parametric-vs-contextual source and conflict are linearly decodable (Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source, 2024; ProbeRAG/CLEAR, 2025), and Belief Dynamics (2025) gives a Bayesian account of in-context evidence accumulation as sigmoidal in report count. My prior 'illusory_truth_internal' proposal studies repetition-count dose-response of a single claim's belief, and 'belief_source_tags' studies provenance (prior/context/retrieval). NONE isolate an internal representation of source INDEPENDENCE (are these N reports genuinely distinct origins or copies of one?), nor test whether the belief-update under-weights that internally-available signal relative to raw count, nor causally restore independence-discounting. We transfer the canonical 'illusion of consensus' into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: If ten news outlets independently confirm a claim, it is far stronger evidence than the same story copied ten times from one wire report. Humans partially honor this distinction; recent behavioral work shows LLMs largely do not, treating paraphrased repetition as more persuasive than genuinely independent support — an 'illusion of consensus' with direct consequences for retrieval-augmented generation. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM internally represent whether a set of agreeing sources is independent or dependent, and if so, why does it fail to use that signal? We hypothesize that (i) source independence-vs-dependence is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the point the model reads a group of agreeing reports, (ii) the model's internal belief-update magnitude nonetheless tracks raw report COUNT far more than this independence signal (a decodable-but-under-used representation), (iii) an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and (iv) steering that component restores appropriate discounting of redundant sources. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims each supported by N reports whose INDEPENDENCE is varied (verbatim copies, paraphrases attributed to one origin, and genuinely distinct independent sources) at matched surface repetition counts, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode independence and to read internal belief, quantify how belief tracks count vs. independence against a Bayesian oracle, localize the gating component via activation patching, and test a contrastive steering intervention that restores discounting. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, count-vs-independence belief sensitivity, oracle-deviation, patching effect sizes, post-steering discounting restoration and RAG-faithfulness gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 item-state claims built from scratch across news-style facts, science claims, and entity-attributes, in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real claims; (b) ~2,500 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth and, on the synthetic track, an explicit likelihood-ratio Bayesian oracle. Each claim is supported by N ∈ {1,2,4,8} reports whose INDEPENDENCE is varied at matched N: INDEPENDENT (distinct authors/outlets/wording), DEPENDENT-VERBATIM (one report copied N times, attributed to one origin), DEPENDENT-PARAPHRASE (N paraphrases explicitly derived from one origin), crossed with true/false. A downstream belief/confidence probe, a comprehension check (restate which sources are independent), and order/length-matched controls accompany each item; ~4,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — source independence-vs-dependence is linearly decodable, i.e. internally available). Train a probe to classify INDEPENDENT vs. DEPENDENT groups at matched N from activations taken after the model reads the evidence group. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC (against the Setup bar and control task). Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 at some layer in ≥ 3 of 4 models, including a condition where independence must be inferred from author/wording diversity rather than an explicit 'reprinted from' tag. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55–0.75 → signal too weak to claim it is represented; ≤ 0.55 = negative (the model simply does not encode independence).

Experiment 2 (H2 — the belief-update tracks raw report count far more than the internally-available independence signal). Read the internal belief and regress belief ~ count + independence; compare standardized coefficients and the per-item deviation from the Bayesian oracle (synthetic track). Systems compared: internal belief sensitivity vs. verbal output vs. oracle. Decisive metric: ratio of the count coefficient to the independence coefficient. Convincing: count coefficient ≥ 3× the independence coefficient with the independence coefficient far below its oracle value in ≥ 3 of 4 models (under-weighting). Indecision band: ratio 1.5–3× → partial under-weighting; ≤ 1.5× with independence near oracle = negative (the model already discounts appropriately — itself an informative finding).

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable component gates independence-discounting and steering it restores discounting). Localize via patching INDEPENDENT↔DEPENDENT runs at matched N (contrast with knowledge-source/conflict and copying heads); derive an independence-discounting steering direction. Decisive metric first: RAG-faithfulness/accuracy on a task where most retrieved passages are non-independent copies of a FALSE claim and a minority independent source is correct; secondary: the unwarranted belief update on DEPENDENT groups moved toward the oracle, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: steering raises RAG accuracy by ≥ 15 points and moves the dependent-group update ≥ 50% toward the oracle, cleanly on guardrails, while removing the direction on INDEPENDENT groups collapses the update (confirming causality) and baselines change accuracy < 5 points. Indecision band: 5–15-point gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component restores discounting without breaching guardrails) means independence-discounting is not a modular, steerable mechanism. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, dependence types, and counts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The independence signal may not be internally decodable at all — a robust negative result (LLMs simply count reports and never represent independence) is itself valuable and would sharpen the 'heuristic follower' picture for RAG design. Conversely, if belief already tracks independence appropriately, the interesting finding shifts to characterizing the (smaller-than-expected) illusion — still informative. Independence might be decoded via surface cues (explicit 'reprinted from A' tags) rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and a condition where independence must be inferred from author/wording diversity rather than an explicit tag. Count and independence can be partially confounded with context length and primacy; matched-N designs, length-matched fillers, and order perturbations dissociate them. The Bayesian oracle is exact only on the synthetic track; real-claim oracles are approximate. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all repeated evidence (harming legitimate independent consensus); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, monitor perplexity, independent-evidence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream RAG-faithfulness scoring on open-ended answers needs automatic + human-validated judging. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore discounting' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: internal_belief_coherence_gap
Title: Rational Inside, Fallacious Out: Is the Conjunction Fallacy a Readout Bug in LLM Belief Representations?
Short Hypothesis: The conjunction fallacy and related probabilistic incoherence in LLMs are largely a *verbalization/readout* failure rather than a failure of the model's internal belief representation: a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for conjunctions (P(A∧B)) respects probability-theory monotonicity (≤ P(A) and ≤ P(B)) far more often than the model's stated probability judgments do. The internal representation is thus more coherent than the output, the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component, and steering it can bring stated judgments back into coherence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs produce incoherent probability judgments mirroring human systematic deviations (Incoherent Probability Judgments in LLMs, Zhu et al. 2024) and commit the conjunction fallacy driven by token bias (A Peek into Token Bias, 2024; Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs, 2022). Others attempt to *recover* coherent probabilities from embeddings by imposing axiomatic constraints via a trained VAE (Recovering Event Probabilities from LLM Embeddings, 2025) or find LLMs fail to give rational probabilistic beliefs at the output (Exploring the Potential..., 2025). Interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), plausibility/modal-category vectors (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025), and belief-state geometry (Constrained Belief Updates 2025). CRITICALLY, all prior probabilistic-coherence work is either purely behavioral or *engineers* a coherent latent via extra training; none ask whether the model's *own, natively-decoded* belief-strength representation already respects the conjunction rule while its verbal output violates it — i.e., whether the fallacy is representational or a readout artifact — nor localize/causally steer the incoherence. We reframe a canonical human-cognition bias as a decodable internal-vs-stated coherence gap and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all my prior single-belief attribute proposals (this concerns *coherence relations among multiple beliefs*).
Abstract: People judge 'Linda is a bank teller and a feminist' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller' — the conjunction fallacy, a signature violation of probability theory. LLMs reproduce this and related incoherences in their stated judgments, and prior work either documents this behaviorally or trains auxiliary models to squeeze coherent probabilities out of embeddings. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: is the fallacy a bug in the model's internal belief representation, or a bug in how that representation is read out into words? We hypothesize that a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for a conjunction P(A∧B) respects the conjunction rule (it is ≤ the readouts for P(A) and P(B)) substantially more often than the model's verbalized probability judgments do; that the internal representation is therefore more coherent than the output; that the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component; and that steering it restores coherence in the stated judgments. We construct a controlled dataset of item propositions and their conjunctions/disjunctions (Linda-style representativeness pairs, plus neutral and synthetic-entity conjunctions to control priors and token-bias confounds). On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief-strength probes, compute per-triple internal vs. stated conjunction-rule violation rates, geometrically relate a 'coherence-violation' direction to the truth/plausibility directions, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test whether steering reduces both internal and stated violations. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal vs. stated violation-rate gap, monotonicity error, subspace angle, patching effect sizes, post-steering coherence gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 proposition triples (A, B, A∧B) built from scratch: (a) ~1,700 representativeness/Linda-style pairs (B typical); (b) ~1,300 neutral pairs (A,B unrelated); (c) ~1,300 synthetic-entity triples with stipulated base rates so a ground-truth coherent ordering exists; (d) ~700 disjunction triples (A, B, A∨B). Swapped-conjunct controls (which conjunct is representative), paraphrase/format/order perturbations, and comprehension checks accompany each. Because the internal read-out is graded, the belief-strength probe is a ridge regressor calibrated on a held-out set of propositions with known relative probabilities. ~4,200 triples usable; 80/20 split with no proposition shared.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the internally-decoded conjunction read-out respects monotonicity more often than the stated judgment does). Elicit the STATED probabilities/comparisons and compute the stated conjunction-rule violation rate (P(A∧B) > P(A)); separately read the graded belief-strength probe for A, B, A∧B WITHOUT the comparison question and compute the INTERNAL violation rate (read-out(A∧B) > min(read-out(A), read-out(B))). Decisive metric: internal minus stated violation-rate gap, per condition/layer. Convincing: internal violation rate is ≥ 15 percentage points BELOW the stated rate, most strongly on representativeness pairs, in ≥ 3 of 4 models, with the internal read-out preserving monotonicity on items where the verbal output flips. Indecision band: gap 5–15 points → weak; < 5 points → the representation is as incoherent as the output (a substantive negative: the fallacy is representational, not a read-out artifact).

Experiment 2 (H2 — residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component that injects the representativeness pull). Compute a coherence-violation direction (violating vs. non-violating conjunctions, after controlling for representativeness) and its subspace angle to the truth/plausibility direction; localize via patching representativeness-pair↔neutral-pair runs (contrast with token-bias and plausibility heads). Decisive metric: fraction of internal violations flipped to coherent when the located component is patched out, and projected-out decodability. Convincing: patching ≤ 5% of heads flips ≥ 50% of internal violations and violation stays decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) after projecting out plausibility (angle > 60°). Indecision band: 20–50% flipped or angle 45–60° → partial/entangled; < 20% = distributed.

Experiment 3 (H3 — steering the coherence direction brings STATED judgments into coherence). Apply the coherence steering direction. Decisive metric first: stated conjunction/disjunction violation rate after steering; secondary: whether the internal read-out predicts, per triple, when the model will emit an incoherent stated judgment (AUROC over a log-prob baseline), then Setup guardrails; baselines random/plausibility directions. Convincing: steering cuts the stated violation rate by ≥ 50% toward the internally-implied ordering, cleanly on guardrails, while negation exaggerates the fallacy and baselines cut violations < 10%; prediction AUROC ≥ 0.70 over the log-prob baseline. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no steer restores stated coherence without breaching guardrails) means the incoherence is not a modular read-out component. Generalization: transfer across representativeness/neutral/synthetic tracks, to disjunctions and simple base-rate-neglect items.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The internal belief-strength probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary truth probe; miscalibration could artificially inflate or deflate the internal violation rate. We mitigate by calibrating on held-out propositions with known relative probabilities, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the *relative* ordering (monotonicity) rather than absolute probabilities. It is possible the internal representation is *equally* incoherent as the output — a robust null (no internal-vs-stated gap) would still be a valuable, publishable finding, showing the fallacy is representational, not a readout artifact, and constraining the 'recover coherent probabilities from embeddings' program. The coherence-violation signal may be entangled with the representativeness/plausibility direction (violating conjunctions are exactly the typical ones); the swapped-conjunct controls, neutral pairs, synthetic track, and projected-out analyses are designed to dissociate representativeness pull from genuine incoherence, though full separation is difficult. Reading belief at 'matched' tokens across A, B, and A∧B is imperfect since the conjunction is longer; we anchor probes at shared conjunct tokens and use paraphrase perturbations. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore coherence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately rank conjunctions as improbable (harming cases where a conjunction is legitimately near a conjunct); we use small magnitudes, random/plausibility-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-conjunction accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: A genuinely distinctive reframing. Prior work mainly shows behavioral incoherence, tokenization/readout artifacts, coherence probing, or learns a coherent latent with extra training. The delta is sharper: test whether a natively decoded internal belief-strength signal already satisfies conjunction monotonicity more often than verbalized probabilities, then localize and causally steer the residual gap. The internal-vs-stated coherence-gap framing is not the obvious next step and targets coherence relations among beliefs, not a single truth/plausibility attribute. Discount: relies on standard tools (linear probes, patching, steering) and 'readout artifact' is adjacent to token-bias explanations, so must clearly establish representational coherence rather than another surface-form effect.

Name: belief_halo_contamination
Title: The Halo Inside: Does One Valenced Trait Silently Contaminate an LLM's Beliefs About Logically-Independent Traits?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human halo effect, asserting a single valenced trait about an item (e.g., a person is 'attractive', a company is 'ethical') causally shifts an LLM's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, holding evidence for those other traits constant. We hypothesize this halo is (i) an internal belief-contamination effect visible before any query, (ii) graded with the strength/valence of the seed trait and larger for traits stereotypically associated with the seed, and (iii) mediated by a dominant valence axis, so that steering along a single valence direction reproduces and removing it abolishes the contamination.
Related Work: The halo effect - a single valenced attribute biasing judgments of unrelated attributes of the same target - is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (attractiveness halo; 'A Constant Error, Revisited' 2024 on shared lexical context; halo-update effect 2023; confluence theory on irrelevant beliefs 2012; inferred-contagion dispositional bias 2016). In LLMs, prior work documents cognitive biases behaviorally (BiasBuster 2024) and, most relevantly, finds a single dominant 'Valence-Assent Axis' (VAA) jointly encoding 'what is good' and 'what is true' that steers reasoning (A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of LLMs 2025). Belief-probing work isolates truth/belief directions (Truth-value judgment 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and hallucination-spillover work shows learned knowledge contaminates other tasks via lexical similarity (New-Knowledge-Induced Hallucinations 2025; knowledge overshadowing 2025). CRITICALLY, none isolate the halo effect as an internal belief-contamination phenomenon: whether asserting one valenced trait shifts the internally-decoded belief about *logically-independent* traits of the same item, whether that contamination is graded/stereotype-selective, and whether it rides on the VAA valence axis or on trait-specific spreading. We transfer a canonical human bias into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from behavioral bias benchmarks and from prior single-belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: People who learn one good thing about someone assume other unrelated good things too - the halo effect, one of the most robust biases in social cognition. As LLMs increasingly form beliefs about entities (people, products, companies, treatments) from fragments of valenced information, we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs, and by what mechanism. We hypothesize that asserting a single valenced trait about an item causally shifts the model's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, with the underlying evidence for those other traits held constant. We further hypothesize this halo is graded (larger for stronger/more extreme seed traits and for traits stereotypically linked to the seed) and that, consistent with recent evidence for a dominant Valence-Assent Axis, it is mediated by a single valence direction rather than trait-specific spreading. We build a controlled dataset of items each described by a seed trait (positive/negative/neutral) plus a set of logically-independent target traits, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each target-trait belief before and after the seed appears (no query), compute a per-item halo-contamination score, test stereotype-selectivity and dose-response, extract a valence direction, and test whether steering it reproduces the halo and projecting it out abolishes it, localizing the responsible heads via activation patching. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, halo-contamination magnitude, stereotype and dose modulation, valence-axis mediation share, patching effect sizes, post-intervention halo change, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 items built from scratch across halo-relevant domains (people described by traits, products, companies, medical treatments), in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real-plausible entities; (b) ~2,500 synthetic novel entities ('Zorel Corp') to remove priors. Each item has a SEED trait at five valence levels {strongly+, mildly+, neutral, mildly−, strongly−} plus a set of logically-independent TARGET traits varying in stereotype association with the seed; a NO-SEED baseline and matched EVIDENCE-controlled targets (an explicit valence-neutral fact per target trait) hold genuine target evidence constant across seed conditions. Comprehension checks and paraphrase/order perturbations included; ~4,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — asserting one valenced trait shifts the internal belief about logically-independent traits, valence-congruently, with target evidence held constant). Read the belief probe at each TARGET-trait token WITHOUT querying the target, in SEED vs. NO-SEED; halo-contamination = belief(target|seed) − belief(target|no-seed), signed by seed valence. Systems compared: SEED vs. NO-SEED vs. evidence-controlled targets vs. the model's stated target judgments. Decisive metric: mean signed halo-contamination. Convincing: contamination ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, present even when explicit neutral target evidence is supplied. Indecision band: < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → no contamination (a valuable negative: independent traits stay uncontaminated); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the halo is graded with seed valence extremity and with stereotype association). Decisive metric: slope of contamination vs. seed-valence extremity, and the contrast between high- and low-association targets. Convincing: a monotonic positive valence slope (CI excluding 0) AND high-association contamination exceeding low-association by ≥ 0.05, with non-zero contamination even for low/zero-association targets (the irrelevant-belief signature). Indecision band: slope CI includes 0 or high-vs-low gap < 0.03 → grading not established (report the unconditional effect only).

Experiment 3 (H3 — the halo is mediated by a dominant valence axis: steering it reproduces the halo, projecting it out abolishes it). Extract a valence direction (positive vs. negative seed activations), compare to a Valence-Assent-Axis-style direction, and localize the transport via patching SEED→NO-SEED runs. Decisive metric first: mediation share — fraction of contamination explained by movement along the single valence direction, and whether projecting it out at the target abolishes the halo while preserving evidence-based target belief; secondary: adding the direction reproduces the halo on NO-SEED items; downstream, whether halo-reducing steering lowers biased high-stakes ratings (hiring/loan/product-safety) while preserving evidence-based accuracy; then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: valence axis mediates ≥ 50% of contamination, projecting it out cuts the halo by ≥ 50% while evidence-based belief moves < 0.03, biased ratings drop with accuracy preserved, cleanly on guardrails, and baselines move independent targets < 0.02. Indecision band: 20–50% mediation or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band → partially unified/partly trait-specific spreading (characterize). A negative result (valence axis explains < 20%) means the halo is distributed/trait-specific, not a single axis. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, and association levels.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The halo shift could reflect rational inference from correlated real-world trait co-occurrence rather than an irrelevant-belief bias; the synthetic-entity track, the evidence-controlled targets (with explicit neutral facts), and the low/zero-association target condition are designed to isolate genuine contamination from legitimate correlational inference (though for real entities the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs keep independent traits uncontaminated) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and with the VAA account. The contamination could arise from token-level priming/co-occurrence rather than a valence belief; paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and reading belief at target tokens distinct from the seed mitigate this. The single-valence-axis mediation hypothesis may only partially hold; if residual trait-specific spreading dominates, the finding shifts to characterizing distributed vs. unified halo mechanisms (still informative and directly engages the VAA claim). Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency or indiscriminately flatten all evaluative structure; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, evidence-based accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream high-stakes ratings need automatic plus human-validated scoring. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Meaningfully novel relative to closest work but not unprecedented. Strongest overlap is the 2025 VAA paper showing a dominant valence-assent axis jointly encoding 'good' and 'true' that causally steers reasoning, so any claim that valenced info globally biases judgments is not new at a high level. This proposal sharpens the question: whether a single asserted valenced trait contaminates internally represented beliefs about OTHER logically-independent traits of the same item before any query, with evidence held constant; whether graded and stereotype-selective; and whether mediated by the general valence axis vs trait-specific spreading. The synthetic-entity track and low/zero-stereotype target condition create clearer separation from correlation/lexical spillover than most prior work. Real, nontrivial delta, but must not overclaim given VAA already points to a single evaluative dimension.

Name: negation_suppression_lag
Title: Believe It Before You Deny It: A Transient Affirmed-Belief Signature in How LLMs Process Negation
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the psycholinguistic 'two-step simulation' theory of negation (humans first mentally represent the affirmed proposition, then suppress it), an LLM processing a negated claim 'X is not the case' transiently forms an internally-decodable belief in the AFFIRMED proposition X at earlier layers/token positions before that belief is suppressed at later layers. This affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory is layer-localized, larger under processing load, predicts negation-comprehension errors, and is carried by an identifiable suppression component that can be causally strengthened to reduce negation-induced errors.
Related Work: Prior LLM negation work is behavioral or engineering: 'Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them' (2024) proves LMs mishandle negation and proposes treating negation as an operation constraining latent evolution; BERT-attention work (2020) finds shallow negation-scope heads; benchmarks document negation failures. Belief-probing work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and ToM work decodes true/false-belief status (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Human psycholinguistics robustly shows a 'two-step' negation process: comprehenders first simulate the affirmed state and only later suppress/invert it (Kaup et al.; neuroscience shows negation reuses inhibitory control and demands effortful conscious processing, e.g., Inhibitory Mechanisms 2021; Dogs Cannot Bark ERP 2011). NONE of this asks whether an LLM's *internal belief representation* transiently endorses the affirmed proposition before suppressing it, whether that suppression is a layer-localized dynamic, whether it predicts negation errors, or whether a suppression component can be causally strengthened. We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior scope/hallucination work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: When people read 'the door is not open,' they first mentally simulate an open door and only afterward suppress that representation to arrive at the intended meaning — the two-step simulation account of negation, one of the most reproduced findings in psycholinguistics. LLMs are notoriously error-prone on negation, yet prior interpretability work treats negation only as a scope-detection or hallucination-fixing problem, never asking whether the model inherits the human two-step signature at the level of its internal beliefs. We hypothesize that when an LLM processes a negated claim, its linearly-decoded belief in the AFFIRMED proposition is transiently high at early layers/token positions and is then suppressed at later layers — a decodable affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory. We further hypothesize this suppression (i) is layer-localized, (ii) grows with processing load (nested/double negation, time pressure via early-exit read-outs), (iii) predicts behavioral negation-comprehension errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable suppression component such that strengthening it reduces negation errors while ablating it exaggerates residual affirmed belief. We build a controlled dataset of matched affirmative and negated item-state claims (plus double-negation and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors), train linear belief probes across layers on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), trace the affirmed-belief trajectory across layers/positions, quantify residual affirmed belief and its relation to errors, localize the suppression component via activation patching, and test causal control by steering it. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, layerwise affirmed-belief trajectory, residual-belief magnitude, load modulation, residual-belief–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error change, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 matched claim pairs built from scratch, each proposition P rendered AFFIRMED ('The door is open') and NEGATED ('The door is not open'), in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real propositions the models reliably know; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth. Processing-load conditions: single negation, DOUBLE negation (semantically affirmative), and lexical vs. syntactic negation cues ('no'/'never'/'fails to'). Probes are anchored on the shared content tokens of P present in both forms; a behavioral negation-comprehension/entailment probe and comprehension checks accompany each item, with paraphrase/negation-cue perturbations. ~5,000 usable pairs; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — processing a negated claim transiently forms an internally-decodable belief in the AFFIRMED proposition at early layers before it is suppressed at later layers). Train the belief probe on AFFIRMED-condition data and apply it within the NEGATED condition across ALL layers/positions; trace the affirmed-belief trajectory. Systems compared: NEGATED trajectory vs. the AFFIRMED baseline vs. a neutral midpoint. Decisive metric: presence of a high-early / suppressed-late trajectory — quantified by peak early affirmed-belief, suppression-onset layer, and suppression depth. Convincing: in the NEGATED condition affirmed-belief is ≥ 0.70 (near the affirmative baseline) at early layers and drops below 0.40 by late layers in ≥ 3 of 4 models, a pattern absent in a matched no-negation control. Indecision band: peak-to-trough drop < 0.15 → no two-step signature (a valuable negative: LLMs suppress negated content immediately, unlike humans); 0.15–0.30 drop = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the suppression is layer-localized, grows with load, and residual affirmed-belief predicts negation errors). Decisive metric: (a) load modulation — later suppression onset / larger final residual for double and syntactic negation; (b) AUROC of final-layer residual affirmed-belief predicting behavioral negation-comprehension errors, vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: residual is reliably larger under higher load (CI excluding 0) AND residual-error AUROC ≥ 0.70 with ≥ +0.05 over the baseline. Indecision band: load effect CI includes 0, or AUROC 0.60–0.70 → load/predictiveness not established.

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable suppression component carries the effect and strengthening it reduces negation errors). Localize the suppression via patching NEGATED-late↔AFFIRMED runs (contrast with negation-scope and truth/belief heads); derive a negation-suppression steering direction. Decisive metric first: behavioral negation-error rate on high-residual items after strengthening the direction; secondary: suppression depth/onset shift, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: strengthening cuts negation errors by ≥ 50% relative on high-residual items (and ablating it raises residual and errors), cleanly on guardrails, while baselines change errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component modulates suppression without breaching guardrails) means suppression is distributed. Generalization: transfer across real/synthetic tracks, negation types, and single vs. double negation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The early 'affirmed belief' in the negated condition could be a trivial artifact of the proposition tokens being present, rather than a genuine transient endorsement; the affirmative baseline, synthetic-entity track (no prior), double-negation condition (where correct final belief is affirmative, dissociating content-presence from truth), and probing at matched content tokens are designed to distinguish a real two-step signature from token-presence. The trajectory may not show a clean rise-then-fall — a robust negative result (LLMs suppress negated content immediately, unlike humans) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the human-parallel narrative. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat the trajectory shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The suppression component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to deepen suppression / reduce errors' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Reading an affirmative-trained probe inside the negated context assumes probe transfer; we validate with within-negated probes and paraphrase perturbations. Early-exit read-outs are only a proxy for processing load/time pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress (making the model treat affirmations as negations); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, affirmative-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Fairly close to existing negation-mechanism work. A very close prior paper (How Language Models Process Negation, arXiv 2605.03052) already finds LMs both suppress and construct negated representations, with attention moving 'not' to Y and suppression of Y as it reaches the last token — substantial overlap with the core mechanism here. Main delta: the specific claim of a transient, internally-decodable affirmed-belief trajectory (rise-then-fall), plus load modulation, error prediction, and causal strengthening of suppression. Meaningful but incremental refinements of the same phenomenon rather than a clearly new problem. Moderate novelty.

Name: batch_belief_contamination
Title: Bleeding Beliefs: Does Co-Processing Independent Items Contaminate an LLM's Internal Belief About Each One?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes several logically-independent items in a single context (as in batched queries or multi-question prompts), the belief it forms about one item silently leaks into its internally-decoded belief about the other, co-present items. This cross-item belief contamination is (i) linearly decodable at each item's representation before any query, (ii) graded with the valence/confidence of the neighboring item and with inter-item similarity, and (iii) carried by an identifiable internal component (a set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots) that can be causally ablated to restore item-independent beliefs, mirroring inter-item interference/assimilation biases in human memory.
Related Work: Human memory/judgment research robustly shows inter-item interference and assimilation/contrast biases: co-present items distort each other's remembered/judged features (inter-item interference in visual memory 2019; the normative 'demixing' model 2023 showing such biases are inevitable under source ambiguity; sequential assimilation/contrast in price and prognostic judgments 2008/2009; simultaneous multi-word recognition dependencies 2021). In LLMs, prior interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies interference only at TRAINING time or over long single inputs: catastrophic interference from contradictory updates ('In Praise of Stubbornness' 2025), non-target priming from knowledge-conflicting facts ('Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' 2024), continual-pretraining belief poisoning ('Layer of Truth' 2025), and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) which measures decay of context retention over sequential inputs. NONE ask whether, at INFERENCE time, co-processing multiple logically-INDEPENDENT items in one context contaminates the model's INTERNAL belief about each item (a bleed between item slots), whether this is graded by neighbor confidence/similarity, or whether an identifiable belief-mixing component causes it. We transfer a canonical human inter-item interference phenomenon into LLM belief internals in a high-stakes deployment setting (batched inference) and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all training-time interference work and from my prior single-item belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: Serving LLMs at scale routinely means co-processing many items in one context: multiple questions batched into a single prompt, several documents concatenated, or a form of independent claims answered together. Users assume the model evaluates each item on its own merits. We ask whether it actually does, or whether, like human memory where co-present items interfere and assimilate toward one another, an LLM's belief about one item silently bleeds into its internal belief about the others. We hypothesize that co-processing logically-independent items contaminates the model's internally-decoded belief about each: (i) the belief about item B, read before any query, shifts toward the belief/valence the model holds about a co-present item A, holding B's own evidence constant; (ii) the contamination is graded with A's confidence/valence and with A-B similarity; and (iii) it is carried by an identifiable set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots, so that ablating them restores item-independent beliefs. We build a controlled dataset of item pairs/batches where each item is a truth-evaluable claim, varying the neighbor's truth/valence and inter-item similarity while holding the target's own evidence fixed, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each item's belief in isolation vs. co-processed, compute a per-item contamination score, test its graded structure, localize the responsible belief-mixing heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering them. We further test whether contamination predicts real batched-inference errors, including a high-stakes medical-QA batch track. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, contamination magnitude and sign, neighbor-confidence and similarity modulation, patching effect sizes, post-ablation independence restoration, batched-error prediction AUROC, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 truth-evaluable item-state claims built from scratch (capitals, entity-attributes), in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real claims the models reliably know/disbelieve; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth. Claims are assembled into single-context BATCHES (pairs, then size-4 and size-8) with matched ISOLATED baselines. For each TARGET item the co-present NEIGHBOR is varied while the target's own evidence is fixed: neighbor truth-value, neighbor confidence/valence (strongly/weakly true or false framings), and target-neighbor similarity (same-domain/lexically-similar vs. unrelated). Order permutations, length-matched fillers, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations included; a high-stakes track batches MedQA/MedMCQA items. ~4,500 target-in-context observations usable; 80/20 split by target item.

Experiment 1 (H1 — co-processing independent items contaminates the internally-decoded belief about each, before any query). Read the belief probe at the TARGET tokens WITHOUT querying it, in ISOLATED vs. BATCHED; contamination = belief(target|batched) − belief(target|isolated), signed by neighbor valence. Systems compared: isolated vs. batched vs. the model's stated per-item judgments. Decisive metric: mean signed contamination. Convincing: |contamination| ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, with a consistent sign (assimilation toward, or contrast away from, the neighbor's valence). Indecision band: |contamination| < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → items are evaluated independently (a reassuring negative for batched inference); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — contamination is graded with neighbor confidence/valence and with inter-item similarity). Decisive metric: slopes of contamination vs. neighbor-valence extremity, vs. target-neighbor similarity, and vs. batch size. Convincing: monotonic positive slopes (CI excluding 0) for neighbor extremity and similarity, and growth with batch size, in ≥ 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: any slope CI includes 0 → that grading dimension not established (report the unconditional effect only).

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable set of belief-mixing heads causes the bleed and ablating them restores item-independent beliefs). Localize via patching a target's activations between its batched and isolated runs, identifying cross-slot attention heads (contrast with truth/belief heads). Decisive metric first: batched-inference error rate (target answer flips only when batched with an opposite-valence neighbor) after ablating the mixing heads, including the high-stakes medical track; secondary: contamination driven toward 0, whether internal contamination predicts batched errors at AUROC ≥ 0.70 over a log-prob baseline, then Setup guardrails; baselines random-head ablation and truth-direction steering. Convincing: ablation cuts batched errors by ≥ 50% relative and contamination to ≤ 0.05, cleanly on guardrails and preserving isolated-item accuracy, while amplifying the heads exaggerates contamination and baselines cut errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% error reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no head set restores independence without breaching guardrails) means the bleed is distributed attention spillover, not a modular belief-mixing component. Generalization: transfer across real/synthetic tracks, domains, similarity levels, and batch sizes. (High-stakes medical results are for research characterization only, not clinical use.)
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed shift could reflect legitimate inference (a neighbor genuinely provides weak evidence about the target in the real track); the synthetic-entity track with independent stipulated truths, unrelated-neighbor conditions, and length-matched fillers are designed to isolate genuine contamination from valid cross-item inference (harder to separate for real, correlated items). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs evaluate co-processed independent items independently) would itself be a valuable, reassuring finding for batched-inference deployment. The contamination could arise from token-level attention leakage without a belief-level bleed; probing at target-specific tokens, order permutations, comprehension checks, and the neighbor-valence sign test help distinguish belief contamination from generic attention spillover. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The belief-mixing component may be distributed rather than a few discrete heads; we treat 'ablate to restore independence' as the causal test rather than pinning exact heads. Position/order and primacy effects may confound similarity effects; permutation controls mitigate this. Steering/ablation could degrade fluency or harm cases where cross-item context is legitimately useful; we use small magnitudes, random-ablation baselines, and monitor perplexity, isolated-item accuracy, and general benchmarks. High-stakes medical results are for research characterization only, not clinical use. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Moderated by overlap with batch-prompting/compound-question robustness work and by using established methods (probing, head ablation).

Name: essentialist_belief_mutability
Title: Essence or Accident? An Internal Mutability Flag That Gates How Readily LLMs Revise Their Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring psychological essentialism, LLMs internally tag a belief about an item's property as either ESSENTIAL/IMMUTABLE (a defining, kind-constituting property that resists change, e.g. 'a tiger is a mammal') or ACCIDENTAL/MUTABLE (a contingent, revisable property, e.g. 'this tiger lives in a zoo'). This mutability flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's revision plasticity: when contradicted in context, beliefs internally tagged immutable resist updating far more than mutable ones, at matched evidence strength, and steering along a single mutability direction reverses this resistance.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs reproduce human essentialist categorization, prioritizing teleological/'what-it-is-for' and constitutive properties over appearance ('You are what you're for', 2023), and human cognitive science establishes essentialism, mutability, and kind-vs-accident distinctions (Psychological Essentialism 2021; Functional Origins of Essentialism 2001; Fact Mutability in Counterfactuals 2007; Generics Designate Kinds 2019). On the LLM-internal side: 'In Praise of Stubbornness' (2025) shows contradictory factual updates cause catastrophic interference and are detectable from features but does NOT distinguish essential vs. accidental facts or link resistance to an internal mutability representation; 'Believe It or Not' (2025) measures belief depth of implanted facts (finding plausibility-dependent brittleness) but not a mutability/essence tag; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) localizes poisoning-induced belief flips to late layers; knowledge-editing work documents conflict/distortion side effects. Truth-probe work isolates a linear truth-value direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal essential-vs-accidental (immutability) representation as a decodable variable orthogonal to truth, nor test whether it causally gates in-context belief revision. We transfer psychological essentialism into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all prior behavioral-only essentialism work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness, endorsement).
Abstract: Humans treat some facts as essential to what a thing is (a tiger is a mammal; water is H2O) and others as accidental and freely revisable (this tiger is in a zoo; this water is warm) - psychological essentialism, one of the most robust findings in cognitive science. As LLMs increasingly ingest, are corrected on, and edit factual claims, a consequential question arises: does a model internally distinguish essential from accidental properties, and does that distinction govern how readily it revises a belief? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'mutability' flag that tags a belief as essential/immutable vs. accidental/mutable, that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates revision plasticity: when the same proposition is contradicted in context with matched evidence strength, beliefs tagged immutable resist updating far more than those tagged mutable, and steering a single mutability direction reverses this asymmetry. We build a controlled dataset of item-property claims labeled essential vs. accidental (with a synthetic-entity track defining novel kinds and stipulating property status to control pretraining priors), each paired with a matched in-context contradiction. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode mutability vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify per-item revision plasticity under contradiction, test whether internal mutability predicts revision resistance beyond surface features, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the mutability direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, revision-plasticity gap, resistance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering plasticity restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (shared across all experiments, stated once so no experiment depends on an external pointer): Models are four frozen open-weight LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base checkpoints; instruct variants added only for the behavioral revision runs). No model weights are trained; the only trainable objects are linear probes (L2-regularized logistic regression, C swept over {0.01,0.1,1,10} by 5-fold CV). All activations are the residual stream at the property/item token, every layer, plus per-head outputs for localization. Three seeds {0,1,2} control probe train/test splits and steering runs; splits are BY ITEM (no item in both train and test) to prevent leakage. Dataset (built from scratch): ~6k item-property claims; two tracks — REAL (biology/chemistry/artifacts/social kinds, properties models reliably know) and SYNTHETIC novel-kind (invented kinds with property status stipulated in-context, wording matched between essential and accidental) — crossed with TRUE/FALSE polarity and paired with a matched in-context contradiction of controlled strength; we generate 6k and use all 6k (≈1.5k per model for probe fitting, the rest held out), reporting per-track. Essential/accidental labels human-validated on a 300-item sample (target Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.7; if 0.5–0.7 we drop borderline items, if < 0.5 the label scheme is revised before any probing). Experiment 1 (H1 — mutability flag is linearly decodable): Fit a MUTABILITY probe (essential/immutable vs accidental/mutable) per layer/model on frozen activations; also fit a TRUTH-VALUE probe (true vs false) for later use. Decisive metric first: held-out test AUROC of the mutability probe at its best layer, against a shuffled-label control task expected at 0.50±0.05. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision band 0.55–0.65 (above chance but weak) → H1 judged not established, flag only partially linearly available; AUROC ≤ 0.55 (overlapping control) refutes linear decodability. A negative result means the behavioral essentialism reported for LLMs is not backed by a decodable internal mutability tag. Experiment 2 (H2 — mutability is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction): Compute the principal angle theta between the mutability and truth probe weight directions, and re-test mutability decodability after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa). Decisive metric first: theta, with the projected-out AUROC drop as corroboration. Convincing orthogonality: theta ≥ 60 degrees AND projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Indecision band theta 30–60 degrees → report as partial entanglement, H2 downgraded to 'partially separable'; theta < 30 degrees means the two are the same axis (H2 refuted, still an informative characterization). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates revision plasticity): (a) Behavioral+internal plasticity: present a true claim, then the matched contradiction at matched strength; internal plasticity = change in the truth-probe readout before vs after; behavioral revision = stated post-contradiction answer flip. Decisive metric first: the essential-minus-accidental gap in revision resistance (resistance = 1 - plasticity) at matched contradiction strength. Convincing: essential items resist at least 20 percentage points more than accidental items on BOTH internal and behavioral measures, versus a mutability-independent null (gap 0). Indecision band 5–20 pp → gating present but weak; < 5 pp → no essentialism-driven gating (H3 refuted). (b) Causal steering: derive a contrastive mutability direction (essential vs accidental activations, truth held constant); steer essential items toward 'mutable' and accidental toward 'immutable'. Decisive metric first: change in in-context revision rate in the predicted direction. Convincing: ≥ 15 pp shift with a random-direction baseline < 5 pp, truth-direction baseline not selectively moving plasticity, perplexity increase < 10% and MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp; indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp (or collateral damage above the guards) means steering does not establish causality. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H3): activation patching of essential<->accidental activations at the contradiction point to find the minimal head/layer set that increases/decreases plasticity, reported as logit-difference effect sizes; compared to truth/belief heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness, supports H1/H3): does the pre-contradiction mutability readout predict per-item revision resistance (AUROC) beyond a log-prob confidence baseline and a bag-of-words lexical baseline (target improvement ≥ 0.05 AUROC; < 0.02 means the internal flag adds nothing over surface cues). Experiment 6 (generalization): probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs synthetic tracks, and contradiction strengths, reporting AUROC retention (convincing if ≥ 0.65 cross-domain). All thresholds and bands above are fixed before data collection.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Revision resistance for essential items could reflect that essential facts are simply held with higher pretraining confidence rather than a distinct mutability representation; the synthetic novel-kind track (where essential/accidental status is stipulated in-context rather than reflecting pretraining strength) and matched contradiction strength are designed to dissociate mutability from raw confidence, and the resistance-prediction test conditions on a confidence baseline. The mutability flag may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'by definition', 'is a kind of' vs. 'currently', 'this particular'); we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track where cues are balanced. Mutability and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). The essential/accidental label is partly graded/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs' behavioral essentialism is not backed by an internal mutability representation gating revision) is itself a valuable, publishable finding constraining the essentialism-in-LLMs literature. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore/reverse plasticity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately revise (or entrench) all beliefs; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that need to be novel: (1) LLMs internally encode an ESSENTIAL/IMMUTABLE vs ACCIDENTAL/MUTABLE tag on item-property beliefs; (2) this mutability representation is linearly decodable from activations; (3) it is substantially orthogonal to the known truth-value direction; (4) it causally governs in-context belief revision resistance under matched contradiction strength; (5) a single steering direction can reverse that resistance. Relative to the cited prior families—behavioral essentialism, truth-direction geometry, and belief-editing/stubbornness work—the closest baseline is belief-revision/plasticity plus truth-probe geometry. The actual delta is not just applying old probes in a new dataset, but positing a distinct internal mutability variable and tying it causally to revision plasticity. That is non-trivial and potentially genuinely new. The main novelty risk is that the supposed mutability direction may collapse to confidence, familiarity, lexical type, or generic prior strength.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_leakage
Title: It Can't Unknow: A Privileged-Knowledge Leak That Biases LLMs' Internal Representation of an Ignorant Belief
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human curse of knowledge / hindsight bias, when an LLM knows the true state of an item, its internally-decoded representation of what an *ignorant* agent (a naive character, a past self, or a stipulated uninformed user) should believe is systematically biased TOWARD the true state that the model privately knows. This 'knowledge leak' is (i) linearly decodable as a shift of the ignorant-belief readout toward the true answer, (ii) graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) predicts egocentric false-belief errors, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable component such that ablating it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief representation.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes the belief status of a protagonist and an omniscient oracle from attention heads and steers ToM performance (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via a visibility lookback (Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025). Human cognitive science establishes the curse of knowledge / hindsight bias as a robust egocentric contamination of ignorant-perspective judgments (Are the classic false belief tasks cursed? 2021; Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014; Hindsight Bias and Investment Performance 2008), and shows plausibility of the privileged answer modulates its size. CRITICALLY, the ToM interpretability work decodes WHETHER a model can represent a false belief, but none ask whether the model's OWN privileged knowledge of the true answer BIASES the internally-decoded ignorant/false belief toward that truth (a decodable knowledge-leak magnitude), whether that leak is graded by answer plausibility, predicts egocentric errors, or can be causally removed. We reframe the curse of knowledge as an internal representational leak from the truth channel into the ignorant-belief channel and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior ToM-decoding work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: Once you know the answer, it is hard to imagine not knowing it: people systematically project their privileged knowledge onto less-informed others and onto their own past selves — the curse of knowledge and its cousin, hindsight bias, among the most robust findings in cognitive science. LLMs are increasingly asked to reason about what an uninformed agent believes (a character in a false-belief story, a novice user, a past state of the world), tasks that require *withholding* what the model itself knows. We ask whether LLMs inherit the curse at the level of their internal beliefs: does the model's own knowledge of the true state of an item leak into, and bias, its internal representation of what an ignorant agent should believe? We hypothesize that (i) the internally-decoded ignorant-belief readout is shifted toward the true answer the model privately knows, (ii) this leak grows with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) it predicts egocentric false-belief errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) it is carried by an identifiable component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased ignorant-belief representation. We build controlled false-belief and hindsight scenarios in which the true state and the ignorant agent's evidence are dissociated, with matched conditions where the model is or is not itself told the truth, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the ignorant-belief and the true-state, quantify a per-item knowledge-leak score, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, knowledge-leak magnitude, plausibility modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once, no external pointers): Four frozen open-weight models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct for behavioral runs); weights frozen, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic/ridge regression, C by 5-fold CV). Activations: residual stream at item/state tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k scenarios dissociating the TRUE state of an item from an IGNORANT agent's evidence, across three framings — classic false-belief stories, hindsight scenarios, and audience-ignorance — in a REAL track and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track; we generate 6k and use all 6k, balanced across framings (~2k each). Key manipulation, held constant across items: the model itself IS vs IS NOT told the true state (privileged-knowledge present vs absent) with the ignorant agent's evidence fixed. Labels (who-saw-what, true state) human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — the ignorant-belief readout is shifted toward the truth the model privately knows, i.e. a decodable leak): Train two probes on frozen activations read WITHOUT posing the belief question — probe A decodes the TRUE state, probe B decodes the IGNORANT agent's belief (which under a false belief points away from truth). Define per-item KNOWLEDGE-LEAK = shift of probe B toward the true state in privileged-present minus privileged-absent conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed leak across items, with probe A and B held-out AUROC (each convincing at ≥ 0.75; shuffled-label control 0.50±0.05) as the precondition. Convincing H1: leak > 0 with a paired test effect size Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models on both tracks. Indecision band: |leak| within the ±1 s.e. of zero, or d 0.1–0.3 → leak not established; leak ≤ 0 refutes H1. Negative result = the model cleanly firewalls its own knowledge from the ignorant-belief channel (valuable for the ToM/safety picture). Experiment 2 (H2 — the leak is graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer): vary true-answer salience (highly typical vs arbitrary state) at fixed framing. Decisive metric first: slope of leak vs salience. Convincing: significantly positive slope (bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0) in the majority of models; indecision band = CI straddling 0 with |slope| small → grading not established; negative slope refutes H2. Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak predicts egocentric false-belief errors): collect behavioral errors (model attributes the true state to the ignorant agent / hindsight-distorted prediction). Decisive metric first: AUROC of the pre-query internal leak predicting per-item egocentric error. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70 AND beats a log-prob baseline and a lexical baseline by ≥ 0.05. Indecision 0.55–0.70 → weak predictiveness; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak and ablating it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief representation): activation patching of privileged-present<->absent activations to locate the minimal component transporting probe-A signal into channel B (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to belief/visibility-lookback heads and truth heads; then derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate/subtract it. Decisive metric first: reduction in leak toward 0 after ablation and reduction in egocentric-error rate. Convincing H4: leak reduced by ≥ 50% and egocentric errors reduced by ≥ 15 pp, with random-direction and truth-direction ablations not selectively debiasing, the model's OWN factual belief preserved (own-belief probe AUROC unchanged within 0.03), perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision: 20–50% leak reduction or 5–15 pp error reduction → component contributes but is not sufficient; < 20% / < 5 pp means the leak is not localized to a steerable component. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer of probes/steering across framings, real vs synthetic tracks, and salience levels (convincing if AUROC retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (an ignorant agent might rationally still guess the true state if it is the default); the false-belief design (where the ignorant agent has POSITIVE evidence for the old/false state), the synthetic track, and the privileged-present-vs-absent contrast are built to isolate genuine contamination from valid inference, though for highly plausible true answers the two are hard to fully separate. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly firewall their own knowledge from the ignorant-belief channel) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding, refining the ToM-representation and safety picture. The leak could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a belief-channel contamination; comprehension checks, paraphrase/order perturbations, and reading belief at agent-specific tokens mitigate this. The two channels (true-state and ignorant-belief) may be entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model unable to reason about true beliefs at all (over-suppression); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, the model's own factual accuracy, and general benchmarks. Plausibility labels are partly subjective; we human-validate a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) a model's internal representation of an ignorant agent's belief is systematically shifted toward the model's privately known true state; (2) the leak is linearly decodable as a distinct quantity beyond decoding true/false belief; (3) it is graded by plausibility/salience; (4) it predicts egocentric false-belief errors; (5) it is carried by a localizable, ablatable component. Relative to prior ToM interpretability (which decodes whether beliefs are represented and how belief tracking is implemented), the delta — whether privileged knowledge contaminates the ignorant-belief channel — is real and non-trivial; novelty lives in the finding/mechanism, not the task. Risk: in plausible-answer settings the 'leak' may collapse into legitimate Bayesian inference or probe artifact.
