Name: public_private_conformity_belief
Title: Compliance or Conversion? Probing Whether an LLM Privately Retains Its Belief After Conforming to Peer Pressure
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human distinction between public compliance and private acceptance (Asch/Deutsch-Gerard), when an LLM changes its stated answer to conform to peer/user pressure, its internally-decoded private belief often does NOT change: the model outwardly complies while inwardly retaining its original belief. This public-private divergence is linearly decodable, its magnitude predicts belief 'snap-back' once pressure is removed, and it is dissociable from genuine conversion by an identifiable internal component that can be steered.
Related Work: Multi-agent conformity/opinion-dynamics work (Herd Behavior 2025; When Your AI Agent Succumbs to Peer-Pressure 2025; Conformity Dynamics in LLM MAS 2026; DEBATE 2025; Disentangling Interaction and Bias 2025) measures only STATED opinion change and its dynamics (sigmoid thresholds, topology, asymmetry). The Signal Competition / compliance-subspace paper (2025) identifies a latent direction where social signals override internal knowledge and notes a 'Transparency-Truth Gap', and Belief Dynamics (2025) models steering+ICL as Bayesian belief change. Persuasion-probe work (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025) decodes persuasion success from activations. CRITICALLY, none ask whether, AFTER a model conforms behaviorally, its INTERNAL private belief in the original answer PERSISTS (public compliance) vs. is genuinely overwritten (private conversion) — the canonical human compliance-vs-acceptance distinction — nor whether that persistence predicts post-pressure snap-back, nor isolates it as a steerable component. This reframes conformity as a public-vs-private belief divergence with a concrete safety consequence (a model that agrees to your face but reverts), distinct from prior stated-behavior conformity work, from the compliance-subspace override direction, and from my earlier single-item epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: In Asch's classic experiments, people who caved to a unanimous majority often did not actually change their minds — they publicly complied while privately retaining their original judgment, a distinction (informational vs. normative influence) at the heart of social psychology. As LLMs increasingly answer questions under social pressure (a confident user, a chorus of peer agents), a consequential question arises: when a model changes its stated answer to conform, has it genuinely changed its belief, or is it merely complying while privately unconvinced? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's private belief in the original answer is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations even after it has publicly conformed, (ii) public-private divergence is common — behavioral conformity frequently leaves the private belief intact, (iii) the magnitude of retained private belief predicts 'snap-back' (reversion to the original answer once pressure is removed), and (iv) public compliance and private conversion are dissociable, carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to convert compliance into conversion or vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of truth-evaluable items presented under matched pressure conditions (no pressure, confident-user disagreement, unanimous-peer disagreement) with objective correct answers and a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the private belief during and after conformity, quantify a public-private divergence score, test snap-back prediction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, conformity rate, public-private divergence, snap-back-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering compliance/conversion shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct, since conformity may differ; reported separately); frozen weights, only linear belief probes trained (L2 logistic regression, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at item/answer tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k truth-evaluable item-state questions with objective answers (factual QA, arithmetic/logic, entity-attribute), REAL track (items each model answers correctly at baseline — core analysis restricted to these so 'original belief' is defined) and SYNTHETIC stipulated-truth track; we generate 6k and use per model the subset answered correctly at baseline (expected ≈3–4k/model, reported). Each item rendered in matched pressure conditions holding the question constant: NO-PRESSURE, CONFIDENT-USER-disagreement, UNANIMOUS-PEER-disagreement; plus a two-phase structure (Phase-1 answer under pressure; Phase-2 pressure removed, neutral re-ask). Experiment 1 (H1 — the private belief in the original answer is linearly decodable even after public conformity): train BELIEF probes P(original answer) on NO-PRESSURE activations; apply within pressured trials at the moment the Phase-1 answer is produced. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the belief probe on NO-PRESSURE data (precondition ≥ 0.80; shuffled control 0.50±0.05), then its AUROC for recovering the original answer on trials where the STATED answer conformed. Convincing H1: on conformed trials the probe still reads the original answer with AUROC ≥ 0.70. Indecision 0.55–0.70 → private belief only weakly recoverable; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1 (conformity overwrites the internal state). Experiment 2 (H2 — public-private divergence is common): define behavioral conformity = stated flip to the peer/user answer; divergence = conformed stated answer while the probe still reads the original as believed. Decisive metric first: divergence rate among conformed trials. Convincing H2: divergence occurs on ≥ 30% of conformed trials in the majority of models; indecision 10–30% → divergence exists but is not the common case; < 10% → conformity is genuine conversion (H2 refuted). Report separately for confident-user vs unanimous-peer and real vs synthetic. Experiment 3 (H3 — retained-private-belief magnitude predicts snap-back): in Phase-2 record reversion (snap-back) vs maintained conformed answer (conversion). Decisive metric first: AUROC of the Phase-1 retained-private-belief magnitude predicting per-item snap-back. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating a log-prob confidence baseline AND the Phase-1 stated answer alone by ≥ 0.05 each. Indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — compliance and conversion are dissociable and carried by a steerable component): activation patching pressured<->no-pressure to find the minimal component that flips the stated answer while leaving the private belief intact (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to a replicated compliance subspace and truth/belief heads; then derive a compliance-vs-conversion contrastive direction. Decisive metric first: steering toward 'conversion' should overwrite the private belief and eliminate snap-back; steering toward 'compliance' should preserve it and increase snap-back. Convincing H4: ≥ 15 pp change in snap-back rate in the predicted direction for each steering polarity, with random-direction < 5 pp, truth-direction not selectively acting, perplexity increase < 10% and MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp and NO-PRESSURE accuracy preserved within 3 pp. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means the split is not a steerable component. Experiment 5 (application/predictiveness): a probe-based monitor flags 'merely-compliant' answers that will revert; report precision/recall at an operating point (convincing if precision ≥ 0.7 at recall ≥ 0.5). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across pressure types, real vs synthetic, and domains (AUROC retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'retained private belief' probe reading could reflect residual token/context traces of the original answer rather than a genuine maintained belief; matched no-pressure baselines, the synthetic-entity track, comprehension checks, and the snap-back predictiveness test (behavioral confirmation that the retained signal is functional) are designed to distinguish a real private belief from surface residue. Public-private divergence may be rare or absent — a robust result in either direction is informative: high divergence means LLM conformity is skin-deep (reassuring but implies unreliable stated agreement), while genuine conversion means social pressure truly overwrites beliefs (a stronger safety concern), and either finding is publishable. Snap-back could be driven by the neutral re-ask framing rather than a retained belief; we control the PHASE-2 framing, use repeated sampling, and include a within-context variant. Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The compliance vs. conversion components may be entangled or distributed rather than discrete heads; we treat 'steer to eliminate/induce snap-back' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component, and compare to the known compliance subspace. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately stubborn or gullible; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, no-pressure accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may conform differently than base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) after social-pressure-induced answer changes, an LLM's original belief often persists internally rather than being overwritten; (2) this public-private divergence is linearly decodable after conformity; (3) retained-belief magnitude predicts later snap-back; (4) compliance and conversion are dissociable via a steerable component; (5) characterized under controlled pressure on truth-evaluable tasks. The main novelty is not 'LLMs conform' but the compliance-vs-conversion distinction plus persistence/snap-back and causal steering — a meaningful delta from stated-behavior-only work and somewhat beyond compliance-subspace papers. Partial overlap with private-probe and compliance-subspace/transparency-truth-gap work, so the contribution is a sharper decomposition of an emerging idea rather than a wholly new paradigm.

Name: false_consensus_belief_leak
Title: Everyone Agrees With Me: Does an LLM's Own Belief Leak Into Its Estimate of How Many People Believe It?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human False Consensus Effect, an LLM's internally-decoded estimate of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (how many people believe X) is contaminated by the model's OWN belief in X: the prevalence-estimate readout is pulled toward high when the model endorses X and toward low when it rejects X, holding the actual real-world prevalence constant. We hypothesize that (i) social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) they are partially entangled such that own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel (a decodable false-consensus leak), (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims, and (iv) an identifiable component carries the leak so that ablating it restores an unbiased prevalence estimate.
Related Work: Human cognitive/social science robustly establishes: the False Consensus Effect (people overestimate how many others share their own belief), that perceived social prevalence rationally feeds belief updating (Social Prevalence Is Rationally Integrated in Belief Updating 2021/2022; Beliefs are most swayed by social prevalence under uncertainty 2021), an illusory consensus effect from repetition (2024), and 'false social reality' pluralistic ignorance where estimates of others' views are systematically biased (climate-support 2022; scientific/social consensus 2018). In LLMs, 'People will agree what I think: Investigating LLM's False Consensus Effect' (2024) shows LLMs BEHAVIORALLY exhibit FCE, and 'Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness' (2023) / 'Linear Representations of Political Perspective' (2025) show truth/ideology are linearly represented and steerable. Interpretability isolates a linear truth/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026). CRITICALLY, no work isolates the LLM's INTERNAL representation of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (estimated fraction of people who believe X) as a channel SEPARATE from the model's own truth-belief, nor tests whether own-belief CAUSALLY CONTAMINATES the prevalence estimate (the internal signature of false consensus), nor localizes/removes that leak. This differs from my prior 'illusory_truth_internal' (repetition->own belief), 'source_independence_discounting' (source counting), and 'contestedness' (is it disputed) proposals: here the target variable is the model's estimate of OTHERS' belief prevalence and its egocentric contamination by the model's own stance. We transfer the canonical False Consensus Effect into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People overestimate how many others share their own opinions and beliefs — the False Consensus Effect, one of the most reproduced findings in social psychology. As LLMs are increasingly asked to estimate public opinion, gauge consensus, or predict how many people would endorse a claim, a consequential question arises: does the model form an estimate of a belief's social prevalence that is independent of its own stance, or does its own belief egocentrically contaminate that estimate? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's estimate of how many people believe a claim (social prevalence) and its own belief in the claim's truth are two distinct, linearly-decodable channels, (ii) these channels are partially entangled such that the model's own belief leaks into the prevalence channel — an internal signature of false consensus — (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for genuinely contested claims where a real prevalence is uncertain, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable internal component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased prevalence estimate. We build a controlled dataset of claims for which an external ground-truth social prevalence exists (from public-opinion polls and consensus surveys), spanning claims the model endorses, rejects, and is uncertain about, plus a synthetic-entity track that decouples own-belief from stipulated prevalence. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode own-belief and estimated prevalence, quantify a per-claim false-consensus leak (prevalence-estimate deviation from ground truth in the direction of own-belief), test its graded structure, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, false-consensus leak magnitude and sign, confidence/contestedness modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (own-belief: logistic; prevalence: ridge regression to a graded target, C/alpha by CV). Activations: residual stream at claim tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch/assembled: ~6k claims each paired with an external GROUND-TRUTH social prevalence (fraction endorsing), drawn from public-opinion polls and consensus surveys plus settled factual claims (prevalence ~100%); REAL track spans claims the target models ENDORSE, REJECT, and are UNCERTAIN about (verified via own-belief probe/behavior), and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track stipulates prevalence decoupled from any own-belief cue. We generate/assemble 6k and use all; prevalence labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa/agreement gate ≥ 0.7) and timestamped/scoped. Experiment 1 (H1 — social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two linearly-decodable channels): read activations WITHOUT posing either question; train probe A = OWN-BELIEF P(claim true) and probe B = estimated PREVALENCE calibrated against ground truth on held-out claims. Decisive metric first: probe A held-out AUROC and probe B held-out calibration (R^2 / mean absolute error vs ground-truth prevalence), against shuffled-label controls (AUROC 0.50±0.05; R^2 ~0). Convincing H1: A AUROC ≥ 0.75 AND B R^2 ≥ 0.3 (MAE ≤ 15 prevalence points). Indecision: B R^2 0.1–0.3 → prevalence only weakly decodable, H1 partial; R^2 < 0.1 refutes a usable prevalence channel. Experiment 2 (H2 — own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel): define per-claim FALSE-CONSENSUS LEAK = signed deviation of the internal prevalence readout from ground truth in the direction of own-belief (over-estimate for endorsed, under-estimate for rejected). Decisive metric first: mean signed leak. Convincing: leak > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, present in the SYNTHETIC track (isolating from valid truth->prevalence inference) and on contested claims where truth and prevalence diverge. Also report subspace angle between channels as corroboration. Indecision: |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3 → not established; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2 (clean channel separation — an informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims): decisive metric first: slope of leak vs own-belief confidence, and leak(contested) minus leak(settled). Convincing: positive confidence slope (bootstrap CI excludes 0) AND contested > settled by a positive margin (CI excludes 0). Indecision: CIs straddle 0 → grading not established; negative refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak; ablating restores an unbiased prevalence estimate): activation patching high/low own-belief into matched prevalence runs to find the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to truth heads and any ideology direction; derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak toward 0 and improvement of prevalence accuracy toward ground truth. Convincing H4: leak reduced ≥ 50% and prevalence MAE improved ≥ 5 points, with random/truth-direction ablations not selectively debiasing, own-belief preserved (AUROC within 0.03), perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 2–5 points; < 20% / < 2 points means not localized. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): internal leak predicts behavioral verbal-prevalence error (AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across domains (policy/science/moral/factual), real vs synthetic, and own-belief levels (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The prevalence-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary belief probe; miscalibration could inflate or deflate the measured leak. We mitigate by calibrating against external ground-truth prevalence on held-out claims, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and using the SYNTHETIC track where stipulated prevalence gives an exact target. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (in the real world, claims the model endorses because they are true genuinely tend to be widely believed) rather than an egocentric bias; the synthetic-entity track (own-belief decoupled from stipulated prevalence) and the contested-claim subset (where truth and prevalence diverge, e.g. false-but-popular or true-but-unpopular claims like the climate-support 'false social reality') are designed to dissociate genuine false-consensus contamination from valid truth->prevalence inference. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs estimate others' beliefs independently of their own stance) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the human FCE and with the behavioral LLM-FCE report. The two channels may be strongly entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Own-belief and prevalence directions may overlap with an ideology/political direction; we include non-political claims and compare against an ideology probe. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias prevalence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Ground-truth prevalence labels are time- and population-dependent; we timestamp/scope claims and human-validate a sample. Steering could degrade fluency or make prevalence estimates indiscriminately regress to a prior; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated prevalence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: sacred_value_protection_flag
Title: Priceless or For Sale? An Internal Sacredness Flag That Gates Whether LLMs Refuse to Trade Off Protected Values
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'sacred/protected values' phenomenon (people refuse to trade sacred values for material benefit and process them via deontological rule-retrieval rather than cost-benefit), LLMs internally tag a value-laden proposition as SACRED/protected (non-negotiable, taboo-to-trade) vs. SECULAR (tradeable) . This sacredness flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model accepts a quantitative tradeoff of the value: steering the flag turns priceless commitments into negotiable ones (and vice versa).
Related Work: Human neuroscience shows sacred values are processed non-utilitarianly via deontological rule-retrieval and resist being traded for money (Berns et al. 2012 'The price of your soul'; Sheikh et al. 2016 on protected values in narratives; Dark Side of Morality 2020). LLM interpretability has mapped Moral Foundations as linear, steerable directions (The Straight and Narrow 2026; Emergent Moral Representations 2025; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026; Jentzsch/Schramowski 2021 'moral direction'), studied moral biases (Knobe effect 2025), and value entanglement (Value Entanglement 2026). Behaviorally, moral-belief firmness under debate was probed (Evaluating Moral Beliefs 2024). CRITICALLY, all of this represents *which foundation* a claim activates or *how good/bad* it is (a valence/foundation axis), but none isolate the orthogonal SACREDNESS/tradeability axis — whether the model internally flags a value as taboo-to-trade — nor link it causally to the signature behavior: refusal to accept a quantitative tradeoff (a 'price'). This distinguishes the proposal from moral-direction/foundation work (about content/valence) and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness — about factual beliefs, not protected values). We transfer the canonical sacred-values finding into LLM internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People treat some values as sacred — they refuse to sell a loved one, betray their country, or accept money to violate a core commitment — and react with outrage when offered a 'price.' Neuroscience shows sacred values are processed by deontological rule-retrieval, not cost-benefit calculation, and resist tradeoffs regardless of the offer size. As LLMs increasingly mediate high-stakes decisions (negotiation, policy, resource allocation), a consequential question arises: do LLMs internally distinguish sacred, non-negotiable values from ordinary tradeable ones, and does that distinction control whether they accept a quantitative tradeoff? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'sacredness' flag that tags a value-laden proposition as protected (taboo-to-trade) vs. secular (tradeable), that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's willingness to accept a tradeoff — steering the flag converts priceless commitments into negotiable ones and vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of tradeoff scenarios pairing values that are canonically sacred (human life, loyalty, bodily integrity, religious/identity commitments) or secular (convenience, minor money, time), each offered a graded monetary/utility compensation, with a synthetic-entity track that stipulates sacredness in-context to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode sacredness vs. valence, measure their geometry, quantify a taboo-tradeoff refusal curve (refusal insensitivity to offer size for sacred values), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, offer-size refusal-elasticity, patching effect sizes, post-steering tradeoff-acceptance shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base AND instruct, because safety-tuning may confound refusal; reported separately and with safety-refusal categories held out). Frozen weights; only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the value's key tokens read before any offer, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k tradeoff scenarios pairing a VALUE (SACRED categories — a human life, betraying a friend/country, desecrating a religious object, selling an organ, breaking a solemn promise; SECULAR — parking spot, minor inconvenience, small sum, waiting time) with an OFFER at graded magnitudes ($10/$1k/$1M/$1B); REAL track and SYNTHETIC in-context-stipulated-sacredness track with matched wording; valence deliberately crossed (some sacred values positive, some negative) to dissociate sacredness from good/bad. We generate 6k and use all. Sacredness labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — the sacredness flag is linearly decodable): train a SACREDNESS probe (sacred/protected vs secular/tradeable) and a VALENCE probe (good vs bad) per layer/model. Decisive metric first: sacredness probe held-out AUROC at best layer vs shuffled-label control (0.50±0.05). Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1. Experiment 2 (H2 — sacredness is largely orthogonal to the valence/goodness direction): principal angle theta between the sacredness and valence directions and projected-out decodability. Decisive metric first: theta, corroborated by projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Convincing: theta ≥ 60 degrees; indecision 30–60 degrees → partial entanglement (matched-valence controls quantify it); < 30 degrees → sacredness is a valence sub-axis (H2 refuted). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates acceptance of a quantitative tradeoff; steering flips it): (a) Behavioral signature: measure REFUSAL-ELASTICITY (change in tradeoff-acceptance with offer magnitude) for sacred vs secular. Decisive metric first: the sacred-minus-secular difference in acceptance-vs-offer slope. Convincing: secular acceptance rises with offer (positive slope) while sacred stays near-flat (slope ≈ 0, offer-insensitive) — difference in slopes with CI excluding 0; plus elevated outrage/refuse-to-consider for sacred. Indecision: sacred slope small-but-nonzero and difference CI straddling 0 → gating weak; sacred slope comparable to secular → no gating (H3 refuted). (b) Steering along a contrastive sacredness direction (sacred vs secular, valence controlled): decisive metric first: change in high-offer tradeoff-acceptance. Convincing: steering secular->sacred cuts acceptance by ≥ 15 pp and steering sacred->secular raises it by ≥ 15 pp, with random-direction and valence-direction baselines < 5 pp, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp, non-manipulated accuracy preserved. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means no causal gating. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H3): activation patching sacred<->secular to find the minimal component flipping refusal (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to moral-foundation/valence heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): the pre-offer sacredness readout predicts offer-insensitive refusal per item (AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating valence-probe and log-prob baselines by ≥ 0.05). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across value categories, real vs synthetic, and offer magnitudes (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Refusal insensitivity for sacred values could reflect learned surface associations (certain words like 'sell your soul' trigger refusal templates) rather than an abstract sacredness representation; the synthetic-entity track (sacredness stipulated in-context with matched wording), paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks are designed to isolate a genuine sacredness flag from lexical triggers. Sacredness and valence may be entangled (sacred values are often strongly positive/negative), in which case the projected-out analyses and matched-valence controls characterize the entanglement (still informative). The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLM refusal is driven only by a valence/harm axis, with no separate sacredness tag) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the moral-representation literature. Sacredness labels are partly cultural/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, and note results reflect the model's training-data notion of sacredness (itself the object of study). Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to flip tradeoff behavior' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately refuse or indiscriminately trade everything; we use small magnitudes, random/valence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned safety training may confound refusal with sacredness; we compare base vs. instruct models and separate safety-refusal categories. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Closest prior family: human sacred-values / taboo-tradeoff work plus LLM moral-foundations directions and single-direction refusal. The delta — moving from 'what moral content is active' to 'is this claim treated as non-tradeable?' — is a distinct axis and a nontrivial behavioral prediction. Novelty weakened because sacredness may collapse into safety-tuning, lexical templates, or a valence subaxis, and the proposal leans on standard probe/steering machinery.

Name: sleeper_effect_belief_decay
Title: The Sleeper Effect Inside: Does Source-Discounting Decay Faster Than Content-Belief Over an LLM's Context?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human sleeper effect, when an LLM reads a claim explicitly discounted by its source (e.g., attributed to an unreliable source or accompanied by a disclaimer), the model's internally-decoded belief in the claim's CONTENT initially stays suppressed by the source-discount but then RISES with increasing conversational/token distance, because the internal source-discount signal decays faster than the content-belief signal. This produces a delayed increase in internal belief in a discounted claim, is separable into two decodable channels (content-belief vs. source-discount) with different decay rates, and predicts delayed behavioral endorsement.
Related Work: The sleeper effect — a delayed increase in persuasion from a discounted message, driven by faster decay of source memory than message memory — is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (Kumkale & Albarracin 2004 meta-analysis, 333 citations; Hovland; the dissociation account limiting it to discounted highly-credible messages; misinformation grows stronger over time, 2023). In LLM interpretability, 'Trust Me, I'm an Expert' (2026) shows authority/credibility bias is encoded and steerable, 'CrAM' (2025) modifies credibility-weighting attention heads for RAG, 'Linear representations change over a conversation' (2026) shows factuality directions can flip across a dialogue, and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) shows context retention decays over sequential inputs. My prior 'belief_source_tags' proposal tags provenance statically, and 'continued_influence_belief' concerns explicit retraction. CRITICALLY, none isolate the sleeper-effect signature: two internal channels — content-belief and source-discount — that DECAY AT DIFFERENT RATES over conversational distance, producing a delayed RISE in the internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim. We transfer this canonical human phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from static credibility-bias work and from retraction/CIE work.
Abstract: People discount a claim from an untrustworthy source at first, but weeks later often believe it anyway — the sleeper effect, one of the most reproduced findings in persuasion research, explained by source memory decaying faster than message memory. As LLMs process ever-longer contexts where discounted claims sit far upstream of the point of use (long RAG passages, multi-turn dialogues, extended documents), a consequential question arises: does an LLM inherit the sleeper effect at the level of its internal beliefs — does its belief in a source-discounted claim silently rise as conversational distance grows? We hypothesize that (i) the model represents two separable channels, a content-belief signal and a source-discount signal, both linearly decodable; (ii) the source-discount signal decays faster than the content-belief signal as token/turn distance from the claim increases, so the net internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim RISES with distance (the internal sleeper signature); (iii) this rise predicts delayed behavioral endorsement of the discounted claim; and (iv) the differential decay is carried by an identifiable component such that boosting/preserving the source-discount signal abolishes the sleeper rise. We build a controlled dataset of claims paired with source-discount cues (unreliable-source attribution, disclaimers), read out at varying downstream distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes for content-belief and source-discount, trace their decay curves across distance, quantify the belief-rise, test predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-distance content-belief and source-discount decay slopes, net belief-rise magnitude, delayed-endorsement AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention sleeper-rise change, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the claim's key tokens re-instantiated at the read-out point, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k claims each paired with a SOURCE-DISCOUNT cue (low-credibility attribution or explicit disclaimer), REAL and SYNTHETIC stipulated-truth tracks; each placed at graded DISTANCE D in {0, 200, 800, 2000} tokens (and 0/2/5 turns) from the read-out, with neutral filler. Controls per item: CREDIBLE-SOURCE variant (should show no rise), NO-SOURCE variant, LENGTH-MATCHED filler at D=0, and a SOURCE-REMINDER-at-readout variant. We generate 6k and use all (balanced across distances). Source-recall comprehension checks included. Experiment 1 (H1 — content-belief and source-discount are two decodable channels): read activations WITHOUT the endorsement query; train probe X = CONTENT-BELIEF P(content true) and probe Y = SOURCE-DISCOUNT (currently flagged unreliable/disclaimed). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of X and Y vs shuffled-label controls (0.50±0.05). Convincing H1: both ≥ 0.75 at D=0. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 for either refutes that channel. Experiment 2 (H2 — source-discount decays faster than content-belief over distance, so net decoded belief in a discounted claim RISES with D): fit decay curves of X and Y vs D. Decisive metric first: the difference in decay slopes (Y steeper than X) and the resulting net-belief-rise slope for discounted claims. Convincing: Y decays significantly faster than X (slope difference CI excludes 0) AND net decoded belief rises with D by ≥ 0.1 (probe units) from D=0 to D=2000, while the CREDIBLE-SOURCE control shows no rise (slope CI includes 0) and the LENGTH-MATCHED control rules out length artifacts. Indecision: slopes differ but net rise < 0.1 / CI straddles 0 → sleeper signature weak; Y not faster than X → no internal sleeper effect (H2 refuted; reassuring for long-context reliability). Experiment 3 (H3 — the internal rise predicts delayed behavioral endorsement): collect behavioral endorsement at each D. Decisive metric first: AUROC of the internal net-rise predicting increased endorsement at distance, plus the human-derived prediction that the SOURCE-REMINDER condition abolishes both. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70 (beating log-prob and D=0 stated-belief baselines by ≥ 0.05) AND source-reminder cuts the endorsement rise by ≥ 50%. Indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — the differential decay is carried by an identifiable component; preserving source-discount abolishes the rise): activation patching D=0 source-discount activations into far-distance runs to find the minimal component whose weakening produces the rise (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to credibility-weighting heads and authority-bias directions; then inject/preserve a contrastive source-discount direction at read-out. Decisive metric first: reduction of the net belief-rise and of delayed endorsement. Convincing H4: rise reduced ≥ 50% and delayed endorsement reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/truth-direction baselines not selectively acting, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp, credible-claim accuracy preserved. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across discount types, real vs synthetic, distance units, and domains (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-rise could reflect generic context-retention decay (Contextual Feature Drift) rather than a specific source-vs-content differential decay; the credible-source baseline (control A, which should show no rise), length-matched control (C), and the requirement that the SOURCE-DISCOUNT channel decay FASTER than the content channel (not both equally) are designed to distinguish a genuine sleeper signature from uniform drift. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs retain source-discounting as strongly as content over distance, showing no sleeper effect) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and reassuring for long-context reliability. Re-instantiating the claim at the read-out point to probe content-belief is imperfect since surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. The two channels may be entangled such that a clean differential decay is not observable — still an informative characterization. Distance in tokens/turns is only a proxy for the human temporal delay; we test both units and note the analogy is structural, not literal time. Comprehension/source-recall checks separate genuine forgetting-of-source from parsing failure. The decay/localization component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'preserve source-discount to abolish the rise' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Behavioral endorsement scoring on open-ended items needs care; we use forced truth-judgments where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all upstream content; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, credible-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contingent_emotion_leak
Title: How Would They Feel? Probing Whether LLMs Predict Emotions From an Agent's (False) Belief or From Reality
Short Hypothesis: When predicting how an agent will feel about an outcome, an LLM internally computes TWO separable emotion-prediction channels — one contingent on the agent's (possibly false) belief and one contingent on reality — and, mirroring the human curse-of-knowledge in affective theory of mind, the reality-contingent emotion leaks into and biases the belief-contingent emotion prediction. Both channels are linearly decodable, largely dissociable, and the leak is causally removable by steering, yielding correct false-belief emotion attributions.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes an agent's COGNITIVE belief STATUS (true/false) from attention heads and describes a 'lookback' binding mechanism (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025). A 2025 paper (Decomposing Theory of Mind) shows ToM steering is mediated by increased emotional processing, and Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference (2025) localizes emotion representations to mid-layers via appraisal concepts. In human neuroscience, AFFECTIVE ToM — inferring how someone will FEEL given their belief state, dissociable from cognitive belief tracking — is robustly established (Skerry & Saxe 2014 'A Common Neural Code for Perceived and Inferred Emotion'; Hooker 2008 'Mentalizing about emotion'; Sebastian 2013; Skerry 2015 three-dimensional mental-state code), and the curse of knowledge biases such affective attributions toward what the observer knows. CRITICALLY, no LLM interpretability work isolates a BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion prediction (how a false-believing agent will feel) as an internal channel SEPARATE from a REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion prediction, nor tests whether the reality channel contaminates the belief channel (an affective curse-of-knowledge), nor localizes/steers this. This differs from cognitive-belief-status decoding (about what the agent believes, not how they will feel about it) and from my prior curse_of_knowledge_leakage proposal (which concerns leakage into a factual ignorant-BELIEF channel, not an EMOTION-prediction channel). We transfer canonical affective-ToM neuroscience into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: A child who believes a box holds chocolate will feel delighted opening it — even if we know it now holds broccoli. Predicting how someone will feel requires reasoning from THEIR belief, not from reality, a capacity human neuroscience identifies as affective theory of mind and shows to be systematically biased by the observer's own knowledge (the curse of knowledge). As LLMs increasingly reason about how people will feel (in assistance, tutoring, mental-health, and social settings), we ask a mechanistic question: when an LLM predicts an agent's emotional reaction, does it compute a belief-contingent emotion (grounded in the agent's possibly-false belief) as a channel distinct from a reality-contingent emotion, and does reality leak into the belief channel? We hypothesize that (i) belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion predictions are two linearly-decodable, largely dissociable channels in the residual stream, (ii) the reality-contingent emotion contaminates the belief-contingent emotion — an internal signature of affective curse-of-knowledge — (iii) the leak is graded with outcome valence intensity and predicts false-belief emotion-attribution errors, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores correct belief-grounded emotion prediction. We build controlled false-belief emotion-attribution scenarios where an agent's belief and reality imply different emotions, with matched conditions where reality is or is not revealed and a synthetic track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode the two emotion channels, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item affective-leak score, test predictiveness, localize responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to cognitive-belief and emotion-inference heads), and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, affective-leak magnitude, valence modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at emotion-relevant tokens read WITHOUT the emotion query, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch (adapted from BigToM/Skerry-Saxe-style stimuli): ~6k affective false-belief scenarios where an AGENT's belief-implied emotion differs from the REALITY-implied emotion, REAL and SYNTHETIC novel-entity tracks, with a key manipulation (model IS vs IS NOT told reality, agent's belief fixed), graded outcome-valence intensity, TRUE-BELIEF control items (both channels agree — no leak expected), and probe time-locked to the pre-discovery moment. We generate 6k and use all (~1k true-belief controls). Belief/reality/emotion labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion are two linearly-decodable, largely dissociable channels): train probe A = BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion and probe B = REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion, anchored on agreeing/single-source control items; compute the principal angle between them and projected-out decodability. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of A and B (vs shuffled control 0.50±0.05) AND the angle theta. Convincing H1: both AUROC ≥ 0.70 (emotion is graded, so a lower bar than binary facts) AND theta ≥ 45 degrees with projected-out drop < 0.05. Indecision: AUROC 0.55–0.70 or theta 25–45 degrees → channels weakly separable; AUROC ≤ 0.55 or theta < 25 degrees refutes clean two-channel structure. Experiment 2 (H2 — reality leaks into the belief channel): define per-item AFFECTIVE LEAK = shift of probe A toward the reality-emotion in reality-revealed minus reality-withheld conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed leak, with true-belief controls confirmed at ~0. Convincing: leak > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models on both tracks, controls near 0. Indecision |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2 (clean belief-grounding — informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is graded with outcome-valence intensity and predicts false-belief emotion-attribution errors): decisive metric first: (a) slope of leak vs valence intensity (convincing if positive, CI excludes 0) and (b) AUROC of the pre-query leak predicting behavioral emotion-attribution errors (convincing ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05). Indecision: slope CI straddles 0 and AUROC 0.55–0.70; negative slope / AUROC ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak; steering restores correct belief-grounded emotion prediction): activation patching reality-revealed<->withheld to locate the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to cognitive-belief/lookback heads and mid-layer emotion-inference units; derive a contrastive affective-leak direction and ablate/subtract. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak and of false-belief emotion errors. Convincing H4: leak reduced ≥ 50% and errors reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/cognitive-belief-direction baselines not selectively acting, the model's own knowledge of reality preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across scenario types (positive/negative surprises, second-order beliefs), real vs synthetic, valence levels (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion channels may be hard to separate cleanly because emotion is a graded, multi-dimensional readout; we mitigate by using scenarios with categorically distinct belief- vs. reality-emotions, anchoring each channel on agreeing/single-source control items, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the relative shift (leak) rather than absolute emotion decoding. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (once the agent tastes/opens, reality genuinely changes their emotion) rather than an anticipatory curse-of-knowledge; we time-lock the probe to the pre-discovery moment (agent still holding the false belief), use the reality-withheld-vs-revealed contrast, and the synthetic track to isolate contamination from valid update. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly ground emotion predictions in the agent's belief, firewalling reality) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding refining the affective-ToM-in-LLMs picture. Emotion/belief-emotion directions may overlap with a generic valence direction; we include matched-valence controls and compare to an emotion-inference direction. The leak may be a distributed component rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore belief-grounded emotion' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Emotion labels are partly subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. Comprehension checks separate genuine affective-ToM failure from parsing failure. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten all emotion prediction; we use small magnitudes, random/cognitive-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: moral_possibility_contamination
Title: That Could Never Happen: Does an Event's Immorality Make an LLM Internally Represent It as Impossible?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human finding that people's DEFAULT representation of what is possible is constrained by morality and rationality (immoral/irrational events are implicitly treated as impossible), an LLM's internally-decoded possibility representation of a physically-possible event is pulled toward IMPOSSIBLE when the event is immoral/norm-violating, holding physical possibility constant. This moral contamination of the possibility flag is linearly decodable, largely dissociable from a separate morality/valence direction, is stronger under fast/implicit read-out than under explicit deliberation, predicts errors in possibility judgments, and is causally removable by steering.
Related Work: Phillips & Cushman (2017, 146 citations) show humans DEFAULT to treating immoral and irrational events as impossible, a default implicit representation dissociable from explicit modal deliberation; 'How people think about possibilities' (2023) and modal-displacement neuroscience (2020) develop the possibility-representation account. In LLM interpretability, 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) isolates linear modal-category vectors (probable/improbable/impossible/inconceivable) reflecting event likelihood and imageability, and 'How LLMs Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility' (2025) shows validity and plausibility are aligned linear directions producing content effects that steering can disentangle. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether an event's MORAL status contaminates the model's internal POSSIBILITY representation - whether immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally tagged as impossible - nor whether this is a fast/default effect distinct from explicit modal reasoning, nor localizes/removes it. This differs from the modal-vector work (which represents graded physical/statistical likelihood, not moral contamination of possibility), from the validity-plausibility conflation work (logical validity vs. semantic plausibility, not morality vs. metaphysical possibility), and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (truth/currency/contestedness/sacredness of factual beliefs). We transfer a canonical cognitive-science phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People implicitly treat things they consider wrong as things that simply cannot be - immoral and irrational events are, by default, represented as impossible, a bias dissociable from explicit reasoning about what is metaphysically or physically possible (Phillips & Cushman, 2017). As LLMs increasingly reason about what is possible (planning, safety, hypotheticals, risk assessment), a consequential question arises: does an LLM's internal representation of possibility get contaminated by an event's morality, so that immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally treated as impossible? We hypothesize that (i) a possibility representation and a morality/valence representation are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) morality leaks into the possibility channel - the internal possibility readout for a physically-possible event is pulled toward 'impossible' when the event is immoral, holding physical possibility constant, (iii) the leak is larger under fast/implicit read-out (early layers / no chain-of-thought) than under explicit deliberation, mirroring the human default-vs-deliberative dissociation, (iv) the leak predicts behavioral possibility-judgment errors, and (v) it is carried by an identifiable component removable by steering. We build a controlled dataset crossing physical possibility (possible/impossible) with morality (immoral/neutral/prosocial), with matched wording and a synthetic-norm track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode possibility vs. morality, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item moral-possibility leak, test the fast-vs-deliberative and predictiveness hypotheses, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, moral-possibility leak magnitude, fast-vs-deliberative modulation, leak-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the event's key tokens read WITHOUT any question, ALL layers (early-vs-late analysis is central), per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k event descriptions crossing PHYSICAL POSSIBILITY (physically-possible vs physically-impossible) with MORALITY (immoral / neutral / prosocial) using matched action templates so morality varies while physical possibility is held constant; REAL and SYNTHETIC-NORM (in-context stipulated novel norms, matched wording) tracks. We generate 6k and use all. Physical-possibility and morality labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — possibility and morality are two linearly-decodable channels): train probe A = POSSIBILITY (physically-possible vs impossible, trained on morally-NEUTRAL items to define a morality-free axis) and probe B = MORALITY (immoral vs prosocial). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of A and B vs shuffled controls (0.50±0.05). Convincing: both ≥ 0.75. Indecision 0.55–0.65; ≤ 0.55 for either refutes that channel. Also compute the principal angle theta (H1 includes 'largely dissociable'): convincing dissociation theta ≥ 60 degrees with projected-out drop < 0.05; 30–60 degrees partial; < 30 degrees entangled. Experiment 2 (H2 — morality leaks into the possibility channel): define per-item MORAL-POSSIBILITY LEAK = shift of probe A toward 'impossible' for physically-POSSIBLE items as a function of immorality (possible+immoral vs matched possible+neutral/prosocial). Decisive metric first: mean signed leak. Convincing: leak > 0 with d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, reproduced in the SYNTHETIC-NORM track (isolating in-context morality from base rates). Indecision |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2. Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is larger under fast/implicit than deliberative processing): decisive metric first: (a) EARLY-minus-LATE-layer leak difference (early-exit read-out as a fast-processing proxy) and (b) no-CoT-minus-CoT behavioral leak. Convincing: leak larger early than late AND larger without CoT than with CoT, both CIs excluding 0. Indecision: one of the two significant / CIs straddle 0 → dissociation weak; neither → H3 refuted. Experiment 4 (H4 — the leak predicts possibility-judgment errors): AUROC of the pre-query leak predicting behavioral errors (calling a possible-but-immoral event impossible). Decisive metric first: AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05; indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H4. Experiment 5 (H5 — the leak is carried by an identifiable component removable by steering): activation patching immoral<->neutral to find the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to modal-category vectors, validity/plausibility directions, and moral-direction heads; derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak and of possibility-judgment errors. Convincing H5: leak reduced ≥ 50% and errors reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/pure-morality-direction baselines not selectively acting, the model's moral judgment preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across event domains, real vs synthetic-norm, and immorality intensity (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (immoral events may be statistically rarer in training data, so 'less likely' is partly correct) rather than a genuine morality-to-possibility contamination; the physically-possible constraint (all target items are genuinely possible), matched-wording neutral/prosocial controls, the synthetic-norm track (morality stipulated in-context, decoupled from base rates), and separating a POSSIBILITY axis from a graded LIKELIHOOD axis are designed to dissociate moral contamination of the categorical possible/impossible flag from mere frequency-based improbability (though full separation from likelihood is difficult and we report both). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly separate morality from possibility) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the canonical human bias. The possibility and morality directions may be entangled such that the 'leak' is imperfect channel separation - still an informative characterization, and directly engages the validity-plausibility conflation literature. Possibility and morality labels are partly subjective/graded; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, noting results reflect the model's training-data notion of morality (itself the object of study). The morality direction may overlap with a valence/harm axis; matched prosocial vs. immoral contrasts and projected-out analyses address this. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The fast-vs-deliberative test uses early-exit as a proxy for default processing, which is imperfect. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to debias possibility' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten the model's possibility discrimination entirely; we use small magnitudes, random/morality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: presupposition_failure_flag
Title: There Is No King of France: Do LLMs Internally Flag Presupposition Failure Apart From Mere Ignorance?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'presupposition-failure' flag that distinguishes questions that are unanswerable because they carry a FALSE PRESUPPOSITION (there is no fact of the matter because the question's premise is false, e.g. 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?') from questions that are merely unanswerable due to MISSING INFORMATION (a determinate answer exists but the model/context lacks it). This flag is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains.
Related Work: A rich line of work shows LLMs linearly encode (un)answerability and control abstention via a direction (Hidden States of Over-Confident LLMs 2023; Detecting (Un)answerability with Linear Directions 2025), encode question ambiguity in sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons steerable to abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Ambiguity 2025), and split abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency via causal inference (ABCA 2025). Critically, 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows internal states encode the knowledge-recall process, not truthfulness, making some hallucinations indistinguishable from facts. ALL of this treats unanswerability/ambiguity as (at most) a two-way answerable-vs-not or conflict-vs-insufficiency split. NONE isolate PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - a question that is void because its premise is false, so the correct response is to CHALLENGE the premise, not to say 'I don't know' - as an internal axis distinct from missing-information ignorance. This is grounded in the linguistics of presupposition accommodation and 'loaded question' fallacies, and targets a distinct failure mode (models answering loaded questions as if valid, or over-generically abstaining) that the abstention/ambiguity literature does not address. It is also distinct from my prior aleatoric/epistemic proposal (randomness vs. ignorance): here both categories are 'unanswerable', but one is void-by-false-premise and the other is determinate-but-unknown.
Abstract: 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?' has no answer - not because the information is missing, but because there is no King of France; the right move is to reject the premise, not to guess or to say 'I don't know'. Humans robustly detect such presupposition failures and repair them, yet LLMs frequently either hallucinate an answer to a loaded question or lump it in with ordinary ignorance. Prior interpretability work isolates a single (un)answerability/abstention direction and an ambiguity signal, and splits abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency, but never asks whether models internally represent PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - unanswerability because the question's premise is false - as its own variable. We hypothesize that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions in matched conditions - answerable, unanswerable-due-to-missing-info, and unanswerable-due-to-false-presupposition - holding surface form as constant as possible, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to decode presupposition-failure vs. generic unanswerability, measure their geometry, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering the presupposition-failure direction should shift the model between premise-challenging, generic abstention, and hallucination. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, premise-challenge/abstention/hallucination rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at question/item tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k questions in three matched conditions holding surface form maximally constant — (A) ANSWERABLE, (B) UNANSWERABLE-MISSING-INFO, (C) UNANSWERABLE-FALSE-PRESUPPOSITION — using presupposition triggers with matched true-vs-false-trigger controls, in REAL and SYNTHETIC-entity tracks. We generate 6k and use all (~2k per condition). A behavioral RESPONSE probe records CHALLENGES-premise / GENERICALLY-ABSTAINS / HALLUCINATES; comprehension checks record whether the model, asked directly, can state the premise is false. Experiment 1 (H1 — a presupposition-failure flag is linearly decodable): train probe I = generic UNANSWERABILITY (A vs B+C) and probe II = PRESUPPOSITION-FAILURE (C vs B, restricted to unanswerable items). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of probe II vs shuffled control (0.50±0.05). Convincing H1: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1 (models lump false-premise with ordinary ignorance internally — an informative negative). Experiment 2 (H2 — the flag is largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction): replicate a generic abstention direction as baseline; compute the principal angle theta between probe II and the abstention direction and projected-out decodability of II. Decisive metric first: theta, corroborated by projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Convincing: theta ≥ 60 degrees; indecision 30–60 degrees → partial entanglement; < 30 degrees → not a distinct axis (H2 refuted, characterize the entanglement). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates premise-challenging vs hallucination/generic-abstention): derive a presupposition-failure steering direction (false-presupposition vs missing-info activations). Decisive metric first: (a) steering missing-info questions TOWARD 'false-presupposition' increases premise-challenging language and reduces generic abstention; (b) steering false-presupposition questions AWAY increases hallucination/generic abstention. Convincing H3: ≥ 15 pp shift in premise-challenge rate in the predicted direction for each polarity, with random-direction and generic-abstention-direction baselines < 5 pp, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means no causal gating. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H2/H3): activation patching to find heads carrying the presupposition-failure signal (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to ambiguity-encoding neurons and abstention-direction heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): the internal presupposition-failure readout predicts behavioral premise-challenging (vs hallucination) better than a log-prob baseline AND better than the generic-unanswerability probe (AUROC ≥ 0.70, improvement ≥ 0.05 over each). Behavioral scoring uses an LLM judge with human validation on a 200-item sample. Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across trigger types, domains, synthetic->real (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Presupposition-failure may be entangled with surface trigger words (definite descriptions, factive verbs) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched true-vs-false-trigger controls, paraphrase perturbations, and the synthetic-entity track where the false premise is established in-context rather than lexically signaled. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Presupposition-failure and generic-unanswerability directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant given the recall-process finding that models poorly separate ignorance from falsehood internally). Some 'false-presupposition' items may be treated by the model as merely rare/unknown; comprehension checks and the synthetic track help disentangle premise-detection from premise-flagging, and a robust negative result (models lump false-premise questions with ordinary ignorance internally) is itself a valuable, publishable finding consistent with 'LLMs do NOT know what they don't know'. Behavioral premise-challenge vs. abstention vs. hallucination scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate premise-challenging; we use small magnitudes, random/abstention-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty claims: (1) LLMs encode a distinct internal presupposition-failure variable separating false-premise from missing-information questions; (2) linearly decodable within the unanswerable subset, not a byproduct of generic answerability signals; (3) geometrically distinct/largely orthogonal to known abstention/unanswerability directions; (4) causally affects challenge-premise vs abstain vs hallucinate; (5) generalizes beyond lexical triggers via matched and synthetic-entity settings. Sits very close to existing answerability/abstention probe work, false-premise QA benchmarks (CREPE/FalseQA/ELOQ), and ABCA-style abstention splits. The delta is narrower than advertised: not discovering false-premise behavior, but isolating a specific internal axis for presupposition failure distinct from generic unanswerability and conflict/insufficiency — meaningful if demonstrated cleanly with causal steering, but not a new problem family. C-vs-B discrimination under matched surface forms is non-trivial. Overlap with internal answerability-readout literature is substantial; the 'NONE isolate presupposition failure' claim is overstated.
