Name: anchoring_pull_estimate_contamination
Title: Dragged Toward the Number: Does an Arbitrary Anchor Contaminate an LLM's Internal Estimate of a Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human anchoring bias, when an LLM is exposed to an explicitly-arbitrary number before estimating a quantity, its internally-decoded belief about that quantity (read from the known monotonic numeric subspace) is pulled toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence for the quantity constant. This anchor-pull is a distinct, linearly-decodable displacement of the magnitude representation that is dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, is graded with anchor distance, predicts biased numeric answers, and is causally removable by steering the numeric subspace, restoring an unbiased estimate.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring: log-probability shifts and Shapley attribution attribute the bias to anchor reweighting (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024, which also finds a 'round number bias'). A separate line shows LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; Language Models Encode the Value of Numbers Linearly 2024; sinusoidal number probes 2025). Closest is 'Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' (2025), which shows irrelevant numerical context perturbs magnitude representations, but it concerns interference among an entity's own attributes, not the classic anchoring paradigm. CRITICALLY, no work isolates the ANCHOR'S PULL as a distinct internal displacement of the model's estimate-of-the-quantity representation, separable from the genuine evidence-based estimate; tests whether the pull is graded with anchor distance and predicts biased answers; or causally removes it via the numeric subspace to restore an unbiased estimate. We transfer a 50-year, meta-analytically robust human bias (Hedges' g=0.825; A Theoretical Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis 2023) into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment using existing numeric-subspace probing machinery, distinct from behavioral/attribution anchoring work and from my prior belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: Ask people to estimate the height of Mount Everest after seeing an arbitrary number, and their estimate drifts toward that number — numeric anchoring, one of the most robust and durable biases in the behavioral sciences. LLMs are known to reproduce anchoring at the output level, but it is unknown whether an arbitrary anchor actually contaminates the model's internal representation of the quantity, or merely nudges surface tokens. Leveraging prior findings that LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces, we ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does exposure to an explicitly-arbitrary anchor displace the model's internally-decoded estimate of a quantity toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence constant? We hypothesize that (i) the model's estimate of the quantity is linearly decodable from its numeric subspace, (ii) an arbitrary anchor produces a decodable displacement of that estimate toward the anchor — an internal anchor-pull — dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, (iii) the pull is graded with anchor distance, largest under high uncertainty, and predicts biased numeric answers, and (iv) the pull is carried by movement along the numeric subspace such that steering it back abolishes the bias. We build a controlled dataset of quantity-estimation items presented with matched anchor conditions (no-anchor, low-anchor, high-anchor, and an explicitly-random anchor) at graded distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train monotonic numeric probes to read the internal estimate, quantify a per-item anchor-pull, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible subspace/heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe R^2/accuracy, anchor-pull magnitude, distance/uncertainty modulation, pull–bias AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only probes trained (numeric probes: linear + monotonic-subspace + sinusoidal baselines fit by ridge/least-squares, regularization by CV). Activations: residual stream at quantity/answer tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k quantity-estimation items across domains (geographic magnitudes, populations, prices, physical measurements, dates); REAL track (model has partial knowledge, evidence present) and SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (quantity fixed by in-context evidence). Matched anchor conditions holding question+evidence constant: NO-ANCHOR, LOW-ANCHOR, HIGH-ANCHOR (classic compare-then-estimate), and EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor; anchor DISTANCE graded. We generate 6k and use all. Experiment 1 (H1 — the internal estimate of the quantity is linearly decodable from the numeric subspace): fit the numeric probe to decode the model's internal estimate of Q, calibrated against the model's stated estimates on a held-out set. Decisive metric first: held-out decoding R^2 (or rank correlation) vs a shuffled-label control (~0). Convincing H1: R^2 ≥ 0.4 (or Spearman ≥ 0.6) at best layer on both tracks. Indecision R^2 0.15–0.4 → estimate only weakly decodable; R^2 < 0.15 refutes H1. Experiment 2 (H2 — an arbitrary anchor produces a decodable displacement of the estimate toward the anchor, dissociable from the evidence-based estimate): define per-item ANCHOR-PULL = shift of the decoded estimate toward the anchor in anchored minus NO-ANCHOR conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed pull (as a fraction of anchor distance). Convincing H2: pull > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, PRESENT for the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor and in the SYNTHETIC track (isolating pull from valid inference); dissociation shown by decomposing the estimate into an evidence component (recoverable at NO-ANCHOR) plus an anchor displacement aligned with the anchor's numeric-subspace position. Indecision |pull| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; pull ≤ 0 refutes H2 (anchoring is only a surface-token effect — informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the pull is graded with anchor distance, largest under high uncertainty, and predicts biased answers): decisive metric first: (a) slope of pull vs anchor distance (convincing if positive, CI excludes 0), (b) pull(high-uncertainty real items) minus pull(low-uncertainty synthetic items) > 0 (CI excludes 0), (c) correlation/AUROC of internal pull predicting behavioral answer bias ≥ 0.70 beating log-prob and surface baselines by ≥ 0.05. Indecision: CIs straddle 0 / AUROC 0.55–0.70; negatives refute the corresponding sub-claim of H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — the pull is carried by movement along the numeric subspace; steering it back abolishes the bias): activation patching anchored<->NO-ANCHOR to find the minimal component transporting the anchor into the numeric subspace (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to known numeric-property subspaces/heads; then remove the pull by subtracting the contrastive direction OR projecting the numeric-subspace estimate back to its NO-ANCHOR position. Decisive metric first: reduction of behavioral answer bias toward the anchor. Convincing H4: bias reduced ≥ 50% with random-direction/off-subspace steering not selectively debiasing, non-anchored estimation accuracy preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50%; < 20% means the pull is not a steerable subspace displacement. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across domains, real vs synthetic, anchor types (relevant vs explicitly-random), and distances (retention: Spearman ≥ 0.5). Thresholds fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pull could reflect legitimate inference (an anchor might, in some prompts, carry genuine information); the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor condition and the SYNTHETIC track (where the true value is fixed by in-context evidence, so any anchor influence is a bias) are designed to isolate genuine anchoring from valid inference, and we compare relevant vs. random anchors. The numeric-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, harder than a binary belief probe; we mitigate using established monotonic/linear/sinusoidal numeric-probe methods, calibrating against the model's own stated estimates, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on relative displacement rather than absolute values. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — anchoring is only a surface token effect, not a contamination of the internal estimate — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding sharpening the behavioral anchoring picture). The pull could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a magnitude-representation shift; probing at answer tokens distinct from the anchor, order/paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks mitigate this. The anchor displacement and evidence estimate may be entangled in the same subspace such that clean decomposition fails — still an informative characterization. Localization may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer/project back to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all numeric estimation; we use small magnitudes, geometry-aware subspace corrections, random-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-anchored accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) arbitrary anchors shift the model's internal decoded estimate of a quantity, not just its output distribution; (2) a distinct, linearly decodable displacement separable from the evidence-based estimate; (3) graded with anchor distance and uncertainty; (4) predicts answer bias better than surface signals; (5) steering the numeric subspace back removes the bias while preserving numeric competence. Anchoring in LLMs is well established behaviorally, and recent work already localizes anchoring pathways and shows internal reweighting/attributional mechanisms; numeric magnitude subspaces are known and causally editable. The real delta is narrower than advertised: testing whether anchoring specifically contaminates a known monotonic numeric-magnitude representation in a graded, decodable, steerable way while holding evidence fixed — a meaningful integration of two prior literatures, aided by explicit-random anchor + synthetic-evidence tracks. Novelty contested: 'Localizing Anchoring Pathways' and related mechanism papers already claim internal localization/reweighting; the proposal does not crisply distinguish why 'contamination of numeric subspace estimate' is qualitatively beyond them.

Name: belief_hysteresis_asymmetry
Title: Easy to Convince, Hard to Un-Convince: Belief-Installation Hysteresis in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit belief hysteresis: it takes systematically LESS in-context evidence to move the internally-decoded belief in a claim from 'disbelieved' to 'believed' than to move it back from 'believed' to 'disbelieved', even when the evidence pieces are matched in strength. This install-vs-uninstall asymmetry traces a hysteresis loop in the internal belief readout as evidence is added then removed/reversed, is graded, predicts sticky behavioral errors, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to symmetrize belief updating.
Related Work: Prior work studies (a) susceptibility to persuasion/misinformation over turns (The Earth is Flat 2023; Vulnerability of LLM Belief Systems 2026; Accumulating Context Changes Beliefs 2025; Knowledge Drift 2024), (b) catastrophic interference from contradictory continual updates (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025) and continual-pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) belief depth of implanted facts (Believe It or Not 2025), (d) retraction driven by momentary belief (When Do LLMs Admit Their Mistakes 2025), and my own prior proposals on entrenchment (freezing of plasticity), continued-influence of retracted claims, and illusory-truth repetition. NONE isolate a SYMMETRY question: is the internal belief-update operator direction-dependent, requiring more evidence to REMOVE a belief than to INSTALL it, holding evidence strength matched? Entrenchment (my prior) concerns freezing WITHIN a single reasoning trace; continued-influence concerns a discrete retraction event. Here the object is a hysteresis LOOP: sweep evidence up (install), then symmetrically sweep it down (uninstall), and measure the gap and area of the loop in the internal belief readout as a fundamental property of in-context belief dynamics. This reframes 'stubbornness' as a measurable directional asymmetry in the update operator and gives it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: Belief change should, in a rational agent, be reversible: if a certain amount of evidence is enough to make you believe a claim, a symmetric amount of counter-evidence should be enough to make you disbelieve it again. We ask whether LLMs violate this symmetry, exhibiting belief hysteresis: needing systematically more in-context evidence to UN-install a belief than to install it. We hypothesize that (i) sweeping matched-strength evidence pieces up (toward the claim) and then back down (against it) traces a hysteresis loop in the model's linearly-decoded belief readout, with a nonzero loop area; (ii) the install-vs-uninstall asymmetry is graded and larger for plausible/prior-consistent claims; (iii) the internal asymmetry predicts sticky behavioral errors (the model keeps asserting a claim after counter-evidence should have dislodged it); and (iv) the asymmetry is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it symmetrizes updating. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims each embedded in an evidence sequence with a specified likelihood-ratio per piece, presented in matched INSTALL sweeps (evidence for, then against) and UNINSTALL sweeps (starting from a believed state), including a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes, trace belief trajectories across the evidence sweep, quantify per-item hysteresis loop area and install/uninstall thresholds, test predictiveness against a Bayesian-symmetric baseline, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal symmetrization by steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, loop area, install-vs-uninstall threshold gap, sticky-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering symmetry restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — installing a belief takes less matched in-context evidence than un-installing it, tracing a hysteresis loop with nonzero area in the internally-decoded belief readout; H2 — the install-vs-uninstall gap is graded and larger for prior-plausible claims than for prior-implausible ones; H3 — the internal asymmetry predicts sticky behavioral errors (the model keeps asserting a claim after matched counter-evidence should have dislodged it); H4 — the asymmetry is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to symmetrize updating.

Data (built from scratch; one shared dataset serves all experiments). ~5,000 item-state claims in two tracks: (a) REAL claims the target models reliably know or reliably reject (drawn from TriviaQA and the CounterFact subject-relation-object set, ~3,000 usable after filtering to items every target model answers consistently closed-book); (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (~2,000, e.g. "Zorblax orbits Kelvath") with stipulated ground truth and an explicit per-piece likelihood ratio, so a Bayesian-symmetric oracle trajectory is computable. We use ~5,000 of the ~5,000 generated (all pass a fluency/parse filter); fewer only if a model's closed-book consistency filter drops an item for that model. Each claim carries an evidence SEQUENCE of k pieces (k up to 6) each with a stipulated strength; two matched sweeps are built per claim holding per-piece strengths and total magnitude identical but mirrored: INSTALL (neutral → k pieces FOR → k matched pieces AGAINST) and UNINSTALL (neutral → k AGAINST → k FOR). Prior-plausibility (prior-consistent vs prior-contradicting) is crossed in. Each item also carries a behavioral ASSERTION probe at every step, comprehension checks ("restate the latest evidence"), and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations. A human validates 200 sampled items for matched strength.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B (base and instruct). Nothing in the transformer is trainable; the only trained objects are linear probes (L2-regularized logistic/linear regression, one per layer) fit on frozen residual-stream activations. Probes: 80/20 item-disjoint train/test split, 5-fold CV for the L2 penalty, 3 seeds {0,1,2}; report mean±sd. Steering uses contrastive activation addition (difference-of-means direction) with coefficient α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer activation std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — hysteresis loop area). For each item, read the internal belief probe at every evidence step of the up-then-down INSTALL sweep, plot belief vs cumulative signed evidence, and compute LOOP AREA and the residual belief at sweep end (should be ≈ the neutral start if updating is reversible). Systems compared: observed loop vs the Bayesian-symmetric oracle trajectory (synthetic track) / a reversible-null bootstrap (real track). Decisive metric: mean loop area, normalized to the probe's belief range, tested > 0 per model/track. Convincing: normalized loop area ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models. Indecision band: normalized loop area in [0.03, 0.10] or CI touching 0 — cannot distinguish hysteresis from probe noise; we then withhold the H1 claim and report the bound. Negative (area ≤ 0.03, CI includes 0): LLMs update reversibly — H1 rejected, a reassuring result reported as such.

Experiment 2 (H2 — install/uninstall threshold gap, graded by plausibility). Define per-item INSTALL THRESHOLD (evidence to cross a "believed" criterion of probe belief = 0.5→0.75) and UNINSTALL THRESHOLD (counter-evidence to drop back below 0.5 once believed), matched in per-piece strength. Decisive metric: (uninstall − install) threshold gap in units of stipulated log-likelihood-ratio, tested > 0 and larger for prior-consistent than prior-contradicting claims (interaction term). Convincing: mean gap ≥ 0.5 LLR units, CI excludes 0, and plausibility interaction significant (p<0.01) in ≥3 models. Indecision band: gap in [0.15, 0.5] LLR — report as weak/graded evidence, no strong claim. Negative (gap ≤ 0.15 or plausibility interaction absent): asymmetry is not graded — the H2 portion is rejected while H1 may still hold.

Experiment 3 (H3 — internal asymmetry predicts sticky errors). Collect behavioral "sticky" errors: after the counter-evidence half of the sweep, does the model still assert the original claim (LLM-judge scored on open output, 300 items human-validated, target κ ≥ 0.7)? Decisive metric first: AUROC of per-item loop area / uninstall-threshold predicting sticky error, compared against a closed-book log-prob baseline. Convincing: probe-based AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 above the log-prob baseline in ≥3 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or within 0.05 of baseline — internal signal is present but not clearly the driver. Negative (AUROC ≤ 0.60): internal hysteresis does not track behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal symmetrization). Use activation patching / causal mediation, patching UNINSTALL-phase activations against a fresh no-prior-belief run to find the minimal head/layer set that resists the belief drop; compare to truth/belief heads. Then derive a contrastive stubbornness/hysteresis steering direction (high- vs low-hysteresis states) and test: (a) subtracting it drives loop area → 0 and uninstall-threshold → install-threshold and lowers sticky errors; (b) adding it exaggerates hysteresis; (c) specificity — random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively symmetrize; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k-item subset) and perplexity on WikiText-103 (2k lines). Decisive metric: reduction in normalized loop area under subtraction. Convincing: ≥50% loop-area reduction with <2% absolute MMLU drop and <5% perplexity increase, and random/truth baselines showing <15% reduction. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction, or collateral MMLU drop 2–5% — a partial/contaminated effect, reported without a clean causal claim. Negative (<20% reduction or effect matched by control directions): no identifiable symmetrizing component — H4 rejected. All effects are planned, not yet measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Hysteresis could partly reflect rational asymmetry (e.g. a prior-plausible claim rationally needs more counter-evidence to dislodge); the synthetic track with explicit matched likelihood ratios and a Bayesian-symmetric oracle, plus the prior-plausibility manipulation, are designed to separate genuine order/direction-dependent stubbornness from justified prior-weighting, though full separation is hard for real claims. The apparent loop could be driven by evidence-order/primacy effects rather than an install-vs-uninstall asymmetry per se; matched reversed sweeps and order-of-piece perturbations disentangle these (both sweeps contain identical pieces in mirrored order). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result -- LLMs update reversibly -- is itself valuable and reassuring). Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat loop shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The stubbornness component may be distributed; we treat 'steer to symmetrize' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately gullible/labile; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-swept accuracy, and general benchmarks. Sticky-error scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: recursive_belief_depth_collapse
Title: Losing the Thread: Do LLMs' Nested Belief Representations Collapse Toward Reality as Recursion Deepens?
Short Hypothesis: As belief-attribution recursion deepens ('A thinks B thinks C believes X'), an LLM's internally-decoded representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief progressively DEGRADES and collapses toward the model's own ground-truth (reality) belief — an internal 'egocentric compression' that grows with nesting order, is linearly measurable as a depth-dependent loss of distinctness between the nested-agent belief channel and the reality channel, predicts higher-order ToM errors, and is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness.
Related Work: Interpretability work decodes first/second-order belief STATUS (true/false) of a protagonist and an oracle from attention heads and shows steering improves ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via visibility (Lookbacks 2025). Behavioral work shows higher-order ToM accuracy DECLINES with recursion order (HI-TOM 2023; Multi-Order ToM 2024; Spontaneous High-Order Generalization 2025) but treats models as black boxes. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether this behavioral decline reflects an INTERNAL representational phenomenon: that with increasing nesting depth the model fails to maintain a distinct representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief and instead reuses its own reality/ground-truth belief (a depth-dependent egocentric collapse). Prior belief-decoding is at fixed order (1st/2nd); my prior curse_of_knowledge proposal concerns a single-level ignorant-belief leak, not a depth-scaling collapse across recursion orders. We reframe higher-order ToM failure as a measurable, mechanistic loss of nested-belief distinctness and give it a causal treatment.
Abstract: Humans can recurse: 'Ann thinks Bob believes Cara knows the ball is in the box.' LLMs reproduce this up to a point, but their accuracy falls as the nesting deepens — a robust behavioral finding whose internal cause is unknown. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does the model actually maintain a distinct internal representation of each nested agent's belief, or does the deepest embedded belief progressively collapse toward the model's own view of reality as recursion depth grows? We hypothesize that (i) the belief attributed to the deepest embedded agent is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) as nesting order increases the deepest-agent belief channel loses distinctness from the reality/ground-truth channel — a depth-dependent egocentric compression — (iii) the degree of this internal collapse predicts higher-order ToM errors, and (iv) the collapse is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness, improving higher-order ToM. We build a controlled dataset of stories with nested belief attributions from order 1 to 5, where at each depth the deepest agent holds a belief that diverges from reality (so the two channels are dissociable), plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the deepest-agent belief and the reality belief at each order, quantify a per-order collapse score (loss of distinctness), test its predictiveness for behavioral errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to belief/lookback heads), and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-order collapse score, subspace angle by depth, collapse–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering distinctness and accuracy gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — the belief attributed to the deepest embedded agent in a nested attribution is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — as nesting order grows, the deepest-agent belief channel loses distinctness from the model's own reality/ground-truth channel (a depth-dependent egocentric collapse); H3 — the degree of internal collapse predicts higher-order Theory-of-Mind (ToM) errors; H4 — the collapse is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness, improving higher-order ToM accuracy.

Data (built from scratch, adapting existing generators). ~5,000 stories with nested belief attributions of order O ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}, generated with the HI-TOM and Multi-Order-ToM templates (public) but constrained so the DEEPEST embedded agent holds a belief that DIVERGES from reality at every order (false-belief chains), making the deepest-agent belief and the reality state dissociable. Matched TRUE-BELIEF chains (deepest belief = reality) are included as controls, and story length is matched across orders to control context length. Two tracks: REAL entities (~3,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-agent/object/location track (~2,000) to control pretraining priors. We use all ~5,000 (fewer for a given model only if a comprehension-check filter drops items). Each story carries a behavioral higher-order QUESTION probe (what does the deepest agent believe?), comprehension checks ("who observed what at each level"), balanced reality-location assignment, and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations; 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression, per layer, item-disjoint 80/20 split, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, report mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — deepest-agent belief is decodable). At the state/object tokens, without asking the question, train linear probes to read (A) the deepest-agent belief and (B) the reality state, anchored on true-belief-agreeing and reality-only items, with shuffled-label control tasks. Decisive metric: order-1 and order-2 deepest-agent probe AUROC vs shuffled-label chance. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.80 at O≤2 in ≥3 of 4 models with the control task at chance. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65–0.80 — decodable but weak, reported as such. Negative (AUROC ≤ 0.65 even at O=1): the deepest-agent belief is not linearly represented — H1 rejected and later experiments reinterpreted as readout failure.

Experiment 2 (H2 — depth-dependent collapse). On false-belief chains, measure across O ∈ {1..5}: (i) deepest-agent probe accuracy, (ii) subspace angle between the deepest-agent and reality directions, (iii) the rate at which the deepest-agent readout reports the reality value. Decisive metric first: slope of the reality-value error rate vs O (positive slope = collapse). Convincing: monotonic increase with a fitted slope whose CI excludes 0 in ≥3 models, and larger collapse on false- than true-belief chains. Indecision band: slope CI touching 0 or non-monotonic — collapse not established; report trajectory. Negative (flat/declining error rate with O): nested beliefs stay distinct — H2 rejected (a valuable finding that higher-order errors are purely readout/parsing).

Experiment 3 (H3 — collapse predicts ToM errors). Collect behavioral higher-order errors per item. Decisive metric: AUROC of the per-item collapse score (read before the question) predicting the behavioral error, vs a log-prob baseline and a surface-feature (length/order) baseline. Convincing: collapse AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models; additionally the per-model collapse-onset order predicts the accuracy cliff order (±1). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive only. Negative (≤0.60): internal collapse does not explain behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — causal restoration). Localize via activation patching the heads carrying distinct deepest-agent belief (patch low-order distinct-belief activations into high-order runs); compare to belief heads and lookback/binding heads. Derive a "nested-belief distinctness" steering direction and test: (a) steering restores deepest-agent distinctness and raises higher-order ToM accuracy; (b) negation exaggerates collapse; (c) specificity — random and reality-direction steering do not selectively restore distinctness and the model's own reality belief is preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), low-order accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric: higher-order (O≥3) accuracy gain under steering. Convincing: ≥10 percentage-point accuracy gain at O≥3, <2 pt drop at O≤2, <5% perplexity rise, controls <3 pt. Indecision band: 4–10 pt gain or collateral drop 2–5 pt — partial/contaminated. Negative (<4 pt or matched by controls): no steerable component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral decline at higher orders could stem from parsing/binding failures (the model loses track of who is who) rather than a belief-toward-reality collapse; comprehension checks, the binding-lookback comparison, and separating 'reports reality' from 'reports a random other agent' errors help distinguish egocentric collapse from generic confusion. The deepest-agent and reality channels may be hard to separate cleanly at high orders precisely because they collapse — which is the phenomenon, but it complicates probe anchoring; we anchor probes on low-order and true-belief-agreeing items and report layerwise results with control tasks. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — nested beliefs stay distinct and errors are purely a readout/parsing issue — would itself be a valuable finding). Collapse could be confounded with context length at higher orders; length-matched controls and the true-belief control chains address this. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer/order; we report layerwise results. The distinctness-maintaining component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore distinctness/accuracy' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or corrupt the model's own reality belief; we use small magnitudes, random/reality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, low-order accuracy, and general benchmarks. Human ToM comparison is structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: global_self_competence_belief
Title: How Good Am I At This? A Domain-Level Self-Competence Belief That Miscalibrates and Biases LLM Per-Item Answers
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human dissociation between local confidence (belief about a specific decision) and global self-performance estimates (belief about one's general skill in a domain), an LLM maintains an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a whole domain/task-type that is (i) linearly decodable and distinct from its per-item correctness signal, (ii) systematically miscalibrated against the model's true domain accuracy, and (iii) causally biases per-item answering behavior (attempt/abstain, confidence, effort), such that steering the global self-competence belief shifts per-item behavior even when the item itself is unchanged.
Related Work: Human metacognition robustly dissociates LOCAL confidence in a single decision from GLOBAL self-performance estimates (SPEs) about one's ability in a domain, with distinct cues, neural substrates, and characteristic drift when feedback is absent (Metacognition prospective vs retrospective, 2016; Formation of global self-beliefs in the human brain, 2020; Learning about Self-Performance in the Absence of Feedback, 2018; Domain-specific updating of self-beliefs, 2023). In LLM interpretability, all self-knowledge probing is LOCAL/per-item: solvability belief per problem (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025), in-advance per-question correctness directions (No Answer Needed, 2025), failure prediction (Gnosis, 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior, 2025), early per-trace outcome commitment (Temporal Predictors, 2025), and difficulty perception per problem (Probing Difficulty Perception, 2025). My prior proposals concern per-item behavioral commitment (behavioral_self_prediction_gap) and endowment of self-generated claims. CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief — the model's estimate of its own ability in a whole domain/task-type, abstracted over individual items — as a channel distinct from the per-item correctness signal, test whether it is miscalibrated against true domain accuracy, or show it causally biases per-item behavior independent of item content. We transfer the canonical human local/global metacognition dissociation into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People carry two kinds of self-knowledge: fleeting confidence in a single answer, and a slower, more global sense of how good they are at a whole domain — 'I'm good at math but bad at names.' These global self-performance estimates are dissociable from local confidence, drift from reality when feedback is scarce, and steer how much effort and risk people take. As LLMs increasingly self-assess (deciding whether to attempt, abstain, or hedge), we ask whether they form an analogous internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a domain, whether it is calibrated, and whether it biases their per-item behavior. We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's global self-competence belief for a task-type is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations and is distinct from its per-item correctness signal; (ii) this global belief is systematically miscalibrated relative to the model's true domain accuracy (over/under-confident in specific domains); and (iii) it causally biases per-item behavior — attempting vs. abstaining, expressed confidence, reasoning effort — so that steering the global belief shifts behavior on an unchanged item. We build a controlled dataset spanning many domains/task-types where the model's true per-domain accuracy is measurable, presenting items with matched framings that make the domain salient. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode global self-competence vs. per-item correctness, measure their geometry, quantify a calibration gap against true accuracy, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the global-competence direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, global-competence calibration gap, per-item behavior shift under steering, patching effect sizes, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — an LLM's GLOBAL self-competence belief for a task-type is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations and is distinct from its per-item correctness signal; H2 — this global belief is systematically miscalibrated relative to the model's true per-domain accuracy; H3 — the global belief causally biases per-item behavior (attempt-vs-abstain, expressed confidence, reasoning effort), such that steering it shifts behavior on an item whose content is held fixed.

Data (assembled from existing sets + a synthetic track). ~8,000 items across many domains/task-types with measurable true per-domain accuracy: MMLU by subject (public, 14k questions; sample ~4,000 across ~20 subjects), GSM8K arithmetic (~1,000), TriviaQA (~1,000), a code track from MBPP (~500), date/entity-attribute facts from CounterFact (~1,000), plus a SYNTHETIC novel-entity-domain track (~500) where true accuracy is set by construction. We use ~8,000 of the available pool (capped per domain to keep domains balanced; fewer only where a domain has too few clean items). Each item is presented in a frame that makes the domain salient ("This is a [domain] question: ..."); true per-domain accuracy is measured empirically per model. Each item carries a global self-competence elicitation ("How good are you at [domain] questions in general?"), a per-item local confidence probe, comprehension checks, and 3 framing paraphrases.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B (instruct). No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen activations (L2 logistic/linear regression per layer; item- and domain-disjoint splits so the global probe is tested on held-out domains; 5-fold CV; seeds {0,1,2}; mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — decodable and distinct global-competence channel). At the domain-salient tokens, before the item is answered, train probes for (A) GLOBAL self-competence (calibrated against elicited/behavioral global estimates) and (B) per-item CORRECTNESS (the in-advance correctness direction). Then compute cosine/subspace angle between the two directions and test whether global competence remains decodable after projecting out the per-item-correctness direction, generalizing to held-out domains and the synthetic track. Decisive metric first: cross-domain global-competence probe AUROC/R² on held-out domains, and residual decodability after projecting out correctness. Convincing: held-out global-competence R² ≥ 0.3 (or AUROC ≥ 0.75 for a high/low split), subspace angle ≥ 30°, and >60% of decodability retained after projecting out correctness, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 15–30° or 30–60% retained — channels partly entangled; report as such. Negative (angle <15° or <30% retained): no distinct global channel, only per-item signals — H1 rejected (a valuable limit on LLM metacognition).

Experiment 2 (H2 — calibration gap). Compare decoded global self-competence per domain to the model's measured true per-domain accuracy. Decisive metric: signed per-domain calibration gap (decoded competence − true accuracy) and its systematicity (e.g. inflated on confident-but-wrong domains). Convincing: mean |gap| ≥ 0.15 (on a 0–1 scale) with a consistent sign pattern across ≥3 models, and decoded-vs-verbal competence agreeing in direction. Indecision band: |gap| 0.05–0.15 — mild/uncertain miscalibration. Negative (|gap| < 0.05): global competence is well-calibrated — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal bias on fixed items). Localize the global-competence signal via activation patching (patch high-competence-domain activations into low-competence-domain runs on a fixed item). Derive a global-competence steering direction and, holding the item fixed, test: (a) steering "high" raises attempt rate and expressed confidence and lowers abstention/hedging; (b) steering "low" does the reverse; (c) specificity — random and per-item-correctness directions do not selectively move global behavior, and the item's actual correctness is not the driver; (d) steering toward the model's TRUE accuracy improves attempt/abstain calibration; (e) collateral — MMLU (1k held-out subset), perplexity (WikiText, 2k lines). Also test that the global readout predicts behavior beyond per-item correctness (incremental AUROC / partial regression). Decisive metric first: change in attempt/abstain rate on fixed items under ±steering, with random/correctness-direction controls. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point behavior swing between +high and +low steering, controls <5 pt, incremental prediction AUROC ≥ 0.05 over the correctness baseline, <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: 5–15 pt swing or incremental AUROC 0.02–0.05 — weak causal role. Negative (<5 pt swing or matched by controls): global competence does not gate behavior — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'global self-competence' probe may in fact recover a domain-identity or difficulty feature rather than a genuine self-referential competence belief; we mitigate by (i) contrasting domains matched on difficulty but differing in the model's actual accuracy, (ii) using the synthetic track where competence is manipulable independent of surface domain, and (iii) testing incremental prediction of self-behavior beyond difficulty/correctness signals — a probe that only captures difficulty would fail these controls. Global and per-item channels may be strongly entangled (the global belief may be a running average of local signals); the projected-out analyses and fixed-item steering (which holds the item and its per-item correctness constant while moving global competence) are designed to dissociate them, and even a finding of entanglement is informative. The global-competence probe requires a calibrated readout, harder than a binary probe; we calibrate against elicited/behavioral global estimates and true accuracy, report layerwise results with control tasks, and focus on relative structure. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs have no distinct global self-competence representation, only per-item signals) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding about the limits of LLM metacognition. Behavioral measures (attempt/abstain, hedging) depend on prompt scaffolding and may reflect instruction-following; matched framings, comprehension checks, and the fixed-item steering test disentangle this. The competence signal may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to shift behavior/improve calibration' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate over/under-confidence; we use small magnitudes, random/per-item-correctness-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may show different self-competence structure than base models (an informative comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: self_consistency_pressure_belief
Title: Sticking to My Story: An Internal Consistency-Pressure Signal That Pulls an LLM's Belief Toward What It Already Said
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM has already asserted a claim earlier in the same context, it forms an internal 'consistency pressure' representation that pulls its subsequently-decoded belief about that claim TOWARD the prior assertion, independent of (and even against) the claim's truth. This consistency-pressure signal is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether the model revises an erroneous prior assertion vs. doubles down to stay consistent with itself.
Related Work: Sycophancy work (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Simulated Adoption 2026) isolates a late-layer preference-shift / orthogonal-interference mechanism driven by EXTERNAL user opinion, and finds user expertise is NOT encoded. Retraction work (When Do LLMs Admit Their Mistakes 2025) shows a momentary correctness-belief probe predicts and causally drives retraction, but does not isolate a self-consistency drive as a variable competing with truth. Behavioral work (How Overconfidence in Initial Choices Modulate Change of Mind 2025) documents a choice-supportive bias and a drive to maintain consistency with prior commitments, and AssertBench (2025) measures 'sticking to one's guns' behaviorally. Stubbornness/interference (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025) and my prior belief_hysteresis_asymmetry proposal concern training-time contradiction damage and evidence-order asymmetry respectively. CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal, decodable representation of SELF-consistency pressure (the pull toward the model's OWN prior in-context assertion) as a channel distinct from the truth-value direction, nor test whether it causally overrides truth to make the model double down on its own error. This differs from sycophancy (external source), retraction (correctness belief, not consistency drive), and hysteresis (evidence order). We isolate self-authored commitment as a truth-competing belief pressure and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People are reluctant to contradict what they have just said, and LLMs show a similar choice-supportive bias, doubling down on an initial answer even when it is wrong. Prior mechanistic work explains sycophancy (caving to a user) and retraction (admitting error via a correctness belief), but no work isolates the internal drive that makes a model stay consistent with ITS OWN prior assertion. We ask a sharper question: after an LLM asserts a claim earlier in a context, does it form an internal 'consistency pressure' signal that pulls its later belief about that claim toward the prior assertion, independent of truth? We hypothesize this signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model revises an erroneous prior assertion or doubles down. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims where the model is first led to assert a claim (correctly or incorrectly), then, later in the same context, its internal belief and its behavioral revision are probed after new evidence is presented. We hold the new evidence and the claim's truth constant while varying whether the model previously asserted the claim, isolating self-consistency pressure from truth and from external pressure. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode consistency-pressure vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item 'double-down' pull, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the consistency-pressure direction to restore or suppress belief revision. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, double-down pull magnitude, revision-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering revision-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — after an LLM asserts a claim earlier in a context, a "consistency-pressure" signal (was the claim previously self-asserted, and in which direction) is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — this signal is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction; H3 — it causally gates whether the model revises an erroneous prior assertion given decisive new evidence, or doubles down to stay consistent with itself.

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 item-state claims across factual QA, arithmetic/logic, and entity-attribute facts. Two tracks: REAL claims the models reliably know (~4,000, sourced from TriviaQA + CounterFact) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000) with stipulated ground truth and controlled PHASE-2 evidence likelihood ratio. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 generated (fewer only where a model cannot be reliably induced to make the target PHASE-1 assertion). Each claim yields matched two-phase contexts: PHASE-1 elicits an ASSERTION engineered to be correct OR incorrect (via a misleading setup), plus a NO-PRIOR-ASSERTION control where the claim is never previously asserted; PHASE-2 introduces decisive evidence that should rationally settle the claim, held constant across the assertion/no-assertion conditions. Also included: a USER-ASSERTS condition (the user, not the model, stated the claim) to dissociate self- from external (sycophantic) consistency. Behavioral REVISION probe, comprehension checks ("restate the PHASE-2 evidence"), 3 paraphrases; core analysis restricted to items where PHASE-2 evidence suffices for a rational agent.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B (base+instruct). No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — consistency-pressure is decodable). At the claim tokens at the PHASE-2 read-out point (without asking the revision question), train probes for (i) TRUTH-VALUE and (ii) CONSISTENCY-PRESSURE (previously self-asserted vs not, signed by assertion direction), with shuffled-label control tasks. Decisive metric first: consistency-pressure probe AUROC on held-out items vs control-task chance. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.80 in ≥3 of 4 models with the control at chance. Indecision band: 0.65–0.80 — weakly decodable. Negative (≤0.65): no decodable self-consistency signal — H1 rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 — orthogonality to truth, and to sycophancy). Compute cosine/subspace angle between consistency-pressure and truth directions; test residual decodability after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa); additionally test the angle to the USER-ASSERTS (sycophancy) direction. Decisive metric: subspace angle to the truth direction and fraction of consistency-pressure decodability retained after projecting out truth. Convincing: angle ≥ 45° and ≥70% decodability retained, plus a nonzero angle to the sycophancy direction, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 20–45° or 40–70% retained — partial entanglement, characterized not claimed as orthogonal. Negative (angle <20°): consistency-pressure is not separable from truth — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal gating of revision / double-down). Measure per-item DOUBLE-DOWN PULL = shift of the internal belief toward the prior assertion in ASSERTION vs NO-ASSERTION at held-constant evidence/truth; localize via activation patching from ASSERTION→NO-ASSERTION runs (compare to late-layer sycophancy heads and truth heads). Derive a consistency-pressure steering direction and test: (a) subtracting it raises revision of erroneous prior assertions and moves belief toward the evidence; (b) adding it increases doubling-down; (c) specificity — random and truth directions do not selectively move revision, and the model's own truth belief on no-prior-assertion items is preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), no-prior-assertion accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Revision on open output is LLM-judge scored (300 items human-validated, κ ≥ 0.7). Also test whether the consistency-pressure readout predicts per-item revision failure (AUROC) beyond log-prob and truth baselines. Decisive metric first: increase in correct-revision rate on erroneous-assertion items under subtractive steering, vs controls. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point revision increase, controls <5 pt, prediction AUROC ≥ 0.05 over baselines, <2 pt MMLU drop, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 5–15 pt or AUROC gain 0.02–0.05 — weak causal role. Negative (<5 pt or matched by controls): self-consistency pressure does not gate revision — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Doubling-down could reflect rational persistence (the prior assertion was itself made on evidence the model still trusts) rather than a truth-independent consistency drive; the matched NO-ASSERTION control (same evidence, no prior commitment), the incorrect-assertion cases (where consistency and truth clearly diverge), and the synthetic track with decisive stipulated PHASE-2 evidence are designed to isolate genuine self-consistency pressure from justified persistence, though full separation is hard for correct assertions. The consistency-pressure signal may be entangled with a generic sycophancy/prior-context direction; the user-asserts comparison condition and projected-out analyses dissociate self- from external-consistency, and even a finding of entanglement is informative. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs revise their own errors based on evidence regardless of prior self-assertion — is itself valuable, contrasting with the behavioral choice-supportive bias literature). Belief may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The consistency-pressure component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore/suppress revision' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Two-phase elicitation may fail to reliably induce incorrect assertions for well-known real facts; the synthetic track and engineered misleading setups mitigate this. Revision scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately labile (flip-flopping) or indiscriminately stubborn; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, no-prior-assertion accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may differ from base models (an informative comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Mechanistic isolation of an internal, decodable SELF-consistency pressure tied to the model's own prior in-context assertion, dissociated from BOTH truth and external-opinion sycophancy, with causal tests of doubling-down on one's own error. Delta over retraction (correctness belief), sycophancy (external source), and behavioral stubbornness is real and non-trivial. Weakest sub-claim = linear decodability alone (unremarkable); strongest = self-vs-external dissociation + causal specificity. Novel but not paradigm-shifting unless the signal is cleanly dissociated.

Name: counterfactual_dual_meaning_belief
Title: Two Worlds at Once: Do LLMs Internally Hold Both the Supposed and the Backgrounded-Factual Meaning of a Counterfactual?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical psycholinguistic 'dual meaning' of counterfactual conditionals (a subjunctive like 'If Tom had studied, he would have passed' conveys BOTH a supposed dependency AND the backgrounded fact that Tom did NOT study and failed), an LLM processing a counterfactual simultaneously maintains two internally-decodable belief layers about the same proposition: the SUPPOSED belief (P holds in the counterfactual world) and the BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false). These two layers are separately linearly decodable, largely orthogonal, and causally dissociable: which layer dominates the model's downstream answer can be steered, and failures to maintain the factual layer produce a characteristic error (treating the counterfactual antecedent as actually true).
Related Work: Cognitive/psycholinguistic work robustly establishes counterfactual DUAL MEANING: subjunctive-counterfactuals express a supposition while implying the opposite factual state of affairs (Understanding Counterfactuality: A Review, Kulakova & Nieuwland 2016, 119 citations; Marking the counterfactual: ERP evidence for pragmatic processing of German subjunctives 2014, 48 citations). In LLM interpretability, 'Counterfactual reasoning: in-context emergence' (2025) finds a latent concept is linearly encoded with noise-abduction heads, and the 'Competition of Mechanisms' line (Ortu et al. 2024; reproductions 2025) traces how factual-recall vs. in-context counterfactual tokens compete, localizing factual/counterfactual info to subject/attribute positions and attention heads. Truth-probe work isolates a single linear truth direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, the competition-of-mechanisms work treats fact vs. counterfactual as a WINNER-TAKE-ALL competition for the output token and does NOT ask whether the model concurrently maintains TWO belief layers (supposed AND backgrounded-factual) about the SAME proposition, as human dual-meaning theory predicts; nor does it isolate these as separately decodable, orthogonal, steerable channels, nor connect the loss of the factual layer to the specific error of endorsing a false antecedent. My prior suppositional_belief_gating proposal concerns a binary endorsed-vs-entertained framing flag; this proposal is specifically about the two CO-PRESENT belief layers that are the signature of counterfactual conditionals. We transfer a canonical cognitive-science phenomenon (counterfactual dual meaning) into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: When we say 'If the dice had been rigged, the game would have been unfair,' we simultaneously entertain a hypothetical world (rigged dice, unfair game) AND signal a fact about the real world (the dice were NOT rigged, the game WAS fair). Decades of psycholinguistics establish this counterfactual 'dual meaning' as a hallmark of human comprehension. LLMs increasingly reason under counterfactual premises (planning, causal reasoning, hypotheticals, safety scenarios), yet it is unknown whether they preserve both layers or collapse into one. We ask a sharp mechanistic question: when an LLM reads a counterfactual conditional, does it internally maintain TWO separable belief layers about the antecedent proposition P — a SUPPOSED belief (P holds, in the counterfactual world) and a BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false)? We hypothesize both layers are (i) separately linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal, and (iii) causally dissociable, such that steering can shift which layer governs downstream answers, and that incomplete maintenance of the factual layer produces a characteristic error — treating the false antecedent as actually true. We build a controlled dataset of counterfactual conditionals, matched indicative/factual and simple-suppositional frames, and synthetic-entity items to control priors, plus factual-inference probes ('In reality, is P true?') and consequent-inference probes. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes for the supposed and factual layers, measure their geometry, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to competition-of-mechanisms heads), and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, layer-dominance shift under steering, patching effect sizes, factual-endorsement error rate, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — when an LLM reads a counterfactual conditional, both the SUPPOSED belief (antecedent P holds in the counterfactual world) and the BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false) about the same proposition are separately linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — the two layers are largely orthogonal directions; H3 — they are causally dissociable, so steering can shift which layer governs the model's downstream answer, and incomplete maintenance of the factual layer produces a characteristic error: treating the false antecedent as actually true.

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 items, each anchored on a proposition P and rendered in three matched frames: (a) COUNTERFACTUAL subjunctive ("If P had been the case, Q would have happened" — implies NOT-P in reality); (b) INDICATIVE/FACTUAL control ("P is the case, so Q"); (c) SIMPLE-SUPPOSITION control ("Suppose P; then Q" — no factual implication). Two tracks: REAL propositions (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000, e.g. "If Zorblax had orbited Kelvath...") with stipulated truth to control priors. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (fewer only where a comprehension filter drops items). Probes attached: FACTUAL-INFERENCE ("In reality, is P true?" — correct answer NO for counterfactuals), SUPPOSED/CONSEQUENT-INFERENCE ("Within the scenario, does Q hold?"), comprehension checks, and 3 mood-cue paraphrases (to prevent decoding from "had"/"would" surface cues); 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — both layers decodable and co-present). At the antecedent P tokens, without asking a question, train probes for (A) SUPPOSED belief in P and (B) BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief in P, anchored using the indicative-factual and simple-supposition frames plus reality-only items, with shuffled-label control tasks. Decisive metric first: in the COUNTERFACTUAL condition, the co-presence rate = fraction of items where supposed-P reads high AND factual-P reads low simultaneously. Convincing: co-presence rate ≥ 0.70 with both probes ≥ 0.80 AUROC in their anchor conditions, in ≥3 of 4 models. Indecision band: co-presence 0.5–0.70 or a probe at 0.65–0.80 AUROC — partial evidence for two layers. Negative (co-presence < 0.5 or no separable factual layer): the model collapses to one belief (winner-take-all) — H1 rejected, reported as a contrast with human dual-meaning comprehension.

Experiment 2 (H2 — orthogonality). Compute cosine/subspace angle between the supposed and factual directions; test residual decodability after projecting out one from the other; also chart per-layer emergence (does the factual/backgrounded layer arise later?). Decisive metric: subspace angle and fraction of factual-layer decodability retained after projecting out the supposed layer. Convincing: angle ≥ 45° and ≥70% retained in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 20–45° or 40–70% retained — partial entanglement, characterized. Negative (angle <20°): layers not separable — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal dissociation and false-antecedent error). Localize each layer via activation patching (patch counterfactual↔indicative activations; compare to factual/counterfactual competition heads, subject/attribute positions, and noise-abduction heads from prior work). Derive per-layer steering directions and test: (a) amplifying supposed / suppressing factual raises false-antecedent endorsement (model treats the premise as real); (b) amplifying factual restores correct factual inference while preserving in-scenario consequent reasoning; (c) specificity — random and truth directions do not selectively move layer dominance; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), indicative-frame accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Also test whether the pre-query factual-layer strength predicts correct factual inference (AUROC) beyond log-prob/surface baselines. Decisive metric first: change in false-antecedent-endorsement rate between +supposed and +factual steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point swing, controls <5 pt, consequent-inference accuracy preserved (<3 pt drop when amplifying factual), <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: 5–15 pt swing — weak dissociation. Negative (<5 pt or matched by controls): layers are not causally separable — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'supposed' and 'backgrounded-factual' layers may be hard to separate cleanly because both concern the same proposition P; the matched indicative/simple-supposition frames, synthetic-entity track, and probes anchored on frames where the two layers agree vs. diverge are designed to dissociate them, and projected-out analyses quantify any residual entanglement (which is itself informative). The dual layers might not be genuinely co-present internally — the model may simply implement a winner-take-all competition (as the competition-of-mechanisms work suggests) collapsing to one belief; a robust negative result (no separable factual layer during counterfactual processing) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting LLM processing with human dual-meaning comprehension and sharpening the competition-of-mechanisms picture. The layers could be decoded via surface mood cues ('had'/'would') rather than abstract belief representations; paraphrase/mood perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track mitigate this. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The responsible components may be distributed rather than discrete heads; we treat 'steer to shift layer dominance / restore factual inference' as the causal test rather than pinning exact heads. Steering could degrade fluency or destroy the model's ability to reason within the counterfactual scenario (over-suppressing the supposed layer); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, consequent-inference accuracy, indicative-frame accuracy, and general benchmarks. Human dual-meaning comparison is structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Transfer of psycholinguistic dual meaning alone is not novel; the delta is co-presence+separability+manipulability. Risk: could collapse to reinterpreting competition or to cue/truth decoding.

Name: defeasibility_flag_belief
Title: Rule or Rule-of-Thumb? An Internal Defeasibility Flag That Gates How a Single Counterexample Revises an LLM's Belief
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally tag a general belief about a category as either DEFEASIBLE (a default/generic that tolerates exceptions, e.g. 'birds fly') or STRICT (an exception-intolerant universal, e.g. 'all bachelors are unmarried'). This defeasibility flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates counterexample-driven revision: presenting a single exception should collapse belief in a strict universal but only mildly dent belief in a defeasible generic; steering the flag reverses this asymmetry, and mis-flagging predicts the two canonical human/LLM errors (misreading generics as universals -> overgeneralization; and unstable beliefs that overreact to one exception).
Related Work: Behavioral work robustly shows LLMs mishandle generics and defeasible reasoning: they conflate generics with universals and overgeneralize (Penguins Don't Fly 2022; Exceptions, Instantiations, and Overgeneralization 2024), fail to maintain stable beliefs when exceptions or irrelevant facts are added (Are LLMs classical or nonmonotonic reasoners? 2024), and vary widely on 20 defeasible patterns with CoT often hurting (Generics and Default Reasoning in LLMs 2025); MLMs are insensitive to quantification yet encode a generic-form meaning (Interpretation of Generalization in MLMs 2023). Classic interpretability isolates a linear truth-value direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, all defeasibility/generics work is behavioral or about quantifier probabilities; none isolate an internal DEFEASIBILITY flag (defeasible-default vs. strict-universal) as a decodable variable distinct from truth-value, nor test whether it causally gates how a single counterexample revises the belief. This differs from my prior essentialist_belief_mutability proposal, which tags a specific instance's property as essential vs. accidental; here the axis is the LOGICAL FORM of a general belief (exception-tolerant generic vs. exception-intolerant universal) and its role in counterexample-driven, non-monotonic revision. We transfer a canonical non-monotonic-reasoning phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: 'Birds fly' and 'all squares have four sides' look grammatically similar but behave differently under a counterexample: a penguin leaves the first belief essentially intact, while a single three-sided 'square' would destroy the second. Humans track this difference (defeasible generics vs. strict universals), and LLMs are notorious for confusing them - overgeneralizing generics into universals, or letting one exception (or even an irrelevant fact) destabilize a belief. We ask a mechanistic question: does an LLM internally represent whether a general belief is defeasible or strict, and does that representation govern how a counterexample revises it? We hypothesize that a 'defeasibility' flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates counterexample-driven revision - so that beliefs internally tagged strict collapse under one exception while those tagged defeasible barely move, and steering the flag reverses this asymmetry. We build a controlled dataset of general claims labeled defeasible (generics) vs. strict (analytic/definitional universals), matched in surface form, plus a synthetic-category track that stipulates a rule's logical form in-context to control priors, each paired with a single counterexample. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Mistral) we train linear probes to decode defeasibility vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item revision-plasticity gap under a counterexample, test whether internal mis-flagging predicts overgeneralization and instability errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, counterexample-revision gap, error-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering plasticity reversal, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — an LLM internally tags a general belief as DEFEASIBLE (a generic that tolerates exceptions) vs STRICT (an exception-intolerant universal), and this flag is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — the flag is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction; H3 — the flag causally gates counterexample-driven revision (one exception should collapse a strict universal but barely dent a defeasible generic), steering the flag reverses this asymmetry, and internal mis-flagging predicts the two canonical errors — overgeneralization (reading a generic as universal) and instability (revising a generic on irrelevant/supporting info).

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 general claims labeled by logical form: DEFEASIBLE generics ("Birds fly", "Metals conduct electricity") and STRICT universals ("All squares have four sides", "Every prime > 2 is odd"), balanced across biology/artifacts/math-definitions/social, surface-matched where possible (bare-plural vs explicitly-quantified) with paraphrases swapping "birds fly"↔"all birds fly" to separate form from cue. Two tracks: REAL (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-category track (~2,000) that stipulates form in-context ("Every zorb is by definition three-eyed [strict]" vs "Zorbs typically have three eyes [defeasible]") to control priors and decouple form from lexical triggers. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (fewer only if the human-validated label filter drops borderline items). Each claim has a matched SINGLE-COUNTEREXAMPLE, an IRRELEVANT-FACT control, and a SUPPORTING-INSTANCE control, plus a behavioral REVISION probe, comprehension checks, and 3 paraphrases; defeasible/strict labels human-validated on 300 items.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — defeasibility flag is decodable). At the claim tokens, train probes for (i) TRUTH-VALUE and (ii) DEFEASIBILITY, with shuffled-label control tasks, testing generalization to the synthetic track and across surface-matched paraphrases (so the probe cannot rely on "all"/"typically" cues). Decisive metric first: defeasibility probe AUROC on the synthetic, cue-balanced held-out set. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.80 on the cue-balanced set in ≥3 of 4 models with control-task at chance. Indecision band: 0.65–0.80 — decodable but possibly cue-assisted. Negative (≤0.65 on cue-balanced items): no abstract defeasibility representation, only lexical cues — H1 rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 — orthogonality to truth). Compute cosine/subspace angle between defeasibility and truth directions; test residual decodability after projecting out truth; test cross-track generalization. Decisive metric: subspace angle and fraction of defeasibility decodability retained after projecting out truth. Convincing: angle ≥ 45° and ≥70% retained in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 20–45° or 40–70% retained — partial entanglement, characterized. Negative (angle <20°): not separable from truth — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal gating of counterexample revision). Present each true general claim, then its single counterexample; measure internal belief change (truth probe) and behavioral retraction, defining a per-item plasticity. Confirm the IRRELEVANT-FACT and SUPPORTING-INSTANCE controls do not revise a well-behaved generic. Localize via activation patching (patch defeasible↔strict activations at the counterexample point). Derive a defeasibility steering direction (controlling for truth) and test: (a) steering strict→defeasible makes universals resist a counterexample; (b) steering generic→strict makes one counterexample collapse them; (c) steering toward the CORRECT form improves calibrated revision; (d) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively move revision, factual belief preserved; (e) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), non-manipulated accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Also test whether the pre-counterexample defeasibility readout predicts overgeneralization and instability errors (AUROC) beyond log-prob and lexical baselines. Retraction/overgeneralization on open output is LLM-judge scored (300 items human-validated, κ ≥ 0.7). Decisive metric first: the strict-vs-defeasible counterexample-revision plasticity gap, and its reversal under steering. Convincing: baseline plasticity gap ≥ 0.3 (normalized belief-change units), reduced/reversed by ≥50% under form-flipping steering, controls <15% change, error-prediction AUROC ≥ 0.05 over baselines, <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: baseline gap 0.1–0.3 or steering effect 20–50% — weak/partial. Negative (gap <0.1 or steering matched by controls): no internal flag gates revision — H3 rejected (a valuable constraint on the generics-in-LLMs literature). All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Revision behavior could be driven by the claim's pretraining confidence rather than a distinct defeasibility flag; the synthetic novel-category track (form stipulated in-context, decoupled from prior strength), surface-matched paraphrases, and conditioning error-prediction on a confidence baseline are designed to dissociate defeasibility from raw confidence. The flag may be entangled with surface cues (bare plural vs. 'all'/'every', 'by definition' vs. 'typically'); we mitigate with paraphrase perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track where cues are balanced. Defeasibility and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). The defeasible/strict label is partly graded/subjective (some generics are near-universal); we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs' behavioral generic/universal confusion is NOT backed by an internal defeasibility representation gating revision) is itself a valuable, publishable finding constraining the generics-in-LLMs literature. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed; we treat 'steer to reverse/calibrate plasticity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Behavioral retraction/overgeneralization scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately rigid or labile; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Moves from behavioral generics/defeasible-reasoning findings to isolating an INTERNAL defeasibility control variable (defeasible generic vs strict universal) distinct from truth, and testing its causal role in one-counterexample belief revision with steering that reverses the asymmetry. Distinct from truth-probes and from the authors' essentialist_belief_mutability (instance property essential vs accidental). Non-trivial conceptual step; novelty depends on controls succeeding (signal not reducible to lexical cues/prior confidence).
