Name: transitive_belief_leakage
Title: Does Belief Survive the Chain? Probing Whether LLMs Propagate Uncertainty Across Inferential Steps or Leak Certainty Into Their Conclusions
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally derives a conclusion C from a chain of individually-uncertain premises (A≈p1, A→B≈p2, B→C≈p3), a rational agent's belief in C should be BOUNDED by (and roughly the product of) the link beliefs, degrading as the chain lengthens. We hypothesize LLMs instead exhibit 'certainty leakage': the internally-decoded belief in the conclusion is systematically HIGHER than the product of the internally-decoded link beliefs and decays far more slowly than probability theory dictates as chain length grows — an internal over-propagation of certainty that is decodable, predicts long-chain overconfidence errors, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to restore proper uncertainty attenuation.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLM internal beliefs skew CoT via confirmation bias (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025), that internal consistency across layers signals reasoning reliability (Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency 2024), that multi-hop reasoning activates a distribution of intermediate answers in middle layers (Distributional Reasoning in LLMs 2024), and that belief/truth directions are linearly decodable and context-sensitive causal mediators of in-context inference (Truth-value judgment 2024; Language Models with Rationality/REFLEX 2023 for belief-graph consistency). Behavioral work on incoherent probability judgments and the conjunction fallacy (my prior internal_belief_coherence_gap) concerns STATIC conjunctions P(A∧B) at a single query, not inferential chains. Belief-manifold work (Shape of Beliefs 2026) shows posteriors' mean/variance are encoded but studies single-distribution updating, not multi-step deductive propagation. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether an LLM's INTERNAL belief in a DERIVED conclusion respects the multiplicative attenuation of uncertainty across a chain of uncertain premises, whether certainty LEAKS (conclusion believed more than the weakest/product of links warrants), how this scales with CHAIN LENGTH, or whether an identifiable component can be steered to restore attenuation. We reframe long-chain reasoning overconfidence as an internal uncertainty-propagation failure and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from static-coherence, confirmation-bias, and layerwise-consistency work.
Abstract: A rational reasoner who is only 80% sure of each of five inferential steps should be far less than 80% sure of the final conclusion — uncertainty compounds along a chain. Yet LLMs are notorious for stating long derivations with unwarranted confidence. Prior interpretability work shows internal beliefs are linearly decodable and shape chain-of-thought, but none ask whether the model's INTERNAL belief in a derived conclusion respects the multiplicative attenuation of uncertainty across the chain that produced it. We hypothesize 'certainty leakage': the internally-decoded belief in a conclusion C is systematically higher than the product of the internally-decoded beliefs in its constituent links, and decays far more slowly than probability theory dictates as chain length grows. We further hypothesize that (i) both link-beliefs and conclusion-belief are linearly decodable, (ii) the leakage magnitude grows with chain length and predicts long-chain reasoning errors, and (iii) it is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores proper attenuation, improving calibration on long chains without harming short ones. We build controlled inference-chain items where each link's belief strength is stipulated (via explicit likelihood-ratio-style premises and a synthetic-entity track to control priors) and chain length is varied from 1 to 6. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each link-belief and the conclusion-belief, compute a per-item leakage score against the product baseline, trace its length-scaling, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, leakage magnitude vs. product baseline, length-decay slope vs. rational, leakage–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering attenuation restoration and calibration gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — both the per-link beliefs and the conclusion belief are linearly decodable, and the internally-decoded conclusion belief is systematically HIGHER than the product (and higher than the weakest link) of the internally-decoded link beliefs ("certainty leakage"); H2 — leakage grows with chain length: the internal conclusion belief decays far more slowly with the number of uncertain links than probability theory dictates; H3 — leakage magnitude predicts long-chain overconfidence errors; H4 — leakage is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores proper attenuation and improves long-chain calibration without harming short chains.

Data (built from scratch). ~5,000 inferential-chain items where conclusion C follows from links (A; A→B; B→C; …) of length L ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}, each link assigned an explicit strength (calibrated hedges "usually/probably/possibly" or explicit "80% of the time") so a rational product-of-links belief is computable. Two tracks: REAL commonsense/factual chains (~3,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000, "Most zorbs are vantar; most vantar glow; so this zorb glows") with fully stipulated link probabilities giving an exact rational conclusion belief. We use ~5,000 of ~5,000. Matched conditions vary chain length while holding the weakest-link strength constant; a CERTAIN-CHAIN control (all links ≈1.0, conclusion should stay high) dissociates leakage from generic length/context decay. Each item carries a behavioral conclusion-confidence probe ("How confident that C? 0–100"), comprehension checks ("restate each link's strength"), and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only a linear/graded BELIEF-STRENGTH probe on frozen activations (ridge/logistic regression per layer, anchored on single-premise items with known stipulated probabilities, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — leakage vs product). Read the internal belief at each link proposition and at the conclusion (without asking the confidence question). Define per-item leakage = internal conclusion-belief − product of internal link-beliefs (also report vs the min/weakest link). Decisive metric first: mean leakage on uncertain chains, tested > 0 against the rational-attenuation null, with the CERTAIN-CHAIN control confirming no spurious decay. Convincing: mean leakage ≥ 0.15 (belief units, 0–1) with CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models, and the belief-strength probe R² ≥ 0.3 on held-out anchors. Indecision band: leakage 0.05–0.15 or probe R² 0.15–0.3 — weak/uncertain. Negative (leakage ≤ 0.05): the model attenuates appropriately — H1 rejected (a reassuring finding).

Experiment 2 (H2 — length scaling). Fit internal conclusion-belief vs chain length L (weakest-link-constant condition) and compare the decay slope to the rational product-decay slope. Decisive metric: (rational slope − internal slope), i.e. how much flatter the internal decay is. Convincing: internal decay slope < 50% of the rational slope in magnitude, CI excluding the rational slope, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: internal slope 50–80% of rational — mild over-propagation. Negative (internal slope ≥ 80% of rational): decay is roughly rational — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — leakage predicts errors). Collect behavioral long-chain errors (asserting a conclusion at higher confidence than warranted, or wrong on synthetic ground truth). Decisive metric: AUROC of per-item leakage (read before query) predicting the error, vs a log-prob baseline and a chain-length-only baseline. Convincing: leakage AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models. Indecision band: 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60): internal leakage does not track errors — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal attenuation). Via activation patching, patch short↔long-chain conclusion activations and weak-link activations into the conclusion representation to find the minimal component that inflates conclusion-belief above the product; compare to belief/truth heads and the middle-layer intermediate-answer distribution. Derive a certainty-leakage steering direction and test: (a) subtracting it lowers conclusion-belief toward the product/rational value on uncertain chains and improves calibration (ECE) and accuracy on long chains; (b) adding it exaggerates leakage; (c) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively restore attenuation, CERTAIN-CHAIN conclusions preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), short-chain accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: reduction in long-chain ECE under subtractive steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥30% relative ECE reduction on L≥4 chains, short-chain accuracy unchanged (<2 pt), certain-chain belief preserved (<0.05 drop), controls <10% ECE change, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 10–30% ECE reduction — partial. Negative (<10% or matched by controls): no steerable attenuation component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The graded belief-strength probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe; miscalibration could bias the leakage estimate. We mitigate by anchoring on single-premise items with known stipulated probabilities, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the RELATIVE comparison between conclusion-belief and the product/weakest-link of internally-decoded link-beliefs (a within-representation contrast that does not require absolute calibration). Apparent leakage could reflect the model using additional valid evidence for C beyond the stated chain (real track); the SYNTHETIC novel-entity track with fully stipulated link probabilities isolates chain-only propagation. Slow decay with length could be a generic context-retention artifact rather than certainty over-propagation; the CERTAIN-CHAIN control (which should stay high) and the length-matched weakest-link-constant condition dissociate genuine leakage from length effects. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs internally attenuate uncertainty appropriately, and overconfidence is only a verbalization artifact) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding. Reading belief at 'link' vs. 'conclusion' tokens is imperfect since positions differ; we anchor probes at matched proposition tokens and use paraphrase perturbations. The leakage component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore attenuation' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately under-confident on valid chains; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, short-chain and certain-chain accuracy, and general benchmarks. Long-chain error scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Delta over output-level UQ (SAUP/UProp/CoT-UQ) and internal-consistency/confirmation-bias/Distributional-Reasoning is real: a quantitative internal chain-propagation law — 'certainty leakage' where internal conclusion belief exceeds the product of internal link beliefs, scaling with chain length, predicting long-chain overconfidence, with a steerable restoring component. Ingredients (belief decoding, steering, length effects) are individually known; novelty is the specific multiplicative-attenuation test and leakage concept. Distinct from static conjunction fallacy (authors' internal_belief_coherence_gap).

Name: recognition_truth_leak
Title: It Feels Familiar, So It Must Be True: A Recognition-to-Truth Leak in LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human recognition-based truth effect (statements that merely feel recognized are judged truer, an effect that outweighs actual repetition), an LLM's internally-decoded belief in a claim's TRUTH is inflated by its internal FAMILIARITY/RECOGNITION signal for the claim's entity, independent of (and even against) whether the model actually knows the relevant fact. This recognition-to-truth leak is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to whether the fact is genuinely known, predicts familiarity-driven hallucination, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth.
Related Work: Human research establishes a recognition-based truth effect: statements JUDGED old (recognized) receive higher truth ratings, and this effect exceeds the effect of actual factual repetition (Recognition-based truth effect 2023); prospective feeling-of-knowing (FOK) is dissociable from actual knowledge and can rest on mere cue-familiarity rather than target-accessibility (FOK & partial knowledge 2016; metacognitive domain specificity 2020). In LLM interpretability, sparse-autoencoder 'entity recognition / knowledge-awareness' directions detect whether the model recognizes an entity and causally gate refusal/hallucination (Do I Know This Entity? 2024); 'factual self-awareness' linear features predict correct recall (Factual Self-Awareness 2025); internal states encode the knowledge-RECALL PROCESS, not truthfulness, so associated hallucinations look like facts (LLMs Do NOT Know What They Don't Know 2025); and truth is linearly decodable (Geometry of Truth 2023). CRITICALLY, none ask whether the RECOGNITION/FAMILIARITY signal CONTAMINATES the TRUTH judgment — whether merely recognizing an entity inflates the internally-decoded belief that a claim about it is true, independent of actual knowledge. Prior recognition work links recognition to refusal/hallucination-likelihood, not to a truth-inflation bias; my prior illusory-truth proposal concerns IN-CONTEXT repetition, whereas here the source is PARAMETRIC recognition/familiarity. We transfer the canonical recognition-based truth effect into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People rate statements they merely recognize as truer, even when recognition carries no diagnostic information — a recognition-based truth effect that can outweigh the effect of genuine repetition, and a cousin of the feeling-of-knowing that rests on cue-familiarity rather than real knowledge. LLMs are known to encode an entity-recognition signal (whether they 'know' a subject) and a separate truth signal, and to hallucinate confidently about familiar-but-unknown entities. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does the model's recognition/familiarity signal leak into and inflate its belief in a claim's truth, independent of whether it actually knows the relevant fact? We hypothesize that (i) an entity-recognition/familiarity channel and a truth channel are separately linearly decodable, (ii) the recognition channel contaminates the truth channel — claims about recognized entities are internally believed truer, holding actual knowledge constant — an internal signature of the recognition-based truth effect, (iii) the leak is graded with familiarity and largest when the model recognizes the entity but lacks the specific fact, predicting familiarity-driven (associated) hallucination, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth. We build a controlled dataset crossing entity FAMILIARITY (recognized/popular vs. unrecognized/rare, plus synthetic entities) with claim VERACITY (true/false) and KNOWLEDGE status (fact actually known vs. not). On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode recognition, truth, and knowledge, measure their geometry, quantify a per-claim recognition-to-truth leak, test its predictiveness for hallucination, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, leak magnitude, leak–hallucination AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering decoupling, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — an entity-recognition/familiarity channel, a truth channel, and a knowledge channel are separately linearly decodable; H2 — the recognition channel contaminates the truth channel (claims about recognized entities are internally believed truer, holding actual knowledge and veracity constant), and this leak is graded with familiarity and largest in the recognized-but-unknown cell; H3 — the leak predicts familiarity-driven (associated) hallucination; H4 — the leak is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth.

Data (built from scratch, entities from existing knowledge bases). ~6,000 subject-relation-attribute claims crossing three factors: (A) ENTITY FAMILIARITY — highly-recognized/popular entities, low-familiarity rare real entities, and fully SYNTHETIC novel entities (never seen), with familiarity set by Wikidata/pretraining-frequency proxies; (B) CLAIM VERACITY — true vs false; (C) KNOWLEDGE status — whether the model actually recalls the correct attribute (measured empirically closed-book). We deliberately populate the diagnostic RECOGNIZED-BUT-UNKNOWN cell (familiar entity, fact not reliably recalled) alongside RECOGNIZED-AND-KNOWN and UNRECOGNIZED cells. Claim surface form is matched across familiarity levels (3 paraphrases) to guard against lexical confounds. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (cell sizes balanced; fewer only where a model has too few recognized-but-unknown items). Behavioral truth-judgment probe ("Is this true? + confidence"), comprehension checks; 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — three channels decodable). At the entity/attribute tokens (without asking the truth question), train probes for (R) RECOGNITION/FAMILIARITY, (T) TRUTH-VALUE, and (K) KNOWLEDGE, with control tasks. Then compute pairwise subspace angles and test that truth remains decodable after projecting out recognition, and that recognition is distinct from the knowledge direction. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of each of R, T, K vs control-task chance. Convincing: each ≥ 0.75 in ≥3 of 4 models with controls at chance. Indecision band: any channel 0.65–0.75 — weakly decodable. Negative (R or T ≤ 0.65): the required channels are not represented — H1 rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 — recognition-to-truth leak). Define per-claim leak = shift of the internal truth readout toward "true" as a function of recognition, holding knowledge and veracity constant (recognized-but-unknown vs unrecognized cells, matched FALSE claims). Decisive metric: mean leak on matched-false claims, tested > 0, and largest in the recognized-but-unknown cell; additionally compare the leak's size to a matched in-context-repetition manipulation (test recognition > repetition, mirroring the human effect). Convincing: leak ≥ 0.10 (truth-readout units) with CI excluding 0, peaking in recognized-but-unknown, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: leak 0.03–0.10 — weak. Negative (≤0.03): recognition does not contaminate truth — H2 rejected (a valuable contrast with the human recognition-based truth effect).

Experiment 3 (H3 — leak predicts hallucination). Decisive metric: AUROC of the per-claim leak (read before any query) predicting associated hallucination (confidently asserting a false attribute about a recognized entity), vs a log-prob baseline and the knowledge probe. Convincing: leak AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models. Indecision band: 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60): leak does not predict hallucination — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal decoupling). Via activation patching, patch recognized↔unrecognized entity activations to find the minimal component that transports recognition into the truth readout; compare to entity-recognition SAE directions and truth heads. Derive a recognition-to-truth-leak steering direction (controlling for knowledge) and test: (a) subtracting it decouples recognition from truth — lowering unwarranted belief in false claims about recognized entities and reducing associated hallucination; (b) amplifying exaggerates the leak; (c) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively decouple, genuine-knowledge recall preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), known-fact accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: reduction in associated-hallucination rate under subtractive steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥30% relative hallucination reduction, known-fact accuracy preserved (<2 pt drop), controls <10%, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 10–30% reduction — partial. Negative (<10% or matched by controls): no steerable decoupling component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (claims about popular entities are, on average, more likely to be true in training data) rather than a spurious recognition-to-truth contamination; the FALSE-claim cells (where recognition and truth diverge), the matched RECOGNIZED-BUT-UNKNOWN vs. UNRECOGNIZED comparison at held-constant veracity/knowledge, and the synthetic-entity anchor are designed to isolate genuine leakage from valid frequency-based inference (though full separation is difficult). The recognition and knowledge channels may be hard to separate (recognition often co-occurs with knowledge); the recognized-but-unknown cell and projected-out analyses are built to dissociate them, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative and directly engages the 'recall-process-not-truth' finding. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (recognition does not contaminate the truth channel) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the human recognition-based truth effect. Familiarity estimated from subject popularity is noisy; we use multiple frequency proxies and the synthetic anchor. The truth/recognition probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to decouple recognition from truth' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model distrust all familiar content; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, known-fact accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Main real novelty: whether the recognition/familiarity signal INFLATES internally-decoded truth belief independent of actual knowledge/veracity (a truth-inflation bias), graded and peaking in the recognized-but-unknown regime, predicting associated hallucination beyond standard uncertainty signals. Prior SAE entity-recognition / factual-self-awareness / recall-process-not-truth work correlates recognition with refusal/hallucination-likelihood or recall success but does not test truth contamination. Distinct from in-context illusory-truth (parametric familiarity here). Localization/steering is standard; novelty is the target phenomenon. Substantial IF independence from knowledge is convincingly shown, else collapses into reframing recognition/recall-process findings.

Name: belief_dilution_effect
Title: Watered Down: Does Irrelevant Information Literally Dilute an LLM's Internal Belief Signal?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human dilution effect (non-diagnostic information weakens the pull of diagnostic evidence), adding irrelevant, non-diagnostic facts to a context weakens an LLM's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion that its diagnostic evidence supports — the belief regresses toward neutral. We further hypothesize this internal dilution is realized geometrically as a REDUCTION IN MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (a literal 'radial dilution'), not merely an angular rotation, and that it predicts diluted behavioral judgments and is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component.
Related Work: The dilution effect — non-diagnostic information weakening the implications of diagnostic information, yielding less extreme judgments — is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (Tversky & Kleinman 1981, 611 citations; The Dilution Effect and Perceptual Decision Making 2015; The Moral Dilution Effect 2025; Restoration of Diluted Judgment 2008). A long-standing open debate is whether dilution is genuine dilution of the diagnostic signal or an inference of missing evidence. In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is a linearly-decodable, context-sensitive causal mediator that is even sensitive to IRRELEVANT context (Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024), belief posteriors form curved manifolds whose mean/variance shift with evidence (The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and 'Simulated Adoption' (2026) provides the crucial geometric framing for in-context conflict as either RADIAL magnitude dilution or ANGULAR orthogonal rotation of the truth direction. CRITICALLY, no work isolates the classic dilution effect as an internal belief phenomenon: whether appending non-diagnostic facts weakens the internal belief in a diagnostically-supported conclusion, whether this is realized as radial magnitude reduction vs. angular rotation, whether it reflects genuine dilution vs. missing-evidence inference, or whether it can be causally reversed by rescaling the belief signal. This transfers a canonical human bias into LLM belief internals and, by importing the radial-vs-angular decomposition from Simulated Adoption, gives it a novel mechanistic, causal treatment distinct from all my prior belief-attribute proposals (which concern repetition, source independence, anchoring, halo, etc., never non-diagnostic dilution).
Abstract: Told that a student scored in the top 5% of a hard exam, people confidently predict she is excellent; add that she owns a cat and jogs on weekends — utterly irrelevant — and their confidence drops. This dilution effect, one of the most reproduced biases in judgment research, has never been examined inside LLMs at the level of their beliefs. As LLMs increasingly reason over long, cluttered contexts (RAG passages padded with irrelevant text, verbose user messages), we ask a sharp mechanistic question: does appending non-diagnostic information weaken the model's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion its diagnostic evidence supports, and if so, how is that weakening realized geometrically? We hypothesize that (i) adding irrelevant facts regresses the internal belief readout toward neutral — an internal dilution effect; (ii) this is realized as a reduction in the MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (radial dilution) rather than an angular rotation of it; (iii) the internal dilution predicts diluted behavioral judgments and grows with the amount of irrelevant material; and (iv) it is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component along the truth direction, restoring undiluted judgments. We build a controlled dataset of diagnostic-evidence items paired with matched non-diagnostic padding (and length-matched diagnostic and neutral-token controls), with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes, decompose the belief signal into radial and angular components, quantify per-item dilution, test the missing-evidence-inference alternative, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal rescaling. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, dilution magnitude, radial-vs-angular decomposition, dose-response, dilution-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-rescaling restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — appending irrelevant, non-diagnostic facts about an item regresses the LLM's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion its diagnostic evidence supports toward neutral (an internal dilution effect); H2 — this weakening is realized geometrically as a reduction in the MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (radial dilution), not an angular rotation of it; H3 — internal dilution predicts diluted behavioral judgments and grows with the amount of irrelevant material (dose-response); H4 — the dilution is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component along the truth direction, restoring undiluted judgments.

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 judgment items, each with a DIAGNOSTIC evidence statement strongly supporting a conclusion C about an item (e.g. "Alex scored in the top 2% on a rigorous exam" → "Alex is highly competent"; plus entity-attribute inferences). Two tracks: REAL (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000) that stipulates diagnosticity to control priors. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000. Per item, matched conditions holding the diagnostic evidence fixed: (i) DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY; (ii) DILUTED — diagnostic + k non-diagnostic facts about the same item, k ∈ {1,2,4,8}; (iii) LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL padding (filler not about the item); (iv) EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC (a second genuinely relevant fact); (v) a MISSING-EVIDENCE-CUE variant framing the padding as an exhaustive dossier vs an incidental aside, to test the inference-of-missing-evidence alternative to genuine dilution. Behavioral judgment probe ("How confident that C? 0–100"), comprehension checks ("which facts are relevant"), 3 paraphrase/order perturbations; diagnosticity labels human-validated on 200 items.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only a linear/graded BELIEF probe on frozen activations (ridge/logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). The truth direction is estimated by difference-in-means with cross-validation. Steering via magnitude rescaling along that direction, gain g ∈ {1.5,2,3}× the diluted component.

Experiment 1 (H1 — internal dilution). Read the belief probe at the conclusion tokens (without asking the judgment question). Define per-item dilution = belief(DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY) − belief(DILUTED). Confirm the LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL control does NOT produce the regression (so dilution is driven by item-specific non-diagnostic facts, not context length) and EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC does not dilute. Decisive metric first: mean dilution on the DILUTED condition, tested > 0, minus the neutral-padding regression. Convincing: net dilution ≥ 0.10 (belief units, 0–1) with CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models, neutral-padding regression < half of it. Indecision band: net dilution 0.03–0.10 — weak. Negative (≤0.03 or fully explained by length): LLMs ignore non-diagnostic facts — H1 rejected (a reassuring finding for cluttered-context deployment). The exhaustive-vs-incidental contrast (v) is reported to indicate whether any dilution is genuine or missing-evidence inference, without being required for H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 — radial vs angular). Project the conclusion representation onto the truth direction and decompose the change under dilution into a RADIAL component (magnitude loss along truth) and an ANGULAR component (rotation away from truth). Decisive metric: radial share of the total belief change. Convincing: radial share ≥ 60% (CI excluding 50%) in ≥3 models. Indecision band: radial share 40–60% — mixed geometry. Negative (radial share < 40%): dilution is primarily angular — the H2 radial claim rejected while H1 may hold.

Experiment 3 (H3 — predicts behavior, dose-response). Fit dilution vs k (dose-response). Decisive metric first: correlation/AUROC of internal dilution (read before the query) predicting behavioral judgment regression, vs a log-prob baseline and a context-length baseline; plus a positive dose-response slope. Convincing: prediction AUROC ≥ 0.70 (or r ≥ 0.4) and ≥ 0.05 over baselines, with a dose-response slope CI excluding 0, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or slope CI touching 0 — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60 and flat dose-response): internal dilution does not track behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — causal reversal by rescaling). Localize via activation patching from DILUTED→DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY the heads carrying the attenuated belief; contrast with truth heads and heads attending to non-diagnostic tokens. Then apply the geometry-aware RESCALING (amplify the radial belief component under dilution) and test: (a) rescaling restores undiluted internal belief and behavioral judgments; (b) suppressing it exaggerates dilution; (c) specificity — random-direction and pure-angular steering do not restore the belief; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), diagnostic-only accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: fraction of the dilution gap recovered by rescaling, with controls. Convincing: ≥50% of the dilution gap recovered, controls <15%, <2 pt MMLU drop, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 20–50% recovery — partial. Negative (<20% or matched by controls): dilution is not reversible by rescaling — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The regression toward neutral could reflect generic context-length effects or attention diffusion rather than a specific non-diagnostic-dilution phenomenon; the LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL control (irrelevant filler NOT about the item), the EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC control, and the requirement that dilution be driven by item-specific non-diagnostic facts are designed to dissociate genuine dilution from length/diffusion artifacts. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs ignore non-diagnostic facts and preserve the belief signal) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the canonical human bias and reassuring for cluttered-context deployment. The genuine-dilution vs. missing-evidence-inference distinction may not fully resolve; the exhaustive-vs-incidental framing test provides evidence but, as in the human literature, may be only partially conclusive — still an informative contribution to a decades-old debate. The graded belief probe requires calibration; we anchor on diagnostic-only items with known belief and report layerwise results with control tasks, focusing on relative change. The radial-vs-angular decomposition depends on a well-estimated truth direction; we use difference-in-means with cross-validation and report per-layer results, and note architectures may differ (Simulated Adoption found norm dynamics vary by model). Rescaling could degrade fluency or over-amplify belief indiscriminately; we use small magnitudes, random/angular-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, diagnostic-only accuracy, and general benchmarks. Diagnosticity labels are partly subjective; we human-validate a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

novelty.reasoning: Non-trivial transfer + mechanistic sharpening: (1) an internal analogue of the human dilution effect (non-diagnostic facts weaken internal belief in a supported conclusion), (2) realized as RADIAL magnitude reduction vs ANGULAR rotation, (3) distinguished from missing-evidence inference, (4) causally reversible by rescaling (strongest novelty). But closest prior already covers human dilution, context-sensitive truth directions (Truth-value judgment 2024), and the radial/angular decomposition (Simulated Adoption 2026), so the actual delta is narrower than the rhetoric: internal-belief framing + applying the decomposition to irrelevant-context dilution + causal test.

Name: belief_rigidity_ontogeny
Title: Learning to Be Stubborn: The Developmental Emergence of Belief Entrenchment Across Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: As a language model pretrains and a fact's parametric belief strengthens, the model's willingness to OVERRIDE that belief with in-context counter-evidence progressively DECAYS: per-fact, the pretraining checkpoint at which a belief becomes linearly decodable predicts the checkpoint at which that belief becomes context-unrevisable. Belief entrenchment (the failure of RAG-style in-context correction) is thus an emergent ontogenetic property that co-develops with, and is causally tied to, parametric belief consolidation rather than being a fixed trait of the final model.
Related Work: Pretraining-dynamics work characterizes WHEN factual knowledge is acquired and forgotten (How Do LLMs Acquire Factual Knowledge 2024; How do LMs learn facts 2025 - three-phase plateau; Probing Across Time 2021), that linear representations of relations form at frequency thresholds (On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency 2025), and that KNOWLEDGE ENTROPY decays over pretraining, impairing new-knowledge integration (Knowledge Entropy Decay 2024). Component-evolution work tracks head/FFN specialization over training (Time Course MechInterp 2025; Crosscoding Through Time 2025). Inference-time work shows final models over-rely on parametric priors and resist in-context correction (context-vs-prior conflict, RAG faithfulness). CRITICALLY, none link the two: no work asks whether, per individual fact, the emergence of a decodable parametric belief CAUSES the loss of in-context revisability (belief entrenchment), nor traces this acquisition-to-rigidity tradeoff across checkpoints, nor tests whether the same mechanism (e.g. knowledge-entropy decay / consolidated recall circuits) that consolidates the belief is what makes it unrevisable. This reframes belief entrenchment as a developmental phenomenon with a per-fact ontogenetic timeline, distinct from acquisition/forgetting dynamics (which ignore in-context override) and from my prior inference-time-only belief proposals.
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented and correction-based systems assume a model will update its answer when the context contradicts what it knows. Yet models notoriously cling to their parametric priors. We ask a developmental question that prior pretraining-dynamics work has not: does a fact's belief become HARDER to override with in-context counter-evidence as the model learns it more strongly, and are these two timelines causally linked? We hypothesize that (i) for a given fact, there is a checkpoint at which its parametric belief becomes linearly decodable (acquisition) and a later checkpoint at which the model stops revising that belief when the context asserts the opposite (entrenchment); (ii) per-fact acquisition timing predicts entrenchment timing, so belief rigidity co-develops with consolidation rather than being uniform across the final model; and (iii) the consolidation mechanism (a strengthening parametric-recall circuit and declining reliance on context) causally drives the loss of revisability, so that intervening on it restores in-context updatability. Using open pretraining checkpoints (Pythia suite, OLMo-7B) with known training-data frequencies, we build controlled fact sets, present each fact under a matched in-context contradiction, and at each checkpoint measure (a) parametric belief via a linear probe, (b) in-context revision behavior, and (c) an internal 'context-vs-prior reliance' signal. We trace per-fact acquisition and entrenchment curves, test their predictive coupling against frequency and difficulty baselines, localize the consolidating recall component, and causally test whether attenuating it re-opens in-context revisability. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-fact acquisition/entrenchment checkpoints and their correlation, revision-rate trajectories, coupling AUROC vs. baselines, patching/ablation effect sizes, post-intervention revision restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — per fact there is a pretraining checkpoint at which its parametric belief becomes linearly decodable (acquisition) and a later checkpoint at which the model stops revising that belief when the context asserts the opposite (entrenchment); H2 — per-fact acquisition timing predicts entrenchment timing, over and above corpus frequency and item difficulty (belief rigidity co-develops with consolidation rather than being uniform); H3 — the consolidation mechanism (a strengthening parametric-recall component and declining context reliance) causally drives the loss of revisability, so attenuating it restores in-context updatability.

Data (built from scratch, over existing fact sets). ~4,000 subject-relation-object facts spanning a wide range of pretraining-corpus frequencies, drawn from CounterFact/T-REx and paired with published OLMo/Pythia term-frequency estimates, plus a matched difficulty control set. We use ~4,000 of the available pool (fewer only where frequency estimates are unavailable). Per fact: a closed-book PARAMETRIC query ("The capital of X is ___"), an IN-CONTEXT CONTRADICTION prompt ("Document: The capital of X is [wrong value]. Question: …") with matched wording, and a NEUTRAL-context control (context restates the true value or is irrelevant); comprehension checks ("quote the context value").

Models (checkpoint sweep — the core resource). Pythia suite at 160M, 1.4B, and 6.9B across its released checkpoints, and OLMo-7B intermediate checkpoints — all frozen at each checkpoint. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream activations at the object token, retrained per checkpoint (L2 logistic regression, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd), corroborated by closed-book log-prob. Steering/ablation via contrastive activation addition and component down-scaling, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — acquisition and entrenchment checkpoints exist). At each checkpoint, per fact, measure (i) PARAMETRIC BELIEF (probe + log-prob), (ii) IN-CONTEXT REVISION (does the model output the contradicted context value?), (iii) a CONTEXT-vs-PRIOR reliance signal (attention-to-context + patching-based attribution). Define the ACQUISITION checkpoint (first crossing a belief-probe criterion) and the ENTRENCHMENT checkpoint (first checkpoint where revision rate drops below a criterion). Decisive metric first: fraction of facts for which both a well-defined acquisition and a later entrenchment checkpoint exist, with entrenchment lagging acquisition. Convincing: ≥60% of facts show acquisition-then-entrenchment ordering with entrenchment ≥ acquisition, in ≥2 of the model families. Indecision band: 40–60% — ordering unclear for many facts. Negative (<40%, or entrenchment routinely precedes acquisition): the two-timeline picture fails — H1 rejected (still informative: rigidity is present from first acquisition or absent).

Experiment 2 (H2 — coupling beyond frequency/difficulty). Decisive metric: per-fact correlation between acquisition and entrenchment checkpoints, and the partial correlation controlling for corpus frequency and difficulty (partial regression). Convincing: raw correlation r ≥ 0.4 AND partial correlation (after removing frequency + difficulty) with CI excluding 0, in ≥2 families; high-frequency facts entrench earlier. Indecision band: partial correlation CI touching 0 while raw r ≥ 0.4 — coupling may be frequency-driven; report as unresolved. Negative (raw r < 0.2): timings are uncoupled — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal role of the consolidating component). Localize at a mid/late checkpoint via activation patching / attention attribution the parametric-recall component (heads/FFNs) that carries the entrenched belief and suppresses context reliance; track its strength across checkpoints (should rise as entrenchment sets in). Then on late (entrenched) checkpoints attenuate it (ablation / down-scaling, or steering along a context-reliance direction derived from revised-vs-unrevised activations) and test: (a) in-context revision on contradicted facts is restored; (b) specificity — random-component ablation does not restore revision, and neutral-context accuracy is preserved; (c) collateral — a general benchmark subset (1k items) and WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: revision-rate recovery on contradicted facts under attenuation, with random-component control. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point revision recovery, random control <5 pt, neutral-context accuracy preserved (<3 pt drop), <5% perplexity rise, and a monotone component-strength-vs-checkpoint curve. Indecision band: 5–15 pt recovery or a noisy component-strength curve — partial/uncertain. Negative (<5 pt recovery or matched by control): consolidation does not causally drive entrenchment — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Entrenchment could simply track corpus frequency rather than a distinct consolidation-to-rigidity mechanism; the frequency-matched difficulty controls and the partial-regression predictiveness test (belief strength beyond frequency) are designed to isolate the belief-consolidation contribution. The acquisition-then-entrenchment ordering may not hold for all facts, or the two timelines may be inseparable (a fact might be revisable and unlearned, or entrenched from first acquisition) - a robust finding either way (coupled vs. decoupled ontogeny) is informative and publishable. In-context revision behavior depends on prompt scaffolding and could reflect instruction-following rather than belief rigidity; comprehension checks, neutral-context controls, and multiple contradiction phrasings mitigate this, though base (non-instruct) checkpoints may under-follow context, which we treat as part of the developmental signal and compare across contradiction strengths. The linear belief probe may not be cleanly decodable or comparable across checkpoints (representations drift); we retrain probes per-checkpoint with control tasks and corroborate with log-prob measures. The recall component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'attenuate to restore revisability' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact unit. Checkpoint availability limits us to Pythia/OLMo (specific data mixes); results may not transfer to other pretraining regimes or to very large closed models. Restoring context-reliance via intervention could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately gullible to any context; we use small magnitudes, random-component baselines, and monitor perplexity, neutral-context accuracy, and general benchmarks.

novelty.reasoning: Real delta over pretraining-dynamics work (acquisition/forgetting, three-phase, knowledge-entropy decay, frequency thresholds) and inference-time context-vs-prior conflict: a PER-FACT developmental coupling where the acquisition checkpoint (belief becomes decodable) predicts the entrenchment checkpoint (belief becomes context-unrevisable), tested beyond frequency+difficulty, plus a causal test that attenuating the consolidating recall component restores revisability. No prior work links per-fact acquisition timing to loss of in-context override across checkpoints. Novelty risk: could collapse to frequency or early-checkpoint instruction-following weakness.

impact.reasoning: Targets a concrete, widely-observed failure mode (parametric belief overriding supplied evidence) central to RAG, tool use, correction pipelines, knowledge editing, continual learning. If entrenchment emerges predictably from consolidation, faithfulness failures become a training-dynamics problem, not just prompt engineering — connecting knowledge acquisition and inference-time correction. Broad reach across foundation-model science and applied retrieval. Payoff somewhat indirect; if the effect is an artifact of small open checkpointed models under weak context-following, frontier relevance narrows.

review.reasoning: Explicit H1-H3, confound awareness (frequency, prompt dependence, probe drift, distributed circuits), directional criteria. But constructs underspecified: 'belief linearly decodable' depends on probe design and per-checkpoint retraining makes cross-checkpoint thresholding hard to compare; 'entrenchment' (revision rate below criterion) is prompt/calibration-sensitive and early checkpoints may just fail at context use generally. Causal chain too strong for planned evidence (ablation restoring revision doesn't show the SAME consolidating mechanism causes rigidity). 'Attention-to-context + patching attribution' reliance signal is vague; attention weights unreliable. Very heavy compute; controls and statistics thin (no hierarchical model, multiple-comparison handling, or H3 power).
